1808879: Clear day on SUMMA departure, requested a VFR climb to the southwest side of Mt. Rainier through 17,500 then proceed on course, all terrain in sight. Cleared as requested. FO as PF , pointed jet to southwest side of the mountain, but a 50 kt wind out of the southwest showed the aircraft track direct to the mountain. I noticed this and was about to ask the FO to turn slightly right of course, when we received a terrain warning, which he complied with and warning went away. Terrain always in sight, but we should have adjusted to ground track into the wind to avoid the warning.Better ground track to compensate for wind.
1808895: I reviewed the maintenance log when I arrived at the aircraft for the first flight of the day. It had just been released from maintenance. It had previously been written up for a strong smell coming from the lavatory. The corrective action stated that the lavatory had been leaking into the cargo bay. It had been repaired the same day and I was the first to fly the aircraft. I included this information with my crew brief.During the descent to ZZZ1, sometime prior to FL180 because the descent checklist had yet to be completed, the FO (First Officer) and I heard what sounded like an extra loud flushing noise from the FWD LAV (Forward Lavatory), but then developed into a loud sound similar to an engine spooling down, immediately followed by a strange, slightly chemical odor. We both looked at each other and confirmed what we heard and smelled. I called the A F/A (Flight Attendant) to verify if anyone had just flushed the toilet. She said someone was in the lavatory, had just flushed, and it smelled strongly like excrement.The odor quickly subsided. We discussed the possible sources. The LAV was a different style from most of our aircraft so it could have just been a sound [different] than what we were used to. The LAV had just been repaired so the odor could have been related. Since there odor was gone and there were no other indications of abnormality we continued to ZZZ1 but I had the FO start reviewing synoptic pages for any clues and I started reviewing possible diversion airports. We made a list of airports closest to our position as we got closer to ZZZ1, ZZZ2, then ZZZ3, then ZZZ4.During descent after passing through FL180, I started to hear and feel the aircraft surging. It sounded like it was coming from the engines. I de-cluttered the EICAS to check for vibration. There was a notable difference in engine vibration, but they were still in the green and there were no other indications on the EICAS.At approximately 13,000 ft. the FO and I both noticed a strong acrid odor. I called the A F/A who confirmed the LAV was not in use. I then called for the Smoke, Fire, Fumes QRC (Quick Reference Checklist). We donned our oxygen masks and the FO started through the QRC. We were almost exactly on top of ZZZ3, which we had already decided as a suitable airport, so when the FO [read the steps related to ATC] of the QRH (Quick Reference Handbook) I told him to [request priority handling] and ask to land at ZZZ3 immediately.ATC assigned an ALT of 9,000 ft. As I started to descend, the aircraft began shaking violently. ATC continued to vector and assign lower altitudes. When the FO turned off the RECIRC fans per the QRH, I asked him to put the checklist down and set up the aircraft for landing. We were very close to the airport and descending quickly. I decided the priority was for the FO to get our landing numbers and set up the approach while coordinating with ATC and the FA's. I could not help because I suspected external damage to the control surfaces so I did not want to take my attention away from maintaining positive control of the aircraft.Somewhere around the 9,000 ft. mark or lower we received an EICAS PACK 1 FAIL. This was the first time the EICAS provided any kind of indication of an abnormality. We had experienced a loud noise, strong odors, violent shaking, and now a PACK 1 FAIL. It felt as if the aircraft had suffered major damage and safe completion of the flight was at serious risk. ATC had placed us on a downwind for the ILS but, fearing we may be losing more systems and controllability, I told the FO we were turning immediately to final. As we slowed to approach speeds the shaking reduced. The FO contacted the FA's to go over [procedures]. I did not order a brace and I did not intend to evacuate. The aircraft was stabilizing and there weren't any smoke or fire indications in the cabin or flight deck. I landed and stopped on the runway. I requested an inspection by the fire trucks to make sure the aircraft wasn't on fire and we were safe to taxi. I made an announcement for everyone to remain seated and that we had landed due to a maintenance issue, but that the aircraft was safe and we were taxiing to a gate.In our judgement, due to the order and severity of events, we thought the aircraft may be in serious jeopardy. An immediate landing was the safest option available. I have often conducted a very similar scenario with FO's on long flights out of the area and near ZZZ3, during cruise. The scenario is a fume event. The reason this is important is because the QRH for fumes is very long and involves a lot of system isolation for troubleshooting. It would take 20-30 minutes for us to review the QRH in a relaxed, stable environment. Only at the end of the QRH do you see just how much runway would be required if you're heavy and have taken a lot of performance penalties due to the QRH troubleshooting process. Because we were so close to the airport and descending quickly, I prioritized performance and navigation over completing the QRH. There simply was not enough time for the full checklist.Parked at the gate, I called Dispatch and explained what was going on. They weren't aware of the diversion. The FO had asked ATC to notify our company during descent. I was getting bounced around a lot between Dispatch and [Administration] with Maintenance talking to them in the background, but Maintenance immediately insisted that it was a simple air system failure and that the aircraft was safe. Both the FO and I conducted a walk-around. I said the aircraft was not safe to fly. I wouldn't have landed in ZZZ3 if I thought the aircraft was safe. This aircraft needs a full maintenance inspection based on the severity of conditions we had just experienced. [In the past] I've had a hydraulic line rupture at FL200, I've had a brake failure on landing, I've had a full system failure. This was like nothing I had experienced and felt far more severe at the time than just a simple air system failure. It was serious enough that I didn't know if we would make the runway. This aircraft had a recent history of fluids leaking into the cargo bay. How much unseen damage was caused by these fluids? Why wouldn't an inspection be required if the maintenance department is saying 'oh yeah the smell and shaking is from the system blowing out'? As I'm trying to convince Dispatch and Maintenance that an inspection needs to be conducted, this is already approaching about 2 hours after landing, the adrenaline started to fade and the fatigue settled in. The entire crew was exhausted to the point that even the FA's were fatigued. Having drilled this scenario, I believe I acted appropriately given the circumstances. QRH calls for system isolation to identify the source but with odor being cause of the [diversion] and no EICAS indications there is no way to verify the source without taking the O2 mask off, which is extremely dangerous. We were so close and working with so little time that getting on the ground immediately became the top priority.

1808930: This was not a good flight because of compounding errors that happened and the negative effect that they had. The good part is that the flight remained safe, but here below are several things that I learned. The events started when on decent into ZZZ when the lights on the autopilot mode selector began to flicker erratically, however the autopilot appeared to perform normally. This was in IMC descent thru layers with occasional moderate turbulence. (The was second flight after the power supply to the EFIS system failed resulting in loss of the primary attitude indicator and HSI which was repaired and return to service. I mention this only because it attributed to my increase lack of trust in the flight instruments.) The autopilot was on altitude preselect with a vertical speed selected. During the decent I was evaluating the autopilot issue and I think, after the fact, I pushed the altitude capture twice, resulting in me disengaging the capture and descending below the desired altitude. At the time I attributed this to a malfunction autopilot and I decided to disconnect the autopilot and manually flew the plane. This increased the workload. Weather was also a significant factor. There was a line of thunderstorms that were moving over ZZZ (destination) and I was watching the satellite radar utilizing a portable GDL52 communicating to Garmin pilot on my I pad. For this flight I was using ForeFlight for navigation/charts and Garmin Pilot for weather, because the GDL would not communicate satellite radar information to ForeFlight. I have been using ForeFlight for charts and weather in previous aircraft for many years, but this aircraft has only ADSB-out and is scheduled to have an avionics upgrade to a GDL69a (sat WX) and Garmin 345 (ADSB IN/Out) installation in Month. I was also utilizing the onboard radar, but am learning to use this system. Bottom line was too many nav / weather systems in use that resulted in unnecessary and additional workload. Another factor was that I had transitioned from a piston to a turboprop and had about 80 hours in the TBM time at the time of this flight. So I was still low on the TBM experience curve. Based on the weather I requested GPS XX and activated the approach on the 530s. However, as I proceeded to ZZZ GPS XX, the weather changed and the IAF for GPS XX was near the line of thunderstorms and center offered ILS XY and left turn to heading for the IAF - I made a right turn to that heading. I should have recognized that I was starting to make small mistakes. During this time I also was varying from assigned altitude due to increase workload. I entered ILS XX in to the 530S and activated and Center vectored me to the approach. I began the approach and was able to see the ground occasionally. I was handed off the Tower and I waited to capture the glideslope. I continued the approach, my position and altitude were not cross checking, and I began try to determine why. I was high when I was on a 2-3 mile final. While making this evaluation, I was able to see the runway lights and able to make a visual decent and landing. I was not confident after this flight, there were too many mistakes in this flight. When I was on the ground I contacted my flight instructor and went over flight and discussed the avionics and my reaction/ decision I made. We made a plan of how to determine the effect of the flickering light on the mode selector and insure that it was safe for flight. I altered my plans so that weather would have a minimal impact and returned back to ZZZ1. To learn and avoid these errors in the future, I did a full debrief with my instructor when I return home. This focused on both the avionics and cross reference that he recommended to determine status of the navigation system. We also spent a considerable time on how I responded to the apparent situation and decision making. It was at this time, I realized how much some minor errors in my part had a large impact onthe flight. The avionics have also been evaluated by Company in ZZZ2 and determine that the malfunction was limited to the mode selector display and that the autopilot is functioning normally. It is schedule to be repaired. Further I have also flow approaches in VFR conditions to verify operations of the navigation and autopilot systems and apply some of the procedures that my instructor and I discussed.
1808940: While doing pattern work on Runway 30L, we requested a full-stop on Runway 3. Tower instructed us to 'make left downwind.' My student and I turned left to enter the left downwind Runway 3, at this time, Aircraft Y traffic was mid-field downwind Runway 30L. Traffic was cleared touch-and-go Runway 30L. Without further instruction, my student and I proceeded with a standard left pattern Runway 3. On 0.25 nm final, I see the traffic landing the parallel is still rolling on the runway, and I did not anticipate them being clear of my runway by the time my student and I crossed the threshold Runway 3, so I instructed my student to execute a go-around. This resulted in our Aircraft X directly overflying the Aircraft Y right as they rolled across Runway 3 on Runway 30L. They were not yet airborne.In hindsight, I believe Tower's instruction to make left downwind may have been intended as extend downwind, or they would call my base. Since this instruction was not given, we made a normal pattern and did not anticipate a conflict until short final.Earlier on the same flight, we had been doing full-stop-taxi-backs, and we landed Runway 30L, and exited left onto Taxiway B. The same controller gave us taxi instructions 'Runway 30L taxi via Delta' and I asked if I needed 'cross Runway 3.' During this same flight, I had prompted the previous controller a couple of times, and gotten the instruction to cross each time, but only after prompting for it. The next controller volunteered, 'we don't normally do that.' She did give me the crossing, but I am wondering why we do not volunteer that crossing since it is necessary to cross the full-hold bar for Runway 3 in order to turn left onto Taxiway D from Taxiway B, or the other way to turn right onto Taxiway B from Taxiway D.

1808951: I was flying with a family member to go sight seeing around downtown Pittsburgh when we encountered a hazardous situation with another aircraft. In this report I want to describe exactly what happened, how I think this situation could have been avoided, and what could be done in the future to prevent this from happening again.At about XA:30 local time, I was approaching Pittsburgh from the east in Aircraft X. cruising at about 80mph at 2,100 ft. MSL. My intended course of flight was to fly west over the Monongahela river, make a shallow turn over the north side, then proceed outbound over the Allegheny river. When I was approaching downtown, I saw Aircraft Y about 1.5 miles ahead of me flying on a head on course at my altitude. I rocked my wings a few times and turned to the right. When the Aircraft Y pilot saw me, he turned to the right and proceeded behind me.I then continued along my intended route along the Monongahela river and flew at 2,000 ft.. After passing point park, I turned northbound to continue with my plan. I saw off my 2 o'clock position about 1.5 miles out the same Aircraft Y flying westbound towards my intended route. At this point in time, I could not turn to the right due to the skyscrapers downtown and if I continued going straight or to the left we would be converging. I decided to take evasive action and turn around back over the Monongahela river by performing a steep turn to the left. While I was performing the turn to the left, Aircraft Y changed course and was flying over point park at this time doing another lap around the city. At this time, Aircraft Y was converging on my location by flying a southeast heading while I was flying an easterly heading. To give way, I flew as far south as I could with out causing any obstacle hazards, but Aircraft Y continued towards my location. Due to Mt. Washington (a large hill with more skyscrapers on top) was to the south, I could not turn to the right. I also could not turn to the left due to the traffic. I decided to add full power and pitch for Vy to slow down, as well as regain the altitude I loss during my steep turn. Aircraft Y, traveling at a faster speed, turned right directly in front of me and proceeded to AGC to the south.For this flight, I calculated ground elevation to be at 765 ft. using the Pittsburgh TAC (1613-848=765). I decided 2,000 ft. would be a good buffer for obstacle clearance and Class B Airspace clearance. During the steep turn I descended to 1,800 ft. due to lack of concentration caused by the traffic I was avoiding. During this flight, I was flying an aircraft that was not originally manufactured with an electrical system and was complying with Part 91.225(e) and 91.215(b)(3).Reflecting on this incident, I believe this could have been easily avoided if the Aircraft Y pilot would have been scanning for traffic and noticed me. In both encounters, I began making evasive maneuvers over a mile in advance while the other pilot continued turning towards me. If an emphasis on see-and-avoid would have been done in this busy airspace, this problem would have been mitigated.Going forward, I believe that there could be some regulatory measures to improve safety in this particular environment. From my experience flying sightseeing flights over Niagara Falls and the Hudson River, I believe that providing a CTAF frequency for VFR aircraft to communicate with makes flying in dense traffic much safer and organized. My suggestion in the future would be to add a note on the Pittsburgh TAC chart with a CTAF frequency, insert a note requiring pilots to contact AGC Tower or PIT Approach, or add a Part 93 regulation standardizing the direction of traffic flow around the golden triangle area. With Class B boundaries above and to the west of the city, large buildings in the city itself, a mountain with large towers to the south, large radio towers to the north, as well as multiple hospital helicopter pads in the city, I believe this is a very complex airspace that could afford to have special procedures to be complied with in this airspace. In conclusion, this occurrence was a result of lack of visual scanning procedures. With this airspace being particularly complex as well as congested due to medical flights and sightseeing flights, I believe all pilots should exercise extremes caution in this area.
1808954: I was flying a helicopter near the south end of the ZZZ Class C airspace. 1808993: This aircraft was enroute from ZZZ to ZZZ1 on an IFR clearance that was obtained after departing ZZZ VFR. The pilot requested a clearance to ZZZ1 via ZZZ2 direct after climbing to an altitude where we could hear him on the radios over ZZZ. I checked the route which ran directly between a small restricted area and a high terrain box that we are used to dealing with northwest of ZZZ2. I also noticed a terrain box of 8,900 feet, and thought the requested altitude of 9,000 feet and the route of flight was safe. I failed to observe a smaller terrain box which requires a safe altitude of 10,000 feet. When the Minimum Safe Altitude Warning alert went off, the pilot was apparently in a small area of poor radio reception and I was unable to get an acknowledgement from him from either the of the TRANSMITTERS available to me.His position and altitude are generally not a problem from one of the transmitters. I had to switch a commercial aircraft to the low altitude frequency to relay a climb clearance to the pilot, which took an extra minute or two, by which time the aircraft began to transit the 9,900 foot terrain box at 9,000 feet. He climbed to 10,000 feet shortly after and was also able to hear me on the radio a few seconds after the clearance had been relayed by the commercial overflight. Pay more attention to the terrain boxes even if you think after the initial scan that everything looks good.
1809003: I was working Local Control. Ground Control was open as well. Ground Control taxied Aircraft Y to Runway 1. 1809006: Runways 8/15 in use. Arriving Runway 8 and departing Runway 15.I was on CIC at the time of this event. I was monitoring the LC (Local Control) frequency as required, but there are often times when I'm monitoring the frequency and not hearing everything since I am performing other CIC duties such as phone calls, sector assignments, coordination with the airport authority about NOTAMs, weather briefings, facility log updates, etc.At the time this situation started, I was talking to the training team on GC (Ground Control) so I did not hear the clearance given to Aircraft X, who was taxiing up Taxiway A and had been given an IFR release off Runway 15 from TRACON. After I finished talking with GC, I sat back down at the CIC position. Aircraft Y was on about a 1.5 mile final to Runway 8 as I saw Aircraft X taxiing onto Runway 15. This is completely normal to see, as we often LUAW (Line Up and Wait) our Runway 15 departures so that we can clear them for takeoff as soon as the Runway 8 landers roll through the intersection.When Aircraft Y was just about to flare for Runway 8, I noticed that Aircraft X appeared to be starting his roll. I asked LC, 'Is Aircraft X rolling? Did you LUAW him or clear him for takeoff?' LC said he didn't think he had cleared him for takeoff. I told him to cancel Aircraft X's takeoff clearance immediately, which he did. The aircraft had rolled about 1,000 to 1,500 feet by the time they aborted.After this incident, a supervisor listened to the tapes and confirmed that LC had indeed cleared Aircraft X for takeoff. I'm not sure whether it was inadvertent and he meant to give him a LUAW clearance or whether he just forgot about Aircraft Y on final.Don't fall into a sense of complacency.Don't allow distractions to take your focus away from your primary duties. I am often teased about it, but when we are busy with many critical situations happening at once, and especially when we have CIC combined with GC, I will not answer the outside phone line until our traffic isn't as busy. I don't want to take my eyes off the busy operation in order to get a phone call from the airport authority about a NOTAM for a taxiway light bulb that's going to be OTS (Out of Service) during the mid-two weeks from now. (CIC was not combined in this situation)LC's scan should have been focused more heavily on making sure that Runway 15 traffic was not moving when Runway 8 traffic was on short final. When I brought it to his attention seemed to be the first he noticed the situation.

1809070: IFR flight to ZZZ. Weather was not a factor. Departed PHX from Runway 7R, runway heading assigned. After approaching 1,000 feet AGL, assigned heading 050. Switched to Phoenix Departure on 119.2, then 120.7 within a minute or two. Controller gave me instructions to 'turn left heading 360, vectors to intercept the PXR 350 radial.' Knowing I was on a diverging path away from my flight-planned route, I was waiting for at least one more turn that would take me toward the radial. This turn occurred within the next few minutes with the controller saying 'turn left heading 270'. Now on an intercept heading with the radial, I made a right turn to join the PXR 350. The Departure Controller quickly gave me instructions to fly heading 260 (which I immediately complied with) asking why I had made the turn north. The remainder of the flight occurred without incident.In hindsight, here's what I learned during this exchange. Despite the numerous flight hours operating in the PHX ATC system, I somehow mistakenly interpreted 'intercept' with 'join'. I knew a 360 heading would not intercept the planned radial. So, I was expecting that next turn to put me on course to do so. What I wasn't told, was the 270 heading was for spacing from other traffic, not necessarily to intercept or join the PXR 350 radial. Had I known why (traffic) I was being turned to a 270 heading, then my thought process would've completely changed and I would've known, without question, to continue on the assigned heading. Instead, I was thinking this was simply the heading that would allow me to intercept the 350 radial. Despite my error, I should have questioned the heading as the intercept angle was 80 degrees, not the standard 30 degrees one would expect. In doing so, the Controller would have simply advised me to remain on the 270 heading and expect another turn to intercept and join the airway. As pilots, we must deal with many human factors on a daily basis. Some of those factors thwart our efforts to fly safe and reasonably. I feel this was a situation where 'if it doesn't look right or feels oddly different' then say something. Questions are always free. Accidents are costly. Routinely flying the same routes and hearing the same instructions from ATC can also create a unique set of issues. We don't always hear what was said, we hear what we expect. And this human factor is one that all pilots must concentrate on avoiding.
1809079: While level at 5,500 ft. and at 170 kts. and on the RNDRZ 1 RNAV, ATC asked us to fly heading 090. ATC gave us a left turn toward Runway 25L. ATC asked us if we had Runway 25L in sight. 1809084: Flew Korry 4 arrival and proceeding visually up the Hudson River at 4,000 feet. Cleared to descend to 3,000 feet. Descending out of 3,500 feet about abeam the museum, noticed an object at our 12 o'clock, flying very stable, and appeared to be flying towards us, at the time our speed was 250 knots. We made no corrective action with our aircraft and continued on descent and heading as there was very little time for it to come and go. It passed approximately 100 feet under the aircraft and was flat oval in shape and a very shiny black in color. I have seen many Mylar Balloons and it definitely wasn't one of them. It had the appearance and actions of a DRONE. We immediately reported it to Air Traffic Control and followed up with law enforcement.We were at the end of a 4 leg day all flown in high density airspace of DCA and LGA. Luckily it was a beautiful weather day and we were both looking out the window at the river and city when the flying object appeared and flashed under the nose.Vigilance is always required as is protection of airspace.
1809136: There was a momentary unreliable airspeed followed by a brief failure of the PF's (Pilot Flying) PFD. Once the PFD was restored, airspeed was still momentarily unreliable.While operating the flight from ZZZ to ZZZZ, I was the pilot flying. After deviating for weather, we were proceeding directly to ZZZZZ to perform the VOR DME 2 [approach to] Runway XX at ZZZZ. Approximately 20nm from ZZZZZ and descending, we encountered IMC and light precipitation and light turbulence which gradually increased to moderate turbulence. We were partially configured at flaps 1 and gear was down at 200 kts and beginning our turn for the arc when my airspeed began having deviations of +/- 15 kts, I attributed this to the increasing turbulence and precipitation we had encountered. While banked and descending, the PLIs (Pitch Limit Indicator) presented and I had a loss of airspeed below the green dot and a gain of airspeed that presented amber digits. At this point my airspeed completely went away, as if I was on the ground, a grey box was present where the digits would be but there was no V-Speed information. Shortly after this occurred, my PFD went black for a moment, but never reverted to a different display. Once this happened, I transitioned to the IESS (Integrated Electronic Standby System), rolled the wings level, advanced the thrust levers, climbed to ensure terrain clearance, and we returned to VMC.Nearly immediately after establishing the climb, the PFD and all information on it returned, although there were errors with the airspeed. Initially, the airspeed showed faster than we were, as if we had been repositioned in the simulator, and we received one aural 'High-speed' until the airspeed settled back to what the IESS was showing. Our altitude at this point was approximately between 17,000 ft. and 16,000 ft. with a high peak around 9827 ft. in our vicinity. From our descent, I knew I could find VMC around 19,000 ft. so I directed the pilot not flying to tell ATC we would be present heading and climbing to 20,000 ft.I did not direct the PNF (Pilot Not Flying) to declare an emergency as we were busy figuring out what just happened and coordinating a plan between each other. In the climb, we cleaned the aircraft up and ran an after takeoff checklist. Once we were in VMC, we worked with each other to determine that all of our instruments matched and were reliable. We also determined that we could remain mostly VMC by performing the approach from ZZZZZ1 and asked to proceed directly to ZZZZZ1. We successfully performed the approach and landing at ZZZZ. Upon exiting the runway, we received both AFCS (Automated Flight Control System) Fault, and ADS Probe 1 Fail messages. We felt that we could have been struck by lightning, but we could not find any strike points on the aircraft, and all static wicks that were visible to us were found intact. We entered both messages above in the AML as well as an AML entry for a possible lightning strike.I feel my actions were appropriate given that we were not in radar contact any longer. I was unsure if I could trust any pitot or static instruments and I knew where I could find visual conditions away from terrain. I should have declared an emergency but at the time I felt that doing so with the language barrier would have broken down my communication with my First Officer when we needed to focus on flying the aircraft. Additionally, he was able to secure a clearance for the same heading up to 20,000 ft. as soon as I asked him to do so.
1809148: While descending into ZZZ on the STAR, at around 28,000 feet, E1 fuel tank indicated Zero Quantity on EICAS and MFD. 1809158: Pushback crew left headset attached to nose gear. Upon arrival to ZZZ, the station representative noted sparks emanating from behind the nose gear. Upon arrival, the headset was located and removed from the nose wheel. No damage to the aircraft was noted during the post flight walk around. Looking at the situation as a whole, we were lucky. If the headset became dislodged, it could have created the potential for an engine failure during takeoff and/or landing.Both flight crew and ground crew missed the disconnection of the ground crew headset. Both parties need to ensure disconnection of the bypass pin, the departure of the tug and tow bar, all ground crew is clear of the aircraft, and ensure their personal belongings are removed with them as well.
1809165: While waiting to exit the ramp, I pulled up a Takeoff Performance System (TPS) for [Runway] XXL and XYR EE as it appeared both were in use. We were told to follow company to XXL, but the company aircraft we pulled behind was going to XYR EE. We resolved the discrepancy and taxied down [Taxiway] XX toward [Runway] XXL. Being in a MAX, I paid close attention to the engine selection as I entered the TPS data. As a result, I missed the obvious first step of changing the runway on the route page. We completed the before takeoff checklist as we were entering the runway and discovered that XYR was selected for takeoff. I changed the runway to XXL and we initiated the roll. As a result of the runway change the aircraft reverted to TO and we didn't have V speeds displayed. The takeoff was uneventful otherwise.Serious congestion on the ZZZ ground frequency. They are still using the same frequency for both outbound and inbound aircraft. First time flying the MAX since it's return. Late in the evening after a long duty period. Confidence in being able to fix the issues on the fly.Slow down and be willing to stop when task saturated.
1809171: Supervising a requalification of a Captain who has not flown in over 14 months. He was Pilot Flying. Given clearance to 'cross ZZZZZ at 8,000 [feet], cleared ILS [Runway] XXC'. We had briefed ZZZ note about not flying glide slope until Final Approach Fix. Captain set 2,200 feet Final Approach Fix altitude and instead of pushing managed descent, pulled open descent. We were outside of ZZZZZ1 and I noticed the Flight Mode Annunciator and that aircraft was not going to level at 8,000 feet. I announced LEVEL OFF three times then intervened with Push to Level about 7,500 feet. I instructed Captain to climb to 8,000 feet as ATC said, '...I see you are going to 7,000, re-cleared to cross ZZZZZ2 at 7,000', re-cleared ILS XXC.'Not having flown in 14 months, the muscle memory may or may not be there. We must always VERIFY what input we make and MONITOR aircraft for compliance, being ready to intervene if necessary.
1809205: After a normal flight from ZZZ we descended for the visual approach to ZZZZ, due to no response from anybody on the ground at ZZZZ, I elected to do an over flight of the airport at pattern altitude of 1,500 ft. with the autopilot disconnected, crossing over midfield from north to south on the east west runway to enter a left hand crosswind for the left pattern landing east, we started configuring the aircraft for landing by selecting flaps to the #2 position, on the left downwind leg we selected the gear handle down, at that point we received an amber CAS message of GEAR MISCOMPARE R The nose gear and left main indicated down(GREEN) the right main gear was an AMBER X. While the First Officer (FO) looked for the message in the Emergency Procedures checklist I engaged the Auto Pilot and Auto throttles and climbed to 2,000 and stayed in an extended racetrack pattern around ZZZZ. At this point we informed the passenger of the situation and was thinking that the procedure should work and we would land at ZZZZ. We followed gear will not extend checklist, pulling the blow down handle, no change, the pulling the main gear uplock handle, no change the last procedure in the checklist was to try and yaw the airplane. We informed the passengers what to expect, and tried the yaw left then right twice, no change. At this point I made the decision to divert to ZZZ1 again informing the passengers what the plan was, they were fine with that because they had used a local company at ZZZ1 to take them to ZZZZ before. We pickup a clearance to ZZZ1 with ZZZ2 Center, and informed them of our situation. After that hand off to ZZZ2 Approach Control, the controller asked us if we would like a fly by for visual verification of the gear status. We chose to do this option, and he coordinated with the tower. I felt very confident that the gear was down because when the FO pulled the uplock handle he felt very little resistance, from my past experience that is a good indication the gear was not in the uplock. With blow down in the system the gear only has one place to go, so I felt with a very high degree of certainty that the right main was down and locked. The weather at ZZZ1 was VMC 10 miles 5,000 ft. Scattered wind was 110/18 gusting 24. After being vectored for the visual low pass over Runway XXR at ZZZ1 Tower informed us that Airfield Operations was in a position to observe our low pass, we had the aircraft fully configured for landing and made the low pass at 300 AGL and 140kts. Airfield Ops confirmed that he saw three gear. We executed the climb out instructions cleaned up the aircraft except for the gear remaining down, then we were vectored for another visual approach to land Runway XXR at ZZZ1. During our patterned we went ahead and [received priority], to have the trucks just in case. Also the FO radioed Company ZZZ1 if they could have a van meet us to take our passengers to their requested destination on the field, and if they would call the Company1 maintenance facility and let them know we were inbound. We reconfigured the aircraft for landing while on a 3mile final we slowed to final approach speed and with Airfield Ops and the fire trucks standing by we made a normal landing with an extended rollout, confirming the gear was indeed down. We cleared the runway and taxied to the Company1 maintenance facility. We deplaned the passengers and got them on their way immediately. I informed the maintenance staff of the issue and they pulled the aircraft in the hanger and did a visual inspection of the gear. They found that the uplock switch, which is a plunger type, was stuck in the gear up position making the computer think the gear was still in the well.
1809224: Departing ZZZ in a 737 MAX. Planned TO data was flaps 1 reduced. We had briefed a gusty wind TO procedure utilizing full power, reduced speeds and VR max as we were holding short of the runway. Previous departures on our RNAV SID we getting headings on departure for weather. As we took the runway, we could see weather in our departure route and anticipated a heading too. We sat in position for a few minutes before ATC announced a 5 minute stop on departures to sort out the previous departures. I suggested to FO see if we can get Flap 5 data and do the same full power, reduced speed, VR max procedure with flaps 5, if time permitted. He agreed. We ordered data then I made a very brief PA about a temporary stop on departures, but we would be airborne shortly, please stay seated.The data came up and I announced the new speeds to include VR max and FO loaded it. My intention was to run a new before Takeoff checklist to clean it up and be ready to go. At this time, a FA called to ask if someone could use the restroom to which I said no. Then ATC called 2 or 3 different time to inquire about a desired heading on departure. The stop was then lifted and we departed. Upon reaching acceleration altitude the FO realized we were still at flaps 1 when he was looking to clean up. At that point I realized I had failed in following up on the before Takeoff checklist.The takeoff itself was uneventful with no more than light chop and moderate rain during initial climb. We debriefed our error for the next hour and a half on our way to ZZZ1. I clearly had failed in letting the distractions take my focus off of the checklist. The weather itself was just a rain shower with no gusts, no wind shear, no lightning and our fancy MAX radar didn't show any of the severe weather cues that it is capable of showing. My FO had told me he had flown very little during the pandemic so my flaps 1 vs 5 concern was more related to his recent experience that to the weather.Another threat was the MAX. We don't get to fly them that often (yet) and I find my eyes are 'lost' when trying to scan the gauges that have always been in the same place for the last XX+ years. Now, many of them have moved. The flap indicator was not where it normally is. That may have caught my attention before accepting a takeoff clearance in an NG.Fortunately for us we were utilizing VR max procedures as this gave us additional speed over and above the flap 1 speeds. Our flaps 5 VR max was 167 which was 8 knots higher than our flaps 1 VR of 159. The tail strike potential of utilizing the published flaps 5 speed on a reduced takeoff with flaps 1 selected is very clear to me. I will no longer be doing flaps 1 takeoffs in [other make/model] airplanes. Most FOs ask me about my flap preferences for takeoff. I gather many captains don't do flaps 1 in the bigger airplanes.
1809236: Turning onto the LOC on 36R in CLT a drone passed extremely close to our aircraft. Same altitude heading the opposite direction. We both saw what we thought was a bird but as drone passed by the First Officer side he saw the propellers of the drone and confirmed that it was a drone. It was black in color. Continued on the approach. Encountered a UAV drone at 2,700 feet while flying an intercept to the 36R localizer between LANSR and CIKDU for a visual approach to 36R at CLT. I originally called out 'bird 12 o clock;' then it maneuvered to our right, where I watched it pass off of our right wing, co altitude. I notified the Captain it was a drone, and we immediately made a PIREP to CLT 36R Tower. Notify other pilots and attempt to inform the general, drone flying public how dangerous and illegal it is operate drones in Class B airspace.
1809244: During our landing, about 1-2 miles from the FAF (final approach fix), we were at 2900 ft I noticed a drone flying above us. It was close to us, seemed like 50 ft above. It was hard to tell if it was flying to the opposite direction or just standing. Any way we passed below it. I immediately informed ZZZ tower about it. We continued and landed at the destination.
1809270: The Captain and I were unfamiliar with this airfield so we reviewed the Jeppesen charts and NOTAM's in detail prior to departing. After landing and then turning into the Mobile Downtown ramp on Taxiway H, we noticed several GA aircraft and barriers in the area where the chart shows a left turn in the ramp. After proceeding on that taxi line, we questioned whether this was correct and the Captain stopped aircraft. We called the company ramp and the individual said he would call the contractor. Ground personnel drove out to the aircraft, placed chocks under the wheels, and we shut down. After deplaning, we asked the Contractors if we were supposed to turn left earlier and they said yes. They also said this has happened numerous times previously.Unfamiliarity with the ramp combined with the construction, barriers in the area the chart depicts a left turn, and an actual taxi line that is not depicted on our charts led to our mistaking that taxi line for the one mentioned in the NOTAMS. We had reviewed everything thoroughly. Upon entering the ramp, we noticed small airplanes and construction barriers in the area where a left turn is shown on the chart. There is an actual taxiline that proceeds straight and we followed that line, believing it was the temp taxilane from the NOTAMS. I stopped the aircraft when I questioned if this was the correct route. The First Officer contacted the ramp and they called the contractor who chocked the wheels. I shutdown and they brought stairs over. After leaving the aircraft, we asked if we should have turned and the contractor said yes, but this has happened many times before.A lot of construction combined with incorrect chart depiction and confusing NOTAMS.
1809286: Aircraft X was on route from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. While proceeding on the RNAV arrival to ZZZ and just prior to ZZZZZ intersection the aircraft was just leveling off at 20,000 feet when the number 2 inverter failed and the aircraft immediately pitched and rolled the while coupled on the autopilot. We immediately pulled the power back to correct the speed increase and I took the controls, decoupled the autopilot and righted the aircraft returning the aircraft to course and altitude. During the upset the aircraft lost approximately 1,800 feet and we deviated off the arrival course about 90 degrees. Center inquired as to our status and we advised them that we had an equipment failure and that we had regained control of the aircraft. We also advised that we required no assistance and that we were able to proceed without incident. The corrective action was to switch to the number 1 inverter, re-couple the autopilot once the attitude indicators re-stabilized and to continue the flight normally. As soon as we were on the ground we advised the company and appropriate corrective action was initiated. Aircraft X was in route ZZZ1-ZZZ. We were descending on an RNAV arrival, assigned to 20,000 feet. As we were approaching ZZZZZ just prior to level off, we had an inverter failure and autopilot failure. Autopilot failed to capture altitude and deviated from assigned heading. We disconnected autopilot and returned aircraft to assigned flight level and heading.
1809353: ZZZ is [near] the BDL 5 nm Class C surface area. During a training flight while returning to ZZZ from BAF, we were using flight following from Y90 TRACON and squawking a discrete code. We were in the Class E airspace beneath the 2,100 MSL shelf of the Class C. As we approached our destination, ATC told us 'Radar services terminated, squawk 1200, frequency change approved.' At this time, we were approximately 1 mile from the Class C surface area. Given our trajectory, it was obvious to the Controller that we were headed direct to our destination and would enter the Class C airspace. Since we were in communication with Y90 and had not been advised to change course or remain clear of the Class C airspace, we assumed that we were cleared into the Class C surface area. We continued into Class C surface area and landed. TRACON usually either advises us to remain clear of the Class C surface area or switches us to the tower frequency.We did not conflict with other traffic in the area as traffic departing BDL was turning away from us and climbing well above our altitude. We were later advised that there could have been an incursion into the Class C airspace.This could have been avoided if we had questioned the Controller to confirm that [we] were cleared into the Class C surface area. We also could have not assumed that we were cleared into the Class C Surface area and altered course to remain clear. The Controller could have told us to remain clear of the Class C airspace or switched us to tower frequency rather than terminating radar services. During a training flight to ZZZ from BAF we were using flight following from BDL TRACON and squawking a discrete code. We were in the Class E airspace beneath the 2100 MSL shelf of the Class C.As we approached our destination, which is located [near] the BDL Class C surface area, ATC told us 'Radar services terminated, squawk VFR, frequency change approved.' At this time, we were just outside the Class C surface area. Given our direct trajectory to ZZZ, and the fact that we had communicated this was our intention to both BDL TRACON (and prior to that, the BAF Tower), we thought it was obvious to the Controller that we were headed directly to our destination and would imminently enter the Class C surface area airspace.This was because we were in communication with BDL TRACON and had not been advised to change course or remain clear of the Class C airspace. This was (in hindsight) a possibly incorrect assumption on our behalf that we were cleared into the Class C surface area.As such, we continued into the Class C surface area and landed. In the past, TRACON BDL has usually either advised us to remain clear of the Class C surface area or has switched us to the BDL tower frequency if they did not want us to pursue a direct route from BAF to ZZZ. We were later advised by BDL Tower (not BDL TRACON) that there could have been an incursion into the Class C airspace.My learning: this could have been avoided if we had questioned the BDL TRACON Controller to confirm that we were indeed cleared into the Class C surface area. We should also have not assumed that we were cleared into the Class C Surface area and we should have altered our direct course to remain clear. I do realize that the BDL TRACON Controller could have told us to remain clear of the Class C airspace or switched us to BDL Tower frequency rather than terminating radar services, but I have to focus on what I can directly control in the future in order to remain a safe pilot.
1809359: Training flight working in the MOA. In comms with ZZZ Center, but operating VFR within the bounds of our assigned MOA block. We were executing a variety of contact maneuvers between 12,000-17,999 MSL, including basic air work, out of control flight, and unusual attitudes. We were monitoring the assigned ZZZ center frequency, but were not able to pay close attention due to focus on the training maneuvers. At one point I heard a civilian aircraft being advised that they were filing a flight plan through an active MOA, but did not hear the aircraft's response. I heard multiple company aircraft checking in for the MOA, including blocks adjacent to mine. Immediately before the NMAC, I set up my student for a nose-low unusual attitude recovery maneuver. I noted a TCAS contact, but it was on a depicted section line for the MOA, so I dismissed the contact as company traffic with the expectation they would be deconflicted through SOP adherence. As we entered a significant nose-low descent for training, we received another traffic advisory, very close to us. We executed a 5G pull and turn for avoidance. Our indicated altitude dropped below the contact. I'd estimate we came within 100 feet of the conflict, though I did not get visual on the other aircraft. Center called us and asked if we had to execute a significant evasive maneuver, and advised that the conflict had been a civilian multi engine aircraft. The controller was apologetic for not providing a traffic call to us, though due to how dynamic our training maneuver was, I don't believe the controller could have anticipated the severity of the conflict.
1809399: Landing practice at ZZZ. All applicable aircraft lighting was on. Level at 1,100 feet in the right downwind. Just after calling position in the downwind a Cessna crossed left to right in front of us at the same altitude overflying the airfield. Aircraft gave a radio call asking if we had a radio. We replied affirmative and that we had been making all applicable radio calls for an untowered airport. Radio was functional as confirmed with a radio check and the fact that we had been sequencing with other traffic at the field for an hour prior to that.
1809400: I was in cruise flight at 40,000 ft. on flight planned route via FTI J58 OAL to my destination. No part of this route crosses or penetrates charted military airspace at 40,000 ft. Prior to reaching ILC ATC initiated change in my routing to keep me clear of 'military airspace '. Revised routing was direct KITTN direct KATTS direct OAL then flight planned route. I entered above fixes in FMS and selected direct KITTN. At this point I pulled up every Jeppesen and government chart available to me and tried to understand this revised routing. ATC said it was to keep me clear of military airspace but there is no charted airspace on J58 above 17,999 ft.Was ATC lying? Was ATC mistaken? What is my elevated level of risk from deviating from flight planned route due to ATC ERROR . Should I query ATC? Is ATC error of immediate danger to me? As I was pouring over charts trying to determine if there was some charted military air space at my altitude that I was simply missing ATC advises turn right 30 degrees . I turn right 30 degrees. ATC advises that I was off course and had appeared to proceed from KITTN direct to OAL rather than KITTN KATTS OAL. I reviewed FMS and ATC was correct. Although I had entered the revised routing in the FMS , the FMS glitched and sequenced in error from KITTN Direct to OAL .I explained what appeared to have happened to ATC . Controller said I had come within 1 mile if penetrating this military airspace which I still could not find on any government or Jeppesen chart at my altitude. I took down the Controller's telephone number and agreed to call him after I landed to discuss this and the reason for me being issued a revised clearance. When I called the Controller he explained that the government has lots of military airspace that represent a hazard to normal flights which they purposely do NOT publish on government Enroute charts. He explained ATC was aware of these uncharted portions of military airspace and it was their job to keep the public away from this hazard. I was somewhat shocked by this admission that the government is publishing knowingly false Enroute charts that do not show military airspace hazards which the controller said in fact do exist and around which they had given me a revised routing. My FMS glitch resulted in a deviation from revised routing. But what I am concerned about is that the Enroute charts we rely on are being willfully and purposely falsified and do not reflect what controller described as many military airspace hazards that do in fact affect the flying public.
1809411: After a normal landing at ZZZ the right brake would not activate. Once rudder authority was lost the aircraft departed the left side of the runway. The nose gear collapsed in the soft dirt and the engines stopped. There were no injuries and we exited the aircraft.
1809415: I the instructor was to take Person X for a refresher flight as he was said to have previously held a Private Pilot certificate. Upon start up and taxi, Person X took questionable action to attempt to start the airplane as well as try to steer the Cessna 152 by use of yolk as if it were a steering wheel. After discussing with Person X that I would be in control of the aircraft and would use positive exchange of controls, I was solely controlling the aircraft while Person X viewed from the left seat. As I positioned the aircraft on Runway XX I advanced power to takeoff and talked through the procedure for Person X to listen. Halfway down the runway, Person X (without permission) positioned his hands on the controls of the aircraft and held the airplane in a position that I was unable to rotate, after several shouts 'LET GO, LET GO, LET GO NOW', my only final action to recover control was to strike Person X to release the controls as we did not have sufficient runway to abort the takeoff. I was able to regain control and climbout to the East where I took time to regroup and kept Person X off the controls. We returned to the airport and discussed the situation. Person X is not welcome to come back for another flight as I find him unfit and dangerous for flight.
1809430: I was on a multi-engine add on training flight with my instructor in Aircraft X. Upon landing at ZZZ I experienced what appeared to be a complete left brake failure. I used right brake to slow down but the brake barely worked. Towards the end of the runway we still had a lot of speed. I tried pumping the left brake which resulted in a slight left turn. My instructor said 'I will help you with the brakes;' which I understood to mean that he will work the brakes so I took my feet off the brakes. He said that he had no brakes at which point I stepped back on the brakes. At this point, the left turn was more aggravated and we were on a trajectory to run over the side of the runway and into the runway lights. My instructor applied right engine power to avoid the lights and stay on the runway. At this point we were near the intersection to the intersecting runway and swerved onto that runway without clearance.We were able to slow down and stop and immediately exited the runway at the nearest intersection. Tower advised us of possible pilot deviation. Contacted Ground. Copied the Tower's number. We called the Tower and advised of the situation. I was later informed that my instructor had been aware of a brake issue with the plane, had the part in hand, but had not wanted to fix it yet so the plane can still be used to finish up instruction for a few students. He said the brakes on the right seat had not worked in weeks, which I was not aware of. The left seat brakes felt soft on previous flight but still allowed adequate braking. I did not notice any anomalies during the pre-flight. Upon landing at ZZZ field on Runway XX pilot advised me that the brakes on his side were soft as were my side on the copilot side, so we both started to pump the brakes to try and regain brakes on either side. As we were pumping brakes we were getting to the end of the runway so I tried to use the hand brake which had no pressure in it either so I checked what my best option was. A taxiway was coming up to fast, not enough room to regain brakes in time before we ran off the taxiway, straight ahead the runway end lights, so getting onto the intersecting runway was that option so I told my student that I had the throttles and I skid the airplane with differential power onto the intersecting runway. By the time we had the airplane pointing down the runway my student had got his brakes back and was able to get the airplane stopped. I did not ask for permission to taxi onto the runway due to the time I had to make a split second decision on where to continue letting the aircraft roll so I looked down the runway and nobody was on final so I wanted the best chance to get our aircraft slowed down without running off and hitting any signs or buildings or hangers, so I used differential power to turn the airplane onto the intersecting runway.
1809433: Witnessed from the surface 2 different quadcopter UAS operating at the above location most likely without ATC authorization. 1809466: Two Controllers in the Tower. I was on Ground Control. Aircraft X landed long on Runway 24 and appeared to be able to exit at [Taxiway] H. 1809471: I was working arrival and departure for the JAX north area. We were on Runway 26. FHB airport is about 15-mile final for JAX [Runway] 26. We are constantly having to vector air carriers and business jets around 1200 codes traffic over and around that airport. Their altitudes and courses are erratic. The air carriers are audibly uncomfortable with it. Just today I had three 1200 codes from 1,500 feet to 3,500 feet MSL orbiting around my final while I'm trying to get jets into JAX. That sector also has multiple Victor routes that are busy with low level GA overflights. So, we have to get these jets as low as we can to miss the overflight traffic but the 1200 codes are blocking our low altitudes. It takes all our focus because we have to watch the tracks and altitudes of these VFR airplanes and constantly update the jet traffic of where they are. We don't like it. The pilots don't like it. It is a wildly unsafe situation there.Our Class C needs to be extended for the final for [Runway] 26. That is the only solution. No one should be flying around our final at crossing altitudes without talking to us. They just opened a flight school at FHB recently so the problem is only going to get worse. It's almost a daily problem now. One air carrier pilot said this is the only airport he flies into where he is dodging Skyhawks on the final. It is the most unsafe operation I have seen in my career.
1809482: Aircraft X ZZZ to ZZZ1. On the beginning of a three-day pairing, during the walk around, the FO (First Officer) found possible evidence of a bird strike in the #2 Engine. ZZZ Maintenance was called out and inspected the aircraft for a bird strike. The inspection was written up and the logbook was cleared in accordance with the maintenance manual. No damage found and Maintenance said the aircraft was good to go, so we departed for ZZZ1 only eight minutes late and landed uneventfully. Upon our arrival Maintenance put a lock on the aircraft for an incomplete inspection. ZZZ1 Maintenance completed the inspection in the first 30 minutes of our ground time. 1809499: Aircraft was directed to taxi from gate 1 to Runway XXL via Taxiways 1, 2, 3, 4. While on Taxiway 3, turning right to join Taxiway 4, both crew members noted an aircraft that appeared to have just been pushed back from gate 2. It was also agreed by both crew members that the tail of the aircraft appeared to be just inside the ramp boundary line. Approaching the aircraft at gate 2, the FO noted that the right wingtip was on the boundary line. The Captain then stated that he was going to deviate left of the taxiway centerline for additional clearance and the FO acknowledged. Approaching the aircraft, the FO was monitoring the right wingtip. From the cockpit angle the wingtip appeared to have approximately five feet of clearance and this was communicated to the Captain. The FO continued to monitor the wingtip until it appeared to initially pass the tail of the other aircraft outside of gate 2 and then announced it was clear to the Captain. It was at this time the right winglet struck the horizontal stabilizer. (Aircraft speed was approximately 5 knots.) The FO then called out to stop multiple times. The Captain stopped the aircraft and made an announcement for the Flight Attendants and Passengers to remain in their seats. The Captain verified with the Flight Attendants that everyone was OK. The crew then coordinated with Ground Control and Operations to return to gate 3. An ACARS message was also sent to Dispatch while waiting for a gate assignment. It is the FO's initial assessment that the wingtip must have started to pass on the opposite side of the horizontal stabilizer of the aircraft outside of gate 2, but incorrectly determined that it was on the near side based off the cockpit angle and understanding that the Captain had deviated left of the taxiway for more clearance. There were no distractions and the crew communicated clearly. Actions that could have prevented this incident would have been if the crew had stopped on Taxiway 4 and waited for the aircraft at gate 2 to move and provide more clearance. Additionally, the FO could have better assessed the wingtip spacing. We were cleared to taxi from [gate] 1 to [Runway] XXL via [taxiways] 2, 3 and 4. As we were joining 4, I noticed an aircraft facing terminal at [gate] 2, which appeared to be just inside of the movement area line. I mistakenly assumed it was an aircraft that had just pushed and that he was waiting to taxi. My expectation bias was that he would not have been pushed deep enough to interfere with Taxiway 4. As we were NE bound on [Taxiway] 4, I steered aircraft left of taxi, centerline to give more clearance around other aircraft. I asked FO how we looked on wingtip clearance. The FO stated, 'We are clear by 5 to 10 feet.' As we were passing behind the aircraft I felt that a main tire hit a pothole. As I asked what that was, I felt another 'bump'. The FO stated 'Stop. Stop.' I brought the aircraft to a stop and the FO told me we struck the other aircraft. I would estimate we were at a speed of 7 to 8 knots when the contact occurred. We began our taxi on #2 engine. I believe the second engine start was complete prior to contact. There was a typical level of chatter on ZZZ Ground frequency, which was busy. After the contact, I stopped the aircraft on Taxiway 4 and set the parking brake. We reported the incident to Ground Control. While I made a PA to the cabin to remain seated, the FO notified operations to coordinate a gate return and contact Maintenance. We returned to Gate 3 without further incident.Task Loading - I did a poor job of managing task loading. ZZZ is very busy and congested on the ground. With multiple aircraft moving in a densely packed area, I should not have opted for Single Engine Taxi (SET). This would have reduced the workload on both crew members and perhaps allowed for better situational awareness as we were moving towards the departure runway. Risk Management- I did not properly balance the risk of aircraft contact with continuing on the taxiway. Had I stopped and waited on the other aircraft to move well clear of taxiway, I would not have assumed that unnecessary risk. This also relates to rushing and trying not to clog up a taxiway. I should have set the brakes and not moved forward until aircraft in question was well clear.
1809513: Upon finishing my three-day paring in ZZZ1 at (time/date) I received a phone call from Scheduling, as I was leaving the aircraft. They told me they had added on to my schedule, they needed me to deadhead to ZZZ, then ferry an aircraft back to ZZZ1. I was concerned because I had already flown quite a bit that day and was afraid that I would not be legal for it. The Scheduler assured me that I was legal and that it was all okay. I asked them to look into it again because I had my doubts. I then asked if they could provide a hotel for rest at the end of the turn as I would be extremely tired. She claimed she would pass it on to the hotel desk. Upon contacting the hotel desk they said they could only provide a room if there was an unused ZZZ1 overnight room, which there was not.I proceeded onto the gate for the first leg of the ZZZ turn. Inside 30 minutes to departure there was no crew or other deadheading crewmember present at the aircraft. The flight to ZZZ was scheduled completely empty except for the Operating Crew, myself and one other deadheader. Again, I was concerned that I would time out before we could complete the turn so took it upon myself to prepare the aircraft for departure and set up the cockpit for the Operating Crew, in order to expedite our departure. We eventually departed 18 minutes later than planned. Upon reaching ZZZ, the operating First Officer left to recover a diverted aircraft back to ZZZ1 and I quickly prepared our aircraft for our return to ZZZ1. Unfortunately, once again, our aircraft experienced multiple delays due to random unexplainable maintenance locks, issues with load and balance calculation and performance. As we sat on the ramp at ZZZ I could tell that I would soon be in danger of timing out and verified my legalities. It showed a Table B Limit of XX42C without extension. At roughly XXX25CI called Crew Scheduling and notified them I was within 20 minutes of reaching the latest takeoff limit, and asked them what their plan was. The Scheduler on the line said that there was someone looking into my legalities and that they would call me back. That call never came. Shortly thereafter the aircraft issues were resolved and we were able to depart at XX37CF, just five minutes before the XX42C takeoff limit. With the aid of computer program and the printed crew legalities sheet, it appeared we had taken off within limits and were completely legal to fly the flight.Upon landing at ZZZ1 at XX04C, we were told that there were no gates available we would have to hold on the pad until one became available. Shortly after parking in the pad, we received an ACARS message referencing my employee number and requesting a flight delay extension. It showed several times, but those times did not match any times on the calculator on computer program. It was confusing and seemed to be in error. Since we were parked in the pad with the parking brake set, the Captain took the radios and I called Crew Scheduling. I explained we were on the ground waiting for a gate, I told them I had received the ACARS message and that it did not make sense - I asked for clarification and the implications of accepting or rejecting. They placed me on a brief hold but when they came back they were not able to answer any of my questions and essentially didn't seem too concerned since we were on the ground in ZZZ1. Since Crew Scheduling was not able to explain the ACARS message I neither accepted nor rejected the extension. Once again I asked for a hotel room, and they said they were not able to accommodate.A gate finally opened, we terminated the aircraft and I left the gate. As I was walking away I got a call from Crew Scheduling, a different Scheduler was on the line telling me that I had violated the limits. I explained to him that I had taken off five minutes before the limit time and that I should have been legal to fly the flight. The Scheduler explained that even though that was true I had violated the 'Last Block In' time of XX15C. I told him that I was not aware of any Last Block In Time, it is not a number that is published or provided to us in the cockpit, either by the Crew legalities sheet or the computer calculator. I also explained that I had called Crew Scheduling multiple times this evening to voice my concern over my proximity to the limits and not once during any of those calls did any member of Crew Scheduling even bother to mention a 'Last Block In' time limitation. The Scheduler tried to explain that it was all okay as long I say I was aware of it and that I was in acceptance. I countered that no, I was not aware of the limit despite my multiple requests to Crew Scheduling to evaluate my limits, and no, I was not aware I had exceeded any limit, yet when I called for an explanation of the ACARS message, it would have been the perfect time to tell me, and finally no, I did not accept the extension, nor did I reject it because nobody at Crew Scheduling could explain it to me. However, by default, a lack of acceptance should be considered a rejection. This was obviously not what the Scheduler wanted to hear, so he told me that he would forward it to a Supervisor, who would subsequently call my Chief Pilot. I said that was fine, asked that he have the Supervisor call me as well and we ended the call.This experience has taught me that Company does not have either the capability or the desire to adequately protect its pilots from exceeding FAR Part 117 Flight Duty Limitations and Rest Requirement restrictions. I understand that FAR 117 responsibilities are shared between the certificate holder (Company) and the pilot (myself). In this case, however, the pilot had expressed concern about the limits three times, asked for clarification from the certificate holder, yet was repeatedly stonewalled with evasive or non-existent guidance in order to complete the operation. Finally, after successfully and safely completing that operation the pilot was criticized for exceeding a limit the he was never provided, warned of, or explained ahead of time. Then finally the certificate holder attempted to coerce the pilot into accepting the extension after the fact.Resolution of this issue and prevention in the future should include: 1. Provide pilots with the latest block-in time on the crew legalities sheet and computer in additions to latest takeoff times for every flight. This allows pilots to clearly understand all limits of the flight. 2. Better and/or more extensive training of Crew Schedulers on FAR Part 117 duty restrictions. 3. Clearer and more proactive communication from Crew Scheduling to pilots about approaching limits. 4. Make available crew rest accommodations, on request, to a pilot that has been flown to the extent of or over the flight limits on the last day of a paring. Accident prevention should extend beyond the confines of the cockpit. After working 13 hours and 48 minutes on duty operating aircraft, nobody should be behind the wheel of a motor vehicle late at night. This event involves a potential exceedance of the Part 117 Maximum Block In (MBI) time for the First Officer at the end of a long duty day that included a re-route (involuntary assignment). It has already been reported by the First Officer, and I agree with and support his report. Rather than repeat his whole narrative, I will highlight important points and add one or two additional observations.In ZZZ, we experienced multiple unexplained maintenance locks which prevented us from receiving takeoff data. (Unknown if this malfunction was due to the new maintenance software, or ZZZ Ops not entering our actual fuel on board - which was tankered in and approximately 3,000 pounds more than expected on the release.) After about 30 minutes, we were able to resolve the situation by correcting fuel on board on a new release (and new takeoff reference number.) Feeling pressure to simultaneously deal with First Officer's legality issue while resolving the maintenance lock issue was a distraction and threat that (unlike weather, passenger issues, or aircraft malfunctions) is created by the system. In other words, although Part 117 is intended to help improve safety, the way it's applied ends up being an unhelpful distraction and a threat to safety.The First Officer tried to raise legality questions on the original call. Later, during the re-assignment, the First Officer called Scheduling at least three times to try to discuss the situation. Although I could not hear the other end of the conversations, it sounded like each time he was told they were aware of it and 'working on it.'The First Officer had accepted an extension the previous night. This caused him / us to wonder whether he was even legal for an extension on a 2nd consecutive night? He attempted to bring this up to Scheduling but never got a good answer from them. (Like everything else in Part 117, it's not as easy to answer as it should be. It certainly isn't a yes/no answer.)Once on the ground in ZZZ1 and holding in the pad for a gate to become available, we received an automated ACARS message asking to accept or reject an extension. This was done at the very last minute, when the only realistic options were: accept the extension, or violate Part 117. That doesn't really give the pilot any option to reject the extension. As previously stated, he had already been trying to work with Scheduling prior to this. And, he also (unsuccessfully) attempted to clarify his block in time and options with Scheduling after the ACARS message. When there was still time to address the issue, Scheduling would only give him a 'we're working on it.' It seems like the only option Scheduling would consider was strong-arming him into accepting the extension 'or else.' As we approach what looks to be a very busy summer flying schedule, with the strong possibility that the pilots being brought back in July from extended time off will arrive on the line too late to fill the gaps, Scheduling and Dispatch might consider being more proactive looking for other solutions (offering more premium open time trips, not diverting aircraft into airports where we only have one scheduled flight per day, etc.) versus pushing so hard and flirting with legality issues. In the interest of fatigue management and safety, I don't think it's reasonable to assume that a pilot who has been involuntarily reassigned more flying at the end of a long trip will automatically desire to voluntarily accept an extension to his flight duty limits. The discussion needs to happen much earlier, and not through an automated message giving the false appearance the pilot has an actual choice in the matter.
1809567: Denver airport is becoming hazardous to fly into due to non-specific ATIS, poor communication between DEN Center and DEN Approach, and the normalization of multiple arrivals and approaches being programmed during a normal arrival into Denver. This has increased substantially in the last few months and is resulting in aircrews being nearly continuously heads down reprogramming and briefing arrivals/transitions, approaches, taxi plan, getting appropriate landing data, briefing such changes, reviewing NOTAMs associated with these changes...etc. This is usually done while dodging weather, and mitigating turbulence, while descending into high terrain and congested traffic into an airport with multiple, parallel, similarly named runways. I feel there are three root causes. 1) ATIS is not very useful. Basically, a direction of traffic flow and a listing of all available approaches DEN has. 2) There seems to be a system now where approach tells Center what runway transition to assign aircraft. This transition frequently doesn't make sense and was not anticipated, programmed and briefed. Then, upon handoff to approach, the transition to another runway is often assigned. Then when the actual runway and approach is assigned, it frequently results in another reprogramming. This is acceptable during rapidly changing weather...it is commonplace all the time, however. On Aircraft X we programmed and briefed the FLATI 2 RNAV, RWY26 transition, RNAV Z Runway 26 approach. (Winds were 25024G34.) After starting the descent, we were given direct BYYKE, for the LONGS RNAV arrival. We programmed the LONGS arrival, Runway 26 transition, Runway 26 RNAV Z approach. We told Center that we were requesting Runway 26. Center directed us to fly the Runway 16R transition. (even though we were planning not to accept this approach). They said they are directed by DEN approach what transition to assign). We reprogrammed the ILS R16 transition and approach (we are now well along in the descent...moderate turbulence, and a VNAV discontinuity resulting from the reprogramming not being executable because of an approach transition altitude in-congruence) This was resolved quickly and safely and flown uneventfully with a 25 knot crosswind landing. The forecast approach winds were spot on, the ATIS hadn't changed substantially in an hour (Though there were about 5 or 6 of them). The point is, there was no significant change in weather driving this. I could have written the same report the last time I arrived to DEN on my last [arrival] from the east. On the flight today, we planned and briefed two different arrivals, one of the arrivals changing the transitions twice, two different RNAV Z approaches, an ILS approach and two different runways/performance numbers, NOTAMs, engine failure procedures taxi plans etc. I wouldn't spend time filing this report if it was a 'one off' It is becoming the norm and accepted scenario into Denver. It is also a contributing factor with DEN historically having issues with RNAVs. Each of these arrivals is complicated with at least 5-10 different altitude or speed constraints associated with them.
1809572: During the last 15 months of the pandemic, with greatly reduced traffic volumes, Newark Tower has used the primary tower frequency for the VFR traffic traversing the Class B airspace (helicopters and VFR sight-seers) which used to be on a discreet frequency with their own controller. 1809599: Approach control cleared us direct to WESEN for ILS [Runway] 08 [approach] at SJU. Captain was Pilot Flying, First Officer was Pilot Monitoring. This was the second leg of the night for this three day pairing of a long duty day. Level at 3,000 ft. (pilot selected) then cleared descent to 2,500 ft. (pilot selected) accomplished in vertical speed. Aircraft pilot selected speed was 180 kts. Controller assigned heading 110 to intercept and then cleared us for ILS [Runway] 08 approach. Approach/Land was armed and 'Land Armed' was displayed on PFD. The localizer remained identified and aircraft turned to intercept inbound course. Glide slope was above. Halfway through the intercept, the aircraft made an abrupt pitch-up followed by a thrust increase. This was very unusual as I have never experienced or seen an aircraft climb to capture a glide slope. While this was happening the aircraft exited approach/land mode and reverted to heading mode and solid bow tie altitude (2,500 ft.) All FMAs were 'white'. During the automation the aircraft pitched up and altitude was approximately 3,000 ft. in an attempt to capture the glide slope. The FO made a quick analysis and quick calls to the pilot flying while I was simultaneously disconnecting the autopilot and manually retarding the throttles to correct this anomaly. The aircraft was stabilized and a hand flown ILS was accomplished without autopilot assistance. This aircraft was scheduled for an 'auto land' for currency requirements and subsequently not accomplished. The First Officer monitoring that was accomplished and the verbal inputs from the FO were timely and appropriate, solid CRM. A note in our company aircrew briefing guide notes: Safety Alert Runway 08 Intermittent Glideslope Weak or intermittent glideslope signals have been reported when using ILS Runway 08. Exercise caution and intercept glideslope at the altitude depicted on the approach chart to guard against following a false glide slope signal. If the crew experiences any anomalies while conducting the approach, report the incident to tower and file an event report.
1809618: We departed ZZZ and climbed to 8,000 feet. Five minutes into cruise flight, we received a LH Engine Fire CASS message.
