1809620: After being cleared for takeoff on Runway 1 in DCA, the Captain transferred the controls to me. Shortly after the '80' knot callout and my response, I noticed Aircraft Y approaching an intersection ahead and it appeared they were moving faster than if they planned to hold short of the runway we were departing. I focused on flying the aircraft while closely monitoring Aircraft Y. Just as I was considering taking action, the aircraft came to a quick stop short of the runway. Around the exact same time the Tower Controller transmitted 'Aircraft X!' with no further instructions. We continued the takeoff uneventfully and Tower gave us their phone number to call upon landing in ZZZ, assuring us we were not in trouble or at fault but wanted to hear our side of the situation. The Captain asked me if I saw the aircraft and after a brief discussion it was obvious we both saw the same situation unfold.I am unaware of Aircraft Y's communication with ATC. With that said, I'm assuming it was either a lack of situational awareness on their part or ATC giving incorrect instructions.I do believe the system in place will normally prevent these occurrences. Maintaining situational awareness. Verifying clearance prior to crossing an active runway. Both pilots being heads-up. Physically checking the runway for aircraft should be the last barrier. We were cleared for takeoff on Runway 01. I turned control of the aircraft over to the First Officer (FO), and after he applied takeoff power I took control of the throttles. Several seconds later I made the '80' call, which the FO acknowledged. About this time I noticed an aircraft (Aircraft Y, I think) up ahead approaching Runway 01 perpendicularly on a taxiway (probably Taxiway G, but maybe M) at a fairly rapid taxi speed. I focused on the aircraft and began to wonder if it was going to stop as it got closer to the runway environment with no sign of slowing. At this point I mentally prepared for performing a rejected takeoff. Just as the aircraft reached the point where I was thinking I would reject the takeoff I noticed the aircraft stop with a pronounced 'dipping of the nose' from hard braking. At this point I knew the aircraft had stopped and takeoff could continue. I estimate our speed to be about 120-130 knots at this point. A second or two later the Tower Controller made a somewhat excited call, 'Aircraft X!...no further transmission'. As we passed the other aircraft I looked over and couldn't determine if it was over the hold short lines, but could tell it was very close. We continued the takeoff and shortly after getting airborne, the Tower Controller asked us if we had the number to call the tower when reaching destination. After retracting gear and flaps I asked the FO 'Did you see that other aircraft?' He replied he did and after further discussion I determined he saw basically the same things I did (aircraft approaching the runway, considering a rejected takeoff, 'dipping of the nose' with hard braking, knowing the aircraft had indeed stopped and comfortable continuing the takeoff). I called the tower when reaching ZZZ. The Controller taking my call informed me the other aircraft had entered the runway environment and asked if we noticed anything. I replied we did, but continued the takeoff because we knew the aircraft had completely stopped and we couldn't determine if it was over line or just very close. The person taking the call also mentioned the Tower Controller started to issue a rejected takeoff command to us but didn't finish because the Ground Controller confirmed the encroaching aircraft had stopped, hence the 'Aircraft X...'SMGCS lighting installed at DCA and used in all weather conditions, not just low visibility. Red lights are very effective in reminding pilots they are not cleared to cross/enter a runway.
1809715: Captain notified the safety cards in seatback pockets and Flight Attendant (FA) demo kits did not match safety cards provided next to emergency equipment in overhead bins (OHB). 1809720: At the end of boarding the agent had passengers in jetway and was doing a visual on seats that were available. I mentioned that the service dog was quite large and needed a bulkhead. She said he was taking [seat] XXF. The dog and handler was boarded and all bins were closed so I cleared all good to close with the Captain and the door was closed and doors armed. I continued to read the remainder of my announcement and also stated once we are in the air we will demonstrate the life vests once again. We did so at level off...Now after level off the passenger at XXF returned to her seat and I knew that I could not send the military service dog (over 80 pounds according to the handler, 2 tours in Country X and 1 in Country Y) and the handler to XXF...so I had the active military officer and his special forces dog sit at the 1L door for the remainder of the flight (he strapped in as needed) and he returned to XC for landing and the passenger once again went back to XXF for landing. 1809783: We were flying at 1,500 feet and to our surprise as we were coming out of a turn, there were two ultralight aircraft slightly higher than us approximately 500 feet horizontally from us in class E airspace. When we came out of a turn, we saw them and took evasive action immediately.
1809785: I rented the Cessna 172, Aircraft X from FBO in ZZZ1 to ZZZ at XA:00 on Date. I did a checkout on the day before. Before takeoff, I followed the checklist to perform the pre-flight and everything was normal, both brakes worked fine.At around XB:10, Aircraft X entered the final leg for Runway XX on ZZZ with 240 at 9 knot wind. I did a short-field landing and touched down smoothly on the second white stripes after the number XX with power idling. After the touchdown, the aircraft was rolling on the runway. I pulled out the yoke and stepped on both pedals to slow down the aircraft. The aircraft slowed down a little bit when taxing near the first exit. However, the airplane was still rolling when it approached the second exit. I checked the pedals and found that the left pedal was lost with no response and the right pedal was OK. So I reached out my right foot to the left pedal on the passenger side to make sure if that one was working, but it was not. In the meantime, my hand turned the yoke to the left subconsciously because the taxiway was on the left of the runway. After I turned the yoke, I saw the aircraft was going left slightly so I decided to turn the yoke all the way down to the left and finally the aircraft turned 180 degrees to the left from the runway to the dirt road. The right-wing struck the fence causing damage when turning. I pulled out the parking brake and the nose turned to the right slightly and stopped. I saw the hydraulic fluid was leaking from the left side of the brake's leg after I got out of the aircraft.
1809786: Aircraft X was on Final approach after calling out turning Final Runway 21, Second call Aircraft X on Short final Runway 21. After first call on Final I saw Aircraft Y pull slowly onto the runway and stop, that's when I cancelled Short Final. Just as I was preparing to go-around he started moving and in my judgement I could land if he kept going. He lifted off as I touched down with full brakes and speedbrakes out. I was gaining on him as he climbed to 100 feet and by the time I made the second to last turn off he was 200 feet above and maybe 300 feet in front of my aircraft.Additional realities information. I never heard Aircraft Y announce anything, entering Runway, or even my call to him after I landed close to him. I also want to point out that as a NON controlled airport no one should pull on the runway and stop for even 10 seconds with an aircraft on final at 110 knots. Since his information indicates he is a commercial pilot I'm sure he realizes that there is no excuse to be on the wrong Frequency XYZ.00 or to stop as in Position and HOLD like you might get at a Towered airport.
1809820: Aircraft X, on vector with ZZZ approach. Sector X calls to coordinate the helicopter on Victor route XX, instead of the filed route Victor route XY. 1809823: When I came into the area, the controller working [Sector X] asked me if I would sit down on the D-side. It was obvious the controller was feeling busy. I asked him if he would like the sector split and he declined. I sat down on the D-side and attempted to get a briefing but the controller was too busy.During the stint, the controllers work was sloppy, he did not seem to have any idea what was happening in the sector at any given time. Several times throughout the stint he did not use positive separation between IFR aircraft and had what I would describe as 'separation by luck.'The reason I decided to report this stint is because the controller nearly caused a midair collision between Aircraft Y that had departed ZZZ1 and Aircraft X that was descending for ZZZ1.When Aircraft X called for a clearance airborne off of ZZZ, the controller did not issue him and IFR clearance but instead instructed the pilot to remain VFR and take up a westerly heading for active military airspace. The only problem with this plan is that the airspace didn't start until 17,000 [ft.]. The aircraft should have been given the clearance to 170 and a heading to get out from under the airspace.Aircraft X was on a heading (for the military airspace) and was descending quickly because he had been left high.I made the following suggestion to the controller. Clear Aircraft Y on a 190 heading and leave Aircraft X on his present heading until they pass.The controller instead cleared Aircraft X direct ZZZ, putting him in conflict with the climbing Aircraft Y that had not yet received a clearance. I just don't understand why he would do this. Direct the airport wasn't even a good way to set the airplane up to land had there not been traffic.When he finally saw the conflict (did not respond when I pointed it out to him). He froze. The control instruction he gave was 'UHHH Aircraft Y maintain VFR' He then called the traffic to Aircraft Y which was at 12'oclock and 10 miles (estimated) opposite direction. Descending.He then followed up the instruction to Aircraft Y to maintain VFR at 8,500. At the time he issued the instruction, Aircraft Y's indicated altitude was 082 and he had been climbing in excess of 3000 ft. per min. The pilot said he could not stop at 085 but could go back down. The next radar hit was at 094. The controller then said 'UHH just maintain VFR.' He should have left Aircraft Y climbing and turned him. It would have cleared the conflict quicker.He then turned Aircraft X 15degrees right for traffic. But when he issued the instruction, he didn't say it with any urgency at all.I don't remember if he eventually issued Aircraft Y a turn or not, but I do remember thinking I was about to witness a midair collision because a bad controller was sitting on the sector.The traffic was not busy, it had some complexity due to the military airspace, but it wasn't bad. It could easily be worked by a competent controller without a D-side.In summary: Bad control judgement, Bad control technique, lack of control instructions, inadequate control instructions, failure to scan the radar environment, and a controller being completely overwhelmed by traffic nearly lead to a collision at near 10,000 ft.

At that moment, the status message POWER TRANSFER UNIT popped up. The captain relayed to Company this information and with the concurrence of all, the election to divert back to ZZZ1 was made based off of all the available information of system degradation, weather conditions in ZZZ and time to complete the extensive HYDRAULIC SYSESTEM PRESSURE - Left (Only) checklist. 1809932: The Ramp Agent on the ground notified the pilot that there was a person in the back with air, and asked if that was okay. I didn't really know what he was saying and I said it was fine. I didn't ask for clarification as to what he was saying. If I had questioned him further about what he was saying it could have been avoided.Proper or additional training regarding what is considered Hazmat for ground crew and more checks before a person with portable oxygen makes it onto the flight. I believe if it was caught at the gate, on the ramp, or if a more clear description was relayed to the flight crew, we could have prevented this situation. The Ramp Agent notified the PIC that there was a passenger 'with air'. He asked the PIC if this was OK but didn't fully explain what he meant. When we landed it we realized that she was using portable oxygen. The [cause of the incident was] lack of communication between the Ramp Agent and flight crew. Had the flight crew asked further questions after the Ramp Agent stated one of the passengers was on air, it would have been clear what the Ramp Agent meant and the situation would have been avoided.Proper or additional training regarding what is considered Hazmat for ground crew and more checks before a person with portable oxygen makes it onto the flight. I believe if it was caught at the gate, on the ramp, or if a more clear description was relayed to the flight crew, we could have prevented this situation.

1810031: I was called to assist in an aircraft spill situation on an A300 aircraft. I arrived as the First Responder was finishing up. I initiated the spill form and another AMT (Aircraft Maintenance Technician) documented the spill in the aircraft logbook. The aircraft had been in ZZZ since about midday and the spill was reported by the unload crew. The aircraft arrived with no containers in the aft lower compartment where the spill was located so a determination as to the source of origin for the spill would not be possible. The aircraft had operated [two] previous flight legs. The spill affected all areas of both the LH side and RH side outboard positions 5 through position 6. The responder said the spill was a 'mild' alkali and that he had used gray spill pads to try to absorb and clean up the unknown material. He said that a sample should be sent out to positively identify the substance. I documented this on the spill form which I completed down to the corrective action field. I inquired as to obtaining an [reference number] but there seemed to be a hesitancy to issue one and the spill form seemed to be met with the same response. The responder showed me the reference material that he used and stated that sodium bicarbonate could be used to clean up the unidentified spill. I informed both him and several on site Supervisors that since it had been identified as an alkali, the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual) Chapter 5 procedures (as per the GMM) would take precedence for any cleanup actions. It appeared that they wanted to load the aircraft but sometime later, the aircraft was ultimately removed from service. I later spoke briefly to the incoming supervisor prior to my leaving my shift for the day and mentioned the spill form which needed the [reference number] and remaining entries after corrective actions were completed. The following day I pulled the history and saw that the log item had been cleared and noted that there was no deferral for a spill on the aircraft. Since I had initiated the spill form, I was concerned and called Company and asked if they had a copy of the completed form. They controller looked but could not find one. I reached out to the [records department] who had the applicable log page but no attached spill form. I inquired as to whether the form had possibly already been scanned and the log page was there but the spill form was not to be found. I informed my Supervisor of my concerns. I understand the GMM (General Maintenance Manual) procedure directs that once the area has been cleaned and a visual inspection accomplished by the AMT, no further action is required but there is more to that procedure. GMM spill response procedures cover roughly two pages and are fairly specific regarding spills determined to be an alkali, a spill that does not have a known source and the requirement for a deferral for a reinspect of the spill area at a later date. The GMM also provides guidance for the disposition of the aircraft spill form. I went upstairs to my manager's office and asked the questions regarding this procedure with the GMM in hand. The response that I got was that the spill was cleaned up by a [company name] vendor that we pay good money for (cleanup service) and at that point, the aircraft spill form is no longer necessary and that is the end of it as far as I was to be concerned. I mentioned that his answer is not in line with what the GMM says. My ultimate concern is for the aircraft and for the AMT's who signed the logbook if any part of this process was misrepresented to them in the name of getting the aircraft back into service. Hopefully this is not the case. The ZZZ Aircraft Hazardous Material Spill Flow Chart, the GMM and the Aircraft Substance Spill Form are very specific with the responsibilities for spill events such as this. It seems like every spill event in ZZZ is like the first time with decisions being made on the fly.

1810049: Last night I flew the airplane across the border from ZZZZ to ZZZ to clear Customs on my way to ZZZ1. Customs held me for about 30 minutes. I was quite tired and stressed because this flight was scheduled very suddenly and I had to drive to ZZZZ to make the flight. By the time I was released from Customs, jumped in the airplane, started the engines, and tried to get my clearance to ZZZ1, ZZZ Tower was long closed. So I tried a phone call to TRACON first, but since ZZZ is so close to the border, my cell phone could not get the proper signal, between Mexico and U.S., so the call did not go through. At that moment, I switched the ZZZ Tower frequency to see if I could get my clearance from TRACON with no success. So, I decided to taxi to the head of Runway XXR, and try it again there. No joy. I began to feel desperate. I tried again calling by phone and this time I made contact, but the call dropped in a second. I kept trying for about four times, until I finally could get my clearance.My 'void if not off by' time was about 8 minutes, so I rushed the flight plan into the FMS, and put Tower frequency again in Comm 1. I then made the call that I was taking off from ZZZ for a straight out departure. Nobody answered, so I began my take off run. I saw some lights down the runway but, from my perspective, looked beyond the runway. Only when I was about to rotate realized and almost froze to see what I think was a helicopter on the runway! I pulled hard on the yoke, since I could not stop the airplane on the ground without hitting the other aircraft. I tried to calm myself down as I was scared to death. I was surprised that I did not hear the helicopter on the Tower frequency. That is when I realized I had not put in the correct Tower frequency! My blood went to my feet and my heart was racing and I felt so bad and miserable to think I could have killed some innocent people along with myself just for that 'little' error. I still feel awful.From now on, I will double and triple check my frequencies, altitudes, headings and runway holding instructions. I assure you that I learned my lesson on how external factors as stress and fatigue can and will affect your judgment. I will do my best to prevent this from happening to me again. Just the thought of the terrible disaster I might have caused, makes me realize the importance of proper focus, concentration and compliance with SOP's, no matter how tired you are. Besides, I will try to fly with a copilot from now on. Another set of eyes and mind are better than one.

1810107: On takeoff from ZZZ we felt a rough bumping at 100 knots. I was distracted by the cause of the roughness and didn't notice the exact speed we initiated the rejected takeoff at but felt it was at least 100 knots, but not above 120 knots. I determined the aircraft was unsafe to fly, called for the aircraft and rejected the takeoff. The First Officer (FO) alerted Tower as we were slowing to a stop. Once we were stopped, I made a Public Address telling the Passengers to remain seated. I was surprised to find that I didn't have a non-normal checklist for the situation and it felt odd as we had so much time to wait for the Fire Trucks to arrive. During that time I communicated with the Flight Attendants FAs to check on them and asked them to look for fire or smoke. They verified no indication of either and also confirmed that there were no injuries. Crew Fire Rescue pulled up and reported the two left main tires were blown and no fire, though they did hose them down briefly. The FO suggested starting the APU, which we did, and I was able to shut down the engine as the Fire Department was tending to the aircraft. We coordinated with Operations by radio and Dispatch by ACARS, and made Public Addresses to keep the Passengers informed and calm. The Passengers were then deplaned by air stairs and bused to the terminal. I had done the walk around and hadn't noticed anything unusual about the tires. The brake-wear pins looked fine. Taxi out was normal and even the initial takeoff roll was normal and didn't notice anything. After I heard the Pilot Monitoring call 80 knots, we felt a jolt and then the aircraft started shaking and getting progressively worse. We rejected the takeoff at about 100 knots with the appropriate flows and callouts. As we were slowing (I believe I saw 43 knots), I called Tower to let them know we were rejecting the takeoff. We got the plane stopped. The Captain called the Flight Attendants. The Tower let us know they actually heard the tires blow and that they were sending out the Fire Department and the Airport Operations. They then switched us over to another frequency to coordinate. We started the APU and shutdown the engines and then the Fire Department sprayed something on the aircraft left side. They used the word hot-spot. The people were then deplaned via air stairs and bused to the terminal, and we again confirmed that no one needed medical attention and were uninjured. After thinking about it, I know in training we had been told to wait until below 60 knots to call the Tower, but I'm not sure if that had changed to being at a complete stop or not before calling and could not find guidance in our manuals.
1810151: On Aircraft X we received an ENOTOC (Electronic NOTOC) from Load Control. While we reviewed the ENOTOC I noticed that there was no UN HAZMAT number and pointed it out to Captain as something I believed was supposed to be on the ENOTOC. Having flown cargo at multiple previous jobs I am very familiar with the HAZMAT paperwork requirements. However, as the ENOTOC is fairly new and the printout is overly confusing to read and decipher Captain contacted Load Control to get further clarification on the matter and to insure that we were in compliance with the procedure and regulations. Load Control assured us that everything was in order and correct for the flight. I do not recall whether we sent to NOTOC acknowledgment before or after we contacted Load Control for clarification. Apparently my initial intuition that something wasn't right with the paperwork was correct and we should have requested new paperwork be sent. Even today I have no idea what HAZMAT was actually on our aircraft. I believe the primary cause of this error is the cumbersome layout of the ENOTOC format to begin with. Every time we receive an ENOTOC it's like trying to decipher a sudoku puzzle. The columns (location, weight, UN number) don't seem to align with what is being listed for the HAZMAT. Even figuring out the location of the HAZMAT requires finding a number on the form and then referring to the bottom of the form for the actual position (at least I think that's what we do because it's a form that is in such disorder that I'm not even sure if I'm looking at a position number or a weight). To compound this ENOTOC issue was the fact that when we inquired with Load Control they assured us that the paperwork was correct and everything was in compliance with procedure. Where the error occurred is unknown, but more awareness from everybody involved could have easily prevented this error. I [suggest] a reevaluation of the ENOTOC procedure and paperwork is in order. The ACARS printout needs to be simpler and easier to read. If it can't, then we should return to the previous procedure with a hard copy of the NOTOC paperwork.
1810168: At ZZZ we were notified by the maintenance technician as part of the maintenance briefing that the autoland system was 'still' deferred and that a part was to be installed when the airplane returned in a few days. We noted that the previous crew had performed an autoland to Cat II standards, and had not written up the airplane with an items. An inspection of the logbook showed multiple issues with the First Officer (FO) raw data glideslope (G/S) indication and other failures over the last few landing cycles. During the flight we received messages from dispatch asking us to perform an autoland in ZZZZ1 to recertify the autoland system as that is how the airplane was deferred, i.e. the aircraft could be recertified by a satisfactory autoland being performed. We thought this strange as the previous crew performed an autoland to cat II standards and did not write anything up. The captain needed a landing for currency anyway, so a few messages were exchanged to that effect with dispatch, which led us to be directed to do an autoland in ZZZZ because the weather at the destination that the airplane would be flying were cat III. We said we would and performed the autoland. On approach we had a no land 3 message on the EICAS and a status message cue. The airplane then indicated the CAT II only on the PFD. We also saw that, as per multiple write ups, the FO's side G/S indication for the raw data portion was not in view. At about 1500 feet above the ground, the FO side glideslope came into view, but the aircraft showed slightly high on glide slope according to the raw data indication (note very slightly high, not out of any parameters, but still a bit unusual for the indication while on autopilot). Atmospheric conditions were VFR and the runway was in sight during the whole approach sequence. At about the time that the FO's raw data for the G/S reappeared, the Captain's side G/S raw data indication disappeared from view, though there was no indication of fault noted on EICAS with either of these issues. We continued the approach and the captain let the airplane land and it landed normally and tracked the centerline normally. The autoland was written up as unsatisfactory due to the loss of both raw data indications during the approach, the FO side data came back, the Captain side never did once it was gone. It appears to me that the autoland system deferral perhaps was not deferred properly as multiple failures over weeks of time suggested a problem with the system, and in the case of our monitoring of the autoland during our flight resulted in the same G/S issues on the FO side as well as a new failure on the Captain side of the raw data indications.

1810194: Aircraft was dispatched with the RT INNER fuel quantity indicating system inop. Per the MEL, the RT INNER fuel tank quantity would have to be verified by an alternate means. As Pilot Monitoring (PM) complied with ECAM and turned the pump off and consulted the QRH. When I brought the FUEL page back onto the ECAM I noticed the RT OUTER tank was burning and we had a fuel split of 1000 lbs between the RT and LT outer tanks. The working pump in the right inner tank showed a green line which I took to mean fuel pressure from the RT inner tank but the RT outer was burning down.I put the crossfeed valve in line so that LT inner tank was feeding the #2 Engine. Fuel stopped burning from the RT outer tank at that time. After a minute or two closed the crossfeed valve to see if the RT inner tank would now burn. Fuel started burning out of the RT outer again. Put crossfeed back in line to manually manage the fuel burn and to minimize the imbalance between outer tanks.FO and I discussed what we thought was going on. At this point I believed there was no fuel in the RT inner tank. We both agreed that we could not continue on to ZZZ1 and talked of possible diverts. We discussed returning to ZZZ but I believed there was no fuel in the RT outer tank and if that was the case, we already had an almost 7000 lb split between left and right sides.At this point we were about 50 miles to the west ZZZ2 and decided that was our best divert option. FO continued flying and worked with ATC to change destination and begin descending. I tried to contact ZZZ2 Ramp on VHF 2 but got no response. Informed operations via ACARS of a fuel discrepancy and that we were diverting to ZZZ2. He acknowledged and sent us routing and new numbers. Coordinated arrival with ZZZ Center and ZZZ2 Approach and shot a visual approach and landing to RWY XXR ZZZ2. Left inner tank was empty by the time we started the approach and were burning tank to engine on both engines.Once in the chocks we discussed what had happened and ran numbers on how much fuel we should have and how much we actually had. We blocked out with 29.2 and as per the fuel burn indicators had burned just a little over 10,000 lbs. We should have had 19,200 lbs. RT inner tank, inop FQIS, showed 5,900 lbs, but was empty. LT outer showed 7.4 and RT outer showed 6.0 for a total for a total of 13.4.ZZZ2 Maintenance verified fuel on board with MIL sticks. LT outer 7.7, LT inner 0.0, RT inner 0.0, RT outer 6.0 for a total of 13.7.A failure in the system ensuring required fuel is on board when dealing with a Fuel System MEL. Aircraft assigned had MEL for RT Inner fuel tank quantity indicator inoperative. When we got to aircraft and I began my walk around, I noticed maintenance moving a ladder over to the right wing inboard of the engine. As I got around to pre-flight the right main gear I asked the maintainer if they were checking the fuel quantity and he confirmed they were. This struck me as a bit odd since the system indicated Flight Ready when we were in ops. I finished my pre-flight and when I got to the cockpit I mentioned to the Captain they were checking the tank on pre-flight, but we both agreed there was no record of the check in the maintenance history. He called Maintenance and they said it was in work. We received an ACARS informing us the aircraft status changed to not flight ready. Shortly after we then received a Flight Ready ACARS notification. I then confirmed the fuel added from the previous flight block in and the fuel slip using the APS. The APS, fuel slip and fuel page all were within +/- 200-300 lbs of total quantity. We blocked out and departed on Runway XXR. After getting a turn east and a climb, ECAM indicated a RT Inner tank pump fault. The Captain began handling ECAM and QRH as Pilot Monitoring (PM). As Pilot Flying (PF), I was not head's down much but I did notice we had approximately a thousand pound split between the LT and RT outer tanks. The fuel page also showed the left pump in the RT inner tank still operational with a green line leading to the right engine. The RT inner showed approximately 5.7. The Captain informed me he was going to place the cross feed valve in-line to feed the right engine from left inner tank. When he did that the RT outer tank burn stopped. After a few minutes he closed the cross feed and again the RT outer tank quantity began decreasing after monitoring it for a minute or two. We then paced the valve back inline to manage imbalance. At this point we were leveling off and we began discussing what was taking place in the fuel system. Despite what the fuel system was indicating, we both came to the conclusion that there was no fuel remaining in RT Inner tank. Based on where we were, and the headwind we would have turning around to ZZZ, we elected to inform Center that we needed to land at ZZZ2. As PF, I took over ATC comms and FMS management to get a descent and set up for approach to ZZZ2 while the Captain attempted contacting operations via ACARS to tell them our situation and plan as well as call ZZZ2 Ramp. We descended and landed at ZZZ2 uneventfully. Once we were blocked in we discussed what we blocked out with-29.2 and had burned-10.0 per the fuel consumption gauges for each engine. The aircraft showed we had 19.2 onboard. We discussed this with Maintenance and they did the manual verification of the tanks confirming that the left and right inner tanks were empty and the actual fuel onboard was 13.7.Unsure other than a discrepancy between what amount of fuel was added and what reading was taken to manually verify RT inner tank quantity.I do not know what took place during the fueling / manual verification timeline to offer feedback on how to prevent future occurrences
1810195: Descending through FL330 enroute to ZZZ, [we] got [an] ECAM warning for green system low quantity. 1810198: While checking the fuel slip and comparing it with the previous flight block in fuel, FO (First Officer) discovered a 6,500-lb. discrepancy. We called Maintenance and asked about another fuel ticket. Maintenance advised us that they could not find one but assumed that fuel was added to the aircraft because of an Inner Tank Fuel MEL was worked on and cleared. I asked if they were going to make the appropriate AML write-up and look for paperwork and they advised that they would and would get back with us. After about 15 minutes, we had not heard from them, so we called and was told that they couldn't find the fuel slip but they were going to come out and check our fuel quantity using the magnetic level indicators. I went downstairs to check on the progress and was informed by Maintenance that they had checked the levels but were going to stick the tanks to recheck. I went back to the cockpit and a several minutes later was informed by an AMT that the Right Inner Tank only had around 4,000 lb. of fuel in it versus the 10,500 lb. that was reading on the Fuel Quantity Indicator. Fuel was uplifted, the tank quantity rechecked, and the previous MEL that was cleared was reinstated.The aircraft had the Inner Tank MEL for several flights prior to being worked on. Not sure if part that was replaced failed or what could have happened. Comparing fuel slips with previous flight block-in fuel is a good check, and my FO made a good catch. 1810221: After taking off behind an Airbus 321, we encountered its wake causing a significant rolling action right then left 20-25 degrees. The FO was pilot flying and disconnected the autopilot but the encounter ceased. This occurred after being cleared to takeoff before the aircraft ahead had rotated from the runway. We encountered their wake around 1100-1300 AGL.This is caused by ATL clearing aircraft for takeoff while the aircraft ahead is still on the takeoff roll. Despite having different courses and being legal, we frequently encounter wake of varying intensities and I often feel it's only a matter of time before a dangerous/ fatal wake encounter occurs.Either separate aircraft more or change the departure headings to help reduce wake encounters. This happens frequently though this encounter was more severe than normal. The aircraft was fighting the roll right then left with a lot of aileron and if we had encountered a stronger wake, we may have had difficulty controlling the aircraft.
1810249: It was the first flight of the morning and also the first flight of the trip for me. I just met the crew, me and the FO [First Officer] never flew with each other as well as being new. Also, we never had been to this airport before. Everything was normal as far as boarding, we started both engines at the gate because the end of the runway was very close to the ramp. The FO called for taxi and ATC says taxi to Runway 27. While taxing I was telling the FO about the hydraulic procedure and asking him when he turned the hydraulic switches from on to auto. During that brief conversation I passed [Taxiway] A5 and was told by ATC to stop and do a 180 back to [Taxiway] A5. (Which is the beginning of the runway) and given the Tower number. I called them when we landed in ZZZ1 and he said it was common (it happens about once a week) and they will soon be posting that area as a hotspot. Also, it was a new unfamiliar airport with the runway about 100 yards away, combined with a somewhat vague restricted area on the other side of the field. I believe this was the subtle chain of events along with a brief disruption in my situational awareness that was the direct cause.I believe I should have looked a lot closer (zoomed in) at the airport diagram, and should have briefed the FO exactly where the runway entrance was at [Taxiway] A5 and where the restricted area boundaries were. Also, as far as the chart goes, not only should this area be a hotspot but it should be magnified in the corner of the chart as well as having a description on the 10-7 pages that covers both sides of the airport where the boundary is.

I was seen at Trauma Center in City where I reside with the approval of Company. My final diagnosis was- lung injury. I am still taking prescriptions, and I am still on my inhaler. I continue to experience pain in my lungs and I am still under the care of Company. I want to be contacted by the FAA about this report. - [F/A Name, Employee No.] Please accept this report, as this is the first opportunity I've had to file this report. As soon as I stepped onto the aircraft, I noticed a dirty sock smell- an oil smell. It was strong to me. I mentioned this to the #1 and #3. I then stepped into the cockpit to introduce myself. After a few cordial words, I asked 'Do you guys smell that?' The Captain said 'What?'- I said 'it's like an oil, fume or dirty sock smell'. The Captain said 'no, we just brought this aircraft in from ZZZ and had no problems, and the other crew (other flight attendants), never mentioned anything'. I went back to the back galley where I was working. We started boarding, and then departed. I did walk back up to the front during boarding and the smell CLEARLY a dirty sock smell, which we all know only comes from oil, was still lingering. Approximately an hour and twenty minutes into the flight, (maybe and hour and thirty) the number 1 came back to the back galley where the rest of us flight attendants were sitting. I said to all of them 'Hey, I just want you all to know I have a mad headache and I don't feel right and I know it's from that smell I smelled before boarding'. Each flight attendant then shared that they too had headaches, and the number #3 said his fingers were tingling, the #4 said she felt dizzy and had vertigo, and the #1 said he felt like he was going to pass out, was nauseous, and had a bad stomach ache. The lack of ground logistics for the transportation to take us all to the hospital was a huge fiasco. We sat for over two hours before getting transportation that took ONE HOUR to get to the hospital. We had repeatedly stated we wanted to go to the hospital and the delay of care was unacceptable. At one point we were all brought down the stairs to the bottom of the aircraft where an ambulance was waiting. We all got in the ambulance, and then about 20 minutes later were told to get out as the paramedics would not take all 4 of us. Back up into the airport we went. Finally a van was procured for our transportation to The Hospital X. This took over an hour. Name was an agent for Air Carrier in ZZZZ1 and went with us to the hospital. She was extremely helpful. We arrived at the hospital and eventually were all placed in separate rooms, examined, were given IV medication and then prescriptions to go back to the hotel with. NO X-RAYS, EKG's or other tests were taken at this hospital. Not one of us were given oxygen therapy. No blood work was taken. It took several phone calls with Medical, and the company to get the bill paid. This part is unclear as most was spoken in [local language], but from what I gathered, Name (our liaison) was given a credit card to pay the bill. I've never been to this Destination before and it's not like any of us picked a hospital. Medical set it up for us. Well Friday morning, Medical said that wasn't the hospital they are affiliated with and we need to go to Hospital Y. This was about XA:00 am local time. It was XD:00 local when we got into a van to take us to the hospital. This was another huge fiasco, there should be measures in place to easily get medical attention when needed! Finally on [following day] I was contacted and was given instructions to go to the hospital as now my symptoms included a chest tightness, a continued head ache and just a feeling of being 'off'. I was given IV medication, a 12 lead EKG, chest X-rays, oxygen therapy for 1 hour, and several vials of blood work, some of which were repeated after an hour. 1810355: This was a flight [to] ZZZ for pickup of an item. I monitored the AWOS and listened to UNICOM for traffic. I announced my intention to enter the traffic pattern for Runway XX and land at ZZZ with a FULL STOP. It was observing that several aircraft were in the pattern in close spacing on the downwind with an estimated speed of approximately 70 Knots. My pattern entry speed was reduced to 130 KIAS for landing gear deployment and spaced about a 1,000 feet to right, outside of these aircraft. Again, I announced my intention to make a Full Stop landing without interfering with the numerous aircraft doing Touch & Go landings. I reduced the speed 110 Knots on base and 100 Knots on Final Approach. Expecting these aircraft to extend downwind about 30 seconds to give me room, I was surprised when one of them continued on a tight base and turn to final directly in front my plane. At 100 Knots approach speed, I easily overtook the 70-knot aircraft and passed successfully at about 500 feet right of ZZZ Runway XX centerline. I accelerated my plane while retracting the gear and flaps and maintained 180 knots for the climb and turn to crosswind. Again, I observed several aircraft on close spacing downwind and I entered a downwind slightly outside the pattern. For the fourth time, I announced my intention to make a Full Stop landing and turned the normal base for my plane's speed. For a second time, an aircraft made a turn to base and turned to final directly in front of me instead of extending their downwind about 30 second to allow much-faster airplanes to make a Full Stop. On this pattern, I was grateful the other aircraft decided to go-around when the pilot observed the rapid CLOSURE from behind. I said 'Thanks' on the radio and completed a safe Full Stop Landing.After my safe landing, I proceeded to the FBO to pick up the item. Upon reaching the FBO desk, I heard on the FBO radio that Runway XX is now CLOSED for an airplane stopped on the runway. From the FBO windows, it appeared to be an aircraft was sitting on Runway XX without its Landing Gear. The poor soul and retractable aircraft were still out there when I departed. If these aircraft belong to a Flight school, perhaps the instructors should talk to their students about allowing faster, dissimilar airplanes into the traffic pattern for a single full stop landing. There are MANY corporate airplanes that land at ZZZ Airport with approach speed in the 100 - 120 knots range. This would be appreciated by many and certainly may save unwanted distraction during landing. Perhaps the instructor input may save some distracted soul from making a gear-up landing.
1810360: Flight for Part 141 Multi-Engine Instructor (MEI) applicant. Preflight was claimed complete, both instructor and student walked out to [the] airplane, started engines, and taxied out. Run-up was normal, as was taxi. On takeoff, engine checks were complete and in the green. Upon rotation and climbout, both oil temperatures and cylinder head temperatures were rising rapidly. At 500 feet, instructor told MEI student to return to airport, [the] temperatures were rising too fast. Lowered power output and maintained 700 feet AGL. By the end of the downwind, both temperatures were in the red, oil pressure still in the green. Base to final had normal airspeeds. Landed safely with engines operating.Upon landing and rollout to taxi, engines began to stutter. Mixtures were pulled as we exited the runway and airplane was shut down. Post-shutdown examination showed engine plugs were not taken out. Thus, pre-flight had not been completed. Engine malfunction was due to student not completing pre-flight and instructor placing too much responsibility and trust upon [the] student to complete such actions. It is the student's responsibility to complete the pre-flight, but the instructor's responsibility to ensure pre-flight is completed. Corrective action would be for instructor to check the MEI student's pre-flight responsibilities and checklist items.

1810398: This was the first time flying into RIC for both crew members. Captain was PF and FO was PM. Crew planned to fly the SPIDR 4 RNAV Arrival and to connect to the RNAV (RNP) Y Runway 16 (RIC was landing Runways 16 and 20). Crew requested and was approved by Potomac Approach to fly the RNAV (RNP) Y to Runway 16 from DEEER (Potomac directed crossing DEEER at 4,000 feet MSL). We received the approach clearance around REDNG. FMC had given ALERT MESSAGES all flight long there was a steep descent after HEMME waypoint (280 KIAS/11,000 feet - 12,000 feet crossing restriction). FMC was correctly programmed. After passing HEMME, the aircraft began to deviate from the RNAV path by getting high. It became very clear, pilots had to intervene substantially in order to correct the aircraft back onto the VNAV PATH to successfully fly the RNAV (RNP) Y Runway 16 Approach. PF used maximum inflight speedbrake, elected not to use extending flaps. Aircraft airspeed was restricted to 250 KIAS or less as aircraft was transitioning to below 10,000 feet MSL. The only technique to slow the aircraft and attempt to re-establish the RNAV vertical path was to extend the landing gear about 30 miles from the field. Crew was able to correct aircraft back to RNAV path and complete the approach + landing. If this was another crew with little or no experience flying this RNAV Arrival to RNAV (RNP) Approach into RIC with actual weather, there is a high probability they would not successfully complete the approach and landing (would have to go missed approach, other altitude/speed deviations and/or compromise safety).
1810486: Conducted a standard preflight DG inspection. Post flight, was made aware of a dangerous goods discrepancy via an email forwarded from the Duty Officer. The IDG [Inaccessible Dangerous Goods] container, had not been assigned to the flight either and was loaded in position X. The Sort DG Manifest was in the pouch of the container but there was no card showing anything loaded.The cause was Improper manifesting and handling of cargo.[I suggest] additional training is provided to cargo loaders and Dangerous Goods personnel. I was informed via company email by the Duty Officer of undocumented DG loaded in the aircraft that was discovered during offloading in ZZZ1. [The cause was] ramp personnel loading unmanifested DG in ZZZ.[Suggest ramp] not load unmanifested DG.
1810496: Radioactive materials were incorrectly loaded in position X that should have been loaded [at position] Y or aft. Ramp called after flight departed to seek after the fact approval. Advised the team and the Duty Officers of the situation. It was determined that based on the low exposure rate - TI .8 - that the flight could continue and the crew would be advised on the ground at the destination. The flight was concluded without incident.The cause was due to the ramp agent missed the warnings he got from his software to not proceed.Ramp should be more aware of the special handling required by DG
1810536: After several discussions and phone calls on 5/X/21 it was concluded that the A Flight Attendant was being replaced and not work 5/Y/21 ZZZ-ZZZ1-ZZZ2. Another FA (Flight Attendant) who was scheduled to work 5/Y/21 ZZZ-ZZZ3-ZZZ2 would replace our A FA. At first the C FA and myself (B FA) thought the A FA would have to DH (Deadhead) on our flight and both the C FA and myself decided to take an earlier van ride to avoid any further distress caused by the A FA. But once C FA and myself realized the A FA was to work ZZZ-ZZZ3-ZZZ2 the C FA and me were relieved and comfortable to take the original van time of XA30am. When van came to pick up the D FA, C FA and myself our original A FA showed up as if nothing happened the previous day. On the previous day once the entire crew arrived to the hotel the A FA verbally attacked the Captain and First Officer. The A FA's hostility towards the pilots made the entire crew uncomfortable. I myself was visibly shaken by the A FA yelling and verbal attack on the pilots. Upon arriving to the airport the A FA walked off without us like the previous two days leaving us behind. When the C FA, D FA and me got to the gate the pilots were waiting in the gate area for us to discuss what we all were going to do as we were all in shock that the A FA was back on the trip without our knowledge of any change. The Captain was still backing up the decision to have the A FA removed but then it came down to what to do. The company put us in a situation making us work with the A FA whose behavior distressed the crew enough to adversely affect our work and well-being at work. The company's decision to have the A FA continue to work the flight created an unhealthy work environment. The crew was nervous and uncomfortable not knowing if there were to be another disturbance. It wasn't as if the flight was only an hour long we were flying across the ocean with nowhere to land if another disturbance were to arise. The C FA, D FA and myself all stayed away from the A FA as much as possible to avoid any further outbursts. The day prior after landing in ZZZ and arriving at the hotel, I, as well as the entire crew, had a situation happen with the A Flight Attendant. After speaking with the Chief Pilot as well as the Supervisor in the Operations Center, the decision was made to have the A Flight Attendant removed from her next flight. This decision was reached between the Supervisor and the B FA and C FA. I informed the Supervisor that I even thought I was OK with flying back with the A Flight Attendant. The B and C Flight Attendants were not, and that I was backing them up and would not force or require them to fly with her, against their wishes. The Supervisor said she would pull the A FA from the trip and we would have a new A FA. The situation was so bad that the B FA and C FA did not want to ride in the same van with the A FA the next day. The following day, when we reported for work, we found out that someone had put the original A FA back on the trip without notifying myself or the rest of the crew.I personally found out 45 minutes prior to departure, when I was given the paperwork to review and noticed her name on the Crew sheet. The B, C and D Flight Attendants were extremely upset about the situation and they were put in a very difficult position standing at the gate with over 160 people who were traveling back to the mainland. I asked the 3 Flight Attendants if they were going to be able to work with the A FA and also called the Operations Center to inform the Chief Pilot and the Supervisor about the situation. After the B, C, and D Flight Attendants agreed to work with her and we departed ZZZ. Upon our arrival in ZZZ2, the B FA informed me that it was a very awkward situation.
1810548: Cabin odors detected at climb and re-occurred at descent. Briefed with other crew and reported to company. Fumes report completed. Slight headache as result. Deplaned after pax de-planing.
1810558: Passenger report to me that she left a laptop in her bag and I asked if it had a lithium battery. Passenger is unsure and I tell my flying partner. She claims its fine and I decide to tell my Captain to be safe. Flying partner proceeds to ask the gate agents in which they state its fine. Flight Attendant proceeds to check the manual to see if laptop can be in the pink tag bag. Captain decides to get the pink tag bag and give the laptop to the passenger. The issue was solved.
1810595: While serving as PF (Pilot Flying) into ZZZ on the ZZZZZ arrival, I was flying the aircraft with autopilot, autothrottle, and VNAV. We had programmed the STAR along with a transition to the ILS XXR into ZZZ and reviewed all the fixes and block altitudes on the Pro Line Fusion MFD screen. The aircraft flew the STAR without incident from FL280 all the way down to about 13000. The VNAV and autothrottle were working. I became distracted when the autothrottle failed to reduce 'FMS speed' for ZZZZZ1 to 250. I manually selected 250 and slowed. I reactivated the FMS speed function and verbally announced that we would monitor the speed and to make sure it made the next speed slowdown proactively at ZZZZZ2. What I failed to properly notice is the VNAV set a floor altitude of 13000 and leveled off. I did not think much of it since the next fix was an 'at or above' 9000 so I thought it was a level-off in lieu of an overly shallow descent.While being distracted in over-monitoring the FMS speed reduction, we got caught in an undesirable aircraft state. To make the alt window at ZZZZZ3, 9000-8000, I manually selected VS and adjusted the descent rate and flight spoilers in order to make that fix's alt window. I believe it was too close to notice if we made it or not and we did not seek relief with ATC since the Captain seemed unsure how to query ATC since he too was interested in watching the VNAV and FMS speed since he had little time on this Pro Line Fusion avionic suite. I flew the remaining alt windows in VS mode since that higher level of automation was not trustworthy or compatible with my state at that time. Later in the arrival, before ZZZZZ4, ATC gave us relief off the arrival and gave a descent to 3000. I dialed 3000 into the FGCP and the Captain confirmed the ALT. Continued down in VS. Since the previous UAS - Undesired Aircraft State - was around 10000, it impeded on the 'in-range check' being completed. We were at about 6500 when the in-range check was started and it distracted us from noticing the aircraft was still in VNAV and had captured the floor of the arrival, 6000, and did not continue [the] descent to 3000. ATC would query us shortly and again I would notice that the aircraft in a UAS. I noticed VNAV still active and disabled it, and continued down. We intercepted the approach and landed without further incident.In hindsight and a word of caution, this is the first avionics suite I have seen where altitudes on a STAR can be superseded by altitudes on an approach. In this example, the ZZZZZ STAR with the ILS XXR ZZZZZ5 transition. There was a discontinuity between ZZZZZ6 and ZZZZZ5. I want to know why in what world should VNAV look ahead of a discontinuity and block the VNAV windows on the STAR. All the stepdowns on the ILS XXR were there for reference as there no way knowing how far in the downwind ATC would take you before a base turn. I don't have a lot of VNAV-capable aircraft experience and I see tremendous issues with not being properly trained in how the aircraft will respond based on what is programmed into the FMS. In general, the avionics differentiation training was lacking and laughable and the differences from the standard avionics in the CL604. It seems half-finished and very retrofit. Having to train on-the-line with the suite to new crew members is frustrating at best and dangerous at worst. I will continue to step up and down levels of automation as my comfort and knowledge adjusts and will try to look for any potential red flags in FMS programming beyond the basic comparing to the approach plate.
1810599: I was practicing traffic patterns at the airport (ZZZ) and when I was turning to the right crosswind, I noticed the plane behind me was already in the upwind. I thought he was going to extend his upwind to give me more space, so I continued normally. As soon as I joined the right downwind for Runway XXR, I heard Tower ask the other plane if he was still following the traffic in front of him, looked towards my right trying to find him and I saw him off my right wing doing a climbing left turn to get away from me.The tower did not tell the other pilot anything after that. I don't know if he did not see how close we were, or he thought it was irrelevant to say something. As for the other pilot, he must have been distracted and lost sight of me. I will be more aware of my surroundings next time. This happened before the tower closed. I am glad it was still controlled airspace, otherwise it would have been another (probably tragic) outcome.
1810601: I was transiting the Bravo airspace and was assigned a specific heading by ATC. I thought I was flying the assigned heading when ATC asked me for my heading. I then noticed that I had failed to set the vacuum driven directional gyro using the magnetic compass. I have flown primarily glass cockpit aircraft for the last 7 years but recently purchased a Cessna 185 which has traditional instruments, and requires that the DG be set manually before flight and periodically during flight. After realizing the omission, I immediately turned to the appropriate heading and then set the DG using the magnetic compass.
1810605: I was on approach to land Runway XX at lake hood ZZZ with an 8 knot cross wind, I decided to carry about 5 knots of extra airspeed into my landing and land long. I touched down with the main landing gear first, parallel with the runway with proper cross wind correction. My trouble came when I set the tail down it began to swing to the right and I gave all of the right break and rudder I possibly could with no avail. I ended up sliding sideways into the left ditch just north of taxiway going roughly 15 kts. The ditch I slid into was very marshy and muddy which caught my right tire making the plane stop abruptly causing the plane to tilt over far enough for right wing tip to make contact with the ground and then settle back on both tires. I first checked my prop to ensure it didn't strike anything and that the motor was still running, I then immediately shut down the engine and contacted Tower to notify them of the situation. I told Tower I would need a minute on the runway to push the plane out of the way and they responded with 'OK'. There were no injuries in the incident and the only damage that occurred was minor to the right wingtip.
1810616: According to my student: While he was doing solo touch/goes at ZZZ, on his second landing, he touched down left of centerline. While rolling with the throttle in the idle position, he turned off the carb heat and began to retract the flaps. The nose of the plane began to veer right. When he applied left rudder he said the plane felt as if it would skid, spin or drop the nose onto the ground. Therefore, he applied just enough left rudder to straighten the nose wheel and rolled onto the grass adjacent to the runway. No contact was made with any runway signage or lights. There was no damage to plane, runway, or grass area, and there were no injuries. Tower cleared for continued movement to the Alpha taxiway. He continued to the transient parking area and called ZZZ Tower per their instructions.As the instructor, my student called me to inform me he had run off the runway, no damage had occurred, and he had spoken with the tower and FAA. I did not know he was flying by himself that day and had received no notification from him. I asked him to recount what happened to me several times trying to understand what happened. I called the Tower and confirmed that the winds were variable at 3 knots and visibility was very good. Based on his recount, I do not fully understand how he thought going off the runway was his safest option. I have not offered him any training or instruction that would indicate that was good judgment. He has never landed far off centerline with me in the plane and has never demonstrated that he would ever act in such a way. He and I have logged extensive dual hours at ZZZ doing pattern work, and he has never flown in a way that indicated he would act or make a decision in this manner. He had demonstrated consistently with me that he was able to maintain directional control of the airplane both in the air and on the ground. I have informed him that all of his solo endorsements are no longer valid. I was planning to spend an extensive amount of time with him on the ground and in the air addressing what happened yesterday through re-training, but he has decided to discontinue his flight training at this time. As a result of this incident, I have re-clarified to all students that they must inform me of any time they plan to solo and must receive my permission before doing so. I have also implemented a strict rule of no solo touch and goes. Solo pattern work will from now on only be full stop landings. While doing solo touch/goes at ZZZ, on my second landing, I touched down just left of center. While rolling with the throttle in the idle position, I turned off the carb heat and began to retract the flaps. The nose of the plane began to veer right. Applying left rudder the plane felt as if it would skid, spin or drop the nose onto the ground and I was too far toward the edge of the runway. I felt it best, to reduce the chances of injury or damage. I applied just enough left rudder to straighten the nose movement and rolled onto the grass adjacent to the runway. No contact was made with any runway signage or lights. No damage to plane, runway or grass area and there were no injuries. Tower cleared for continued movement to the taxiway. I continued to the transient parking area and called ZZZ Tower per their instructions. As a result of this occurrence, training has been suspended for evaluation and scheduling with CFI.
1810628: The aircraft in question came in for a dead left magneto which failed in flight. We troubleshot and determined it was in fact a dead left magneto. We removed and replaced the left magneto with a factory rebuilt magneto. Ops checked everything fine. Mag drop was perfect. The pilot ran it as well. No issues. He loads up his passenger, and they take off. Well, the right-hand magneto fails on takeoff, resulting in him turning back and landing at the airport. Back in (Month) 2020 that right hand magneto failed and we replaced it with a factory rebuilt magneto as well. I am writing this to see what can be done about these factory rebuilt magnetos. I feel they are failing too soon. Only 100 hours in between failures. If the left magneto would've held out and failed at the same time as the right hand just did, it could've been a catastrophic failure and maybe even loss of lives.
1810630: Aircraft Y landing VPS was descending over V198 to FL200. Aircraft X, a departure from CQF in P31, was vectored NE bound to climbing to FL190 to allow Aircraft Y to descend south of the aircraft. Traffic was called to both aircraft. Aircraft X read back '200 Aircraft X' which was not caught or verified by the controller.The controller was busy separating aircraft arriving and descending to the northeast CEW landing VPS. When the controller noticed Aircraft X starting to climb, Aircraft Y was turned 25R to the southeast to try to get some lateral separation. At first since the targets were close, I thought it was MODE C interlace. Since I was unsure what altitude Aircraft X was climbing to I decided to try to get lateral separation instead of vertical. Upon further query Aircraft X misunderstood the traffic call and thought it was a climb to FL200.Traffic at the CEW sector has increased by multitudes over the past year due to numerous airlines starting and expanding service to the FL panhandle. Before COVID, the departure list from the 3 panhandle complexes (P31, Eglin RAPCON, and Tyndall RAPCON) rarely went over 30 proposed departures. Now we are regularly seeing 40-50 proposed departures.When the military airspace gets activated, the sector becomes an inverse T with about 10 MI on either side of the 'T' to separate commercial jets, slow props, military trainers, and fighters.The departures and arrivals are all filed over the same fix CEW creating a dangerous situation with minimal time to solve conflicts. There should be a redesign of this sector.
1810636: Visibility issues arose due to solar panel reflection approximately 1.5 miles South/Southeast of the airport [Newark].Reflection is in line of sight of both arrivals and departures on the Northeast flow.Have panel removed or turned away from Tower.
1810675: I was doing the Captain preflight duties as specified by the Aircraft Operating Manual (AOM). This was the first time in an actual MAX aircraft (not counting the MAX return to service training in the SIM) since the aircraft were grounded 2+ years ago. As I was completing the preflight duties, I neglected to set the autobrakes to RTO. I believe the cause of this was, the autobrake selector in the MAX is in a different position than the NexGen aircraft, specifically in the center console rather than next to the landing gear selector lever. Also, the flight paperwork was placed in such a position as to cover the autobrake selector knob. When we accomplished the Before Start Checklist, of course one of the items is 'AUTOBRAKE' with a response of 'RTO'. I responded with the appropriate call of 'RTO' purely by rote memory without actually looking at the autobrake selector. I recall looking towards the landing gear lever where I expected to see the autobrake selector and for some reason was convinced I saw it and it was set properly to RTO. We taxied out and departed uneventfully. It was only upon accomplishing the clean-up items after flap retraction that we noticed the autobrake selector was in the off position. The rest of the flight continued uneventfully.
1810679: While preparing for departure we were interrupted in the middle of our pre-departure brief several times as a result of not having enough time to complete all required checks to be ready for all other work groups checking in before departure. Scheduled hotel pick up time put us at the airport right at 45 minutes. However, because of the requirement to accomplish COVID temperature check, and health screening, we arrived at aircraft with not enough time to complete all the International/Oceanic checks before the different team members that need to check with us to be ready to depart (i.e.: gate agent, ramp, flight attendants etc.) began to check in. Especially, when all other work groups were ready to depart 10 minutes before departure time and we were trying to catch up with our checks.This time constraint created a significant threat as every time we got interrupted there was the possibility of missing something in addition to the extra mind workload of having to shift attention and re-focus.
1810740: Approximately 80 miles before top of descent MIA Center descended us to FL360 behind a widebody which was left at FL380. There was a quartering left tailwind of approximately 30-35 knots. We were given 280 knots assigned for spacing. The widebody entered the STAR from our left or the east. Our separation grew from less than 10 miles to just at or slightly over 10 miles with our descent and speed. At approximately 60-55 miles from the new top of descent from FL360 we experienced a rapid roll to the left of approximately 30 degrees. I turned off the autopilot and the plane then rolled right rapidly, about 20 seconds later. We [asked] for a speed of 250 [kts]. ATC gave the speed when we reported the wake turbulence. I continued to hand fly for a while until we could assure ourselves the wind dropped a bit and our separation had increased. I had the FO (First Officer) call the FAs (Flight Attendants) everything was secure and everyone was okay. We had them take their seats [and] the seatbelt sign was on at the time of the event. Upon leveling at 8,000 [feet] and turning westbound we had a second event even though the 777 was turning base ahead and we were just entering the downwind and crossing the bay. Approach had kept the 777 high and gave them relief on the restrictions as they descended. The next day, MIA Approach cleared us to 8,000 [feet] behind an aircraft ahead with tight spacing. We did get a slight roll left then right but I immediately slowed to 230 and had the FO tell MIA we were slowing. This time the aircraft ahead was not kept high and so I hand flew slightly above VNAV path to assure at FL230 we would not have wake turbulence. Later [that day] Tower cleared us to takeoff before [another air carrier aircraft] had rotated. After I lined the jet up on the centerline and after takeoff clearance, we waited 8-10 seconds for [the other air carrier aircraft] to rotate. We then took off. We were given heading 105 [on departure, and the other air carrier was given heading 120]. The aircraft behind us was given 090. We encountered wake turbulence behind [the other air carrier aircraft] due to crosswinds. MIA has minimized separation and rushed operations such that it is my experience safety is impacted.First, the next time MIA says keep it rolling and cleared to takeoff, I will ask to exit when an aircraft is still not near rotating. Second, MIA needs to review the operating practices in play. Lack of separation at FL380, being placed below and behind a heavy with a quartering tailwind, 10+ miles separation was not enough with 30+ knot tailwind. Change the practice of [descending] a non-heavy behind and below a heavy to descending the heavy below the following aircraft.
1810741: We were [on] Aircraft X PHX-ZZZ on Date. We pushed back from gate onto taxiway, started engines and performed the before taxi checklist. The First Officer (FO) called for taxi, and clearance was given to taxi. I looked left and said 'clear left'. The FO looked right and said 'clear right'. As I pushed up the thrust levers to taxi, the FO immediately shouted 'stop'. He noticed three people attempting to walk in front of our aircraft. Apparently they were walking from concourse 2 to concourse 1 thru the ramp area. When he noticed them they were about to walk in front of our right engine. When he got their attention, the three folks changed direction and then walked under our right wing and out of sight behind our aircraft. We notified the Ramp Controller of the individuals and waited until they were well clear of our aircraft and then begun our taxi. Never allow people to walk in or around the ramp taxi area after aircraft have been pushed back onto the taxi lines to start engines and taxi. After pushback from gate, with both engines running and all pertinent flows and checklists complete, I called PHX ramp for taxi. Ramp cleared us out the south line to [the] spot. At that point, the Captain and I were unable to ensure the aircraft was clear for taxi out. Out the left side of the aircraft, he noticed a ground crew worker telling him not to taxi. Out the right side of the aircraft, I noticed what appeared to be three aircraft cleaners walking in front of the number two engine. To make matters worse, after realizing their mistake they continued to show their propensity to make bad choices by not doing a 180 degree turn but by turning and walking behind the airplane to cross the ramp. A conversation was had with the Ramp Controller. I encourage you to watch the security video to see just how bad this was. They had no clue the danger they were in and this could have been much worse. Something needs to be done. On our end, no causal factors to list. Everything was done in accordance with standard operating procedures. On their end, I can only speculate but lack of common sense seems first and foremost. Accountability on behalf of these three individuals.
1810757: FAA National Airspace Incident Monitoring System (NAIMS) NOTAMS system stopped uploading new NOTAMS on Date. I revised a flight release on the aircraft. I was relieving Dispatch desks XX and XX1. Both of those dispatchers did not tell me that the FAA NOTAM system was not updating with newly issued NOTAMS. I saw a screen printer message to access Defense Internet NOTAMs Service (DINS) to look-up NOTAMS. Due to task saturation and dealing with multiple storms en-route, multiple re-routes, phone calls and turbulence I was unable to access DINS for the flight. When I could access DINS, the server wasn't responding due to overload. The flight landed and blocked in at ZZZ without incident. The cause was the FAA NAIMS NOTAM system not updating with newly issued NOTAMS. I believe if this happens again in the future there needs to be better communication on turnovers that the issue is occurring. I also think that supervisors should make an announcement in the department shortly after a new shift starts to let them know of the issue. Multiple screen printer messages I think would also help. But most importantly this information needs to be included on turnovers and an announcement over the PA should be made by the ATC desk, Chief Dispatcher or Duty Director.
1810763: At start of shift, we were informed that NOTAMs had not been available since approximately XA:00z due to damage to the FAA servers. Several messages sent by [the] domestic manager to get NOTAMs by calling Airport Operations at our airports to obtain NOTAM information. However, this wouldn't work with many international airports due to language barrier (later resolved when international NOTAM access was restored;) and even with domestic airports, the information is only good until the phone call would be terminated because without new NOTAMs coming in, we would have no way of knowing if a new NOTAM was added later. Additionally, Center, FIR and FDC NOTAMs were not being updated either, so that information also not available as required by FAR and FOM.Consequently, I elected not to release any of my flights until the NOTAM system came back up. I attempted to have the flights all prepped so they could be sent immediately when the NOTAM system started coming back, but I fell behind even doing that, and all 13 flights on my desk released late and took the associated delays. Contributing to the late releases were thunderstorms approaching ZZZ during the inbound and having to focus my attention on those rather than getting flight plans prepped. My purpose with this report is to both self-disclose the fact that I sent releases later than specified by the manual but also to raise concerns about management's solution to 'mitigate' the NOTAM issue. The manual is clear about our requirement to check ALL NOTAMs, and merely calling airport operations does not ensure that all NOTAMs are received. Some NOTAMS, like runway closures, taxiway closures, approach light outages, etc, may come from Airport Operations, but others may be issued by the FAA NOTAM office (FDC NOTAMs;) others are issued by the ATC centers. It's simply unrealistic and imposes too much of a workload on both international and domestic dispatchers to be expected to call dozens of airports (9 alone on one of my ETOPS flights;) along with multiple centers to try and get NOTAM information while also dealing with thunderstorms and all of our other flight following duties.It seemed very much that the overriding concern was getting releases out regardless of whether it was legal or prudent to do so. Apparently, the FAA puts the NOTAM servers on the top floor of one of their building. When thunderstorms moved through, the roof leaked and allowed water to soak all of the servers. Better server placement by the FAA would be a good start along with a robust backup system in a completely different location along with the necessary programming and bandwidth so that failing over to the backup system is a near-instant process rather than requiring hours.
1810775: On left base for visual Runway (RWY) XX, slowing to full configuration and turning final, flaps were extended to 45 degrees while flight spoilers where deployed at 1,500 feet. Speed trend vector was decreasing although thrust setting was at expected thrust setting for approach. Captain called for increased power and crew realized that the flight spoilers were not fully retracted while turning final. The aircraft speed was approx. 150 knots which was below the SOP maneuvering speed of ref + 17 knots with spoilers deployed. At this time the stick shaker activated for approx. 2 seconds and the angle of attack was lowered. The flight spoilers were immediately retracted and the stick shaker stopped. Continued to join the localizer and were on a stabilized approach by 1,000 feet and landed without any incident.While slowing to configure for final approach, Pilot Flying (PF) believed the flight spoilers were fully retracted and called for flaps 8 and 20 at 200 knots. Then the call for gear down and flaps 30 at 180 knots. PF was approaching the localizer course, called flaps 45 at 160 knots. To reduce automation workload the autopilot was disconnected and was preparing to make a left turn to intercept the localizer and glide slope. The stick shaker activated at this time because the flight computer detected a pending stall with the flight spoilers deployed. Immediately after the flight spoilers were fully retracted, the stick shaker stopped and the aircraft was on speed with flaps at 45 degrees. A left turn was made intercepting the localizer and the aircraft was on a stable approach by 1,000 feet.ATC gave direct to the final approach fix for the visual to RWY XX while still descending out of 6,000 and needing to slow to configure for landing. PF could have anticipated needing more distance to reduce airspeed, possibly without flight spoilers, and fully configure the aircraft by 3 miles of the final approach fix by descending sooner and leveling off earlier. This would have reduced pilot workload and automation management allowing for a more thorough scan of the aircraft and its systems before deploying flaps and slowing to final approach speed.
1810783: We were on a local training flight at ZZZ. While holding short at Runway XX, all the engine indications were normal, as we reduced the power to idle, engine shutdown by itself. We tried to restart following the checklist, as it was unsuccessful. I requested the Tower for assistance to tow the airplane back to the ramp. After post-flight inspection airplane was squawked.
1810791: Taxiing into the gate, the visual docking system was reading STOP" but the marshallers were continuing to wave us in. Stopped and called OPS who said they were looking into it. Marshallers continued to wave us in. Had to call OPS again, who said they weren't sure if it was working. We advised them to turn the system off so we were not receiving conflicting information, and after several minutes of all the marshallers trying to wave us in, one of them finally went over and reset/turned off the system. We discussed the situation, and being good daylight visibility, taxied in using the marshallers only. This is not the first time I've had conflicting information between ground crew and the system, usually with the display advising "STOP". I am not Seattle based so don't see the system every day but I have used it fairly often, and I think we are just setting ourselves up for potential issues if we get in the habit of not trusting or ignoring the system sometimes and relying on it other times. The system should either be working and used or completely off when we're relying on marshallers."
