1810811: At 7,000 feet during climb the flight attendants called the flight deck and reported fumes and a smell in the cabin. Both flight attendants reported it and said multiple passengers were aware of it as well. I didn't smell anything in the flight deck. I might have gotten a slight acrid smell but now I'm not sure. I contacted ATC and requested to return to ZZZ and reported fumes in the cabin. They [gave us priority handling]. I sent an ACARS to Dispatch saying we were returning to ZZZ. I called the flight attendants and told them we were returning to ZZZ and would be on the ground in 15 minutes. First Officer was the pilot flying and setup for the approach. I briefed it for him. I pulled the QRH and looked at the fumes procedure. I turned off the recirculating fan and pushed in the dump button. I called the flight attendants again to confirm if they were still smelling the odor and they were. I asked if they saw anything. They started telling me about what they saw on the wings. I clarified my question. Did they see anything in the cabin? Smoke or other signs of heat / fire? They did not. On final to XXC we were number 2 to land when an aircraft reported a bird strike. Tower told the aircraft ahead of us to go around. I asked tower about the bird strike and they told me to expect a low approach. I made the decision to land despite the possibility of bird remains. I felt that was the safer course of action. First Officer agreed. We landed. I had instructed the flight attendants to inform me if the conditions worsened otherwise we would taxi to a gate. [Airport response] services followed us to the gate and inspected the interior with an infrared camera and didn't find any sources of heat. Due to no airflow onboard and the temperature rising in the cabin we deplaned. All passengers were grateful for a safe return.As a crew we worked together, kept each other calm and controlled. We communicated well and I'm grateful for the professionalism each member of the crew displayed to have a successful outcome to this event.
1810831: We were given an ILS clearance into ZZZ in VMC conditions. A VFR airplane was at our altitude and seemed to be tracking to cross the final approach course. We both had the aircraft in sight and changed to a visual approach to maneuver behind the aircraft. At that point the airplane made a sharp right turn and we had to turn further right (away from the final approach course) to maintain separation. It seemed like the plane was on a long final for ZZZ1 and we were then at 90 degrees off of the final approach and unable to make a stable approach into ZZZ. We called the go-around with Tower and were given a heading and altitude toward the east before switching to Approach Control to come back and try it again.The main issue was the VFR traffic no one was communicating with. The crew did not fully brief the location and potential for conflicting traffic for ZZZ1 when approaching from the south. Had the crew not changed to a visual approach and been given ATC vectors, we may not have had the same issues. A go-around may not have been avoidable due to conflicting traffic but a more thorough brief of the airspace and threats may have increased situational awareness and avoided confusion. We should also have not changed the type of approach at the last minute. We were given a heading to intercept the localizer to Runway XXL and given a traffic call that was not on frequency. Controller then had us maintain heading and fly through the localizer to avoid traffic which was about 500 ft. above, crossing our path and that of the localizer track. We decided as a crew that if they gave us clearance for the visual, we could maintain separation from the aircraft into ZZZ. We were given just that and made the right turn back towards the runway and began to descend for landing. The general aviation aircraft ahead of us descended into our path and made an unexpected turn as we were continuing. I disconnected the autopilot and continued the turn towards the east to avoid ZZZ3 airspace and aircraft. Once clear of the aircraft, we elected to scrap the approach and were given vectors for another uneventful approach. We were originally on a 5 mile final to Runway XYR when ZZZ swapped runway configuration and we were then rerouted to the south to land north. We briefed the new approach and had the approach loaded and armed. With the change of runways, perhaps there was not enough time to fully brief the new approach and surroundings to point out a runway to the east that could cause some confusion. Some cumulative fatigue was present, as well as it being our third of four legs for the day added to the stress of the situation. I do think the spacing given into ZZZ was a partial factor with a GA aircraft that wasn't talking to anyone. There are steps to help mitigate issues like this, like ensuring complete situational awareness of self and the possibility of others, but ultimately there might always be general aviation aircraft out there operating around controlled airspace's not on frequency.
1810836: Landed without a locked nose gear. Heading into ZZZ, I did the before landing flow and put the gear handle down. The gear lights only indicated 2 green mains and the red unlocked light with no nose gear indication. Seconds after the lights illuminated for both the Left and Right Hydraulic Flow. I informed Tower I needed to break off my approach for a gear indication issue and troubleshoot. They gave me a heading and altitude then sent me to approach. Approach gave me vectors while I troubleshot. I performed the landing gear will not extend hydraulically checklist. Part of the checklist is to pull the emergency gear extension handle, I did so briskly and without twisting the handle. The indications did not change and I did not hear or feel a thump. I then pulled even harder on the emergency gear handle and braced myself by putting my feet on the floor then tried again and still no response. I finished the checklist then read through the next checklist to land with defective gear. I called approach and said my checklist was unsuccessful. I asked to return to ZZZ and told them there was no indication for the nose gear, and [advised ATC]. They brought me around for [Runway] XX, I ran through the checklist multiple times to ensure I had the procedure down, then left the book open. I landed softly and held the nose off for as long as possible. Performed the ground evacuation checklist then shut everything off and got out.
1810850: Arrived at aircraft. I reviewed the Aircraft Maintenance Logbook (AML) to verify what I had already reviewed on my IPAD. The aircraft had three MEL's: Auto-brakes inoperative, Auto speed brakes inoperative, and External power inoperative. I then found an open write up for the Anti-skid system, and called maintenance to address the issue. (This was the first flight of the day, aircraft was in ZZZ all the previous night).Maintenance arrived, and I showed them the open write-up and gave them the logbook. I then discovered that the B system hydraulic was at 69% with RF displayed. I again called maintenance to address this issue. The technician showed up and filled the system to 88%. I told the technician that I did not put the discrepancy in the AML, and if he wanted me to, I would get the AML from the other maintenance technicians and make an appropriate entry. He said, it's okay. We then pressed on with the other issues. I never made a HYD B low" entry into the AML. Upon landing ZZZ1 and accomplishing our post flight duties, I again noticed that hydraulic system B was at 69% with the RF displayed. I made an AML entry and called Maintenance Control regarding the issue. I then left the aircraft and debriefed the oncoming Captain on all of the above issues. I later called the oncoming Captain and was told that during trouble shooting in ZZZ1, a hydraulic leak was discovered in one of the wings.With the many MEL's and the newly discovered maintenance issues, I failed to make an AML entry regarding the low system B hydraulic quantity prior to having it serviced. I also allowed it to be serviced without an AML entry.Suggestions: Maintenance could clear MEL's on overnights and service low fluid quantities. They could also investigate low fluid quantities that are out of the ordinary."
1810893: Taxiing out of ZZZZ we called the advisory frequency, we were told there was no inbound traffic and we were cleared to back taxi. It's about a 3,500 foot taxi to the end and roughly 1,000 feet from the end my First Officer points out what seems to be a Citation on a visual left base. We advise the VFR tower that there was an aircraft on final for our runway. Both the tower and ourselves attempted to tell the aircraft to go-around and failed. At this point there is brush and trees lining both sides of the runway and there was no turn off. I pull the aircraft to the right edge of the runway in event that he continued the landing. At an estimated 100 feet, the aircraft was seen adding power and retracting the gear. We advised the tower that we were clear of the conflict and we continued our departure.Suggestions: VFR island flying training or VFR plates to advise of traffic flows to certain airports.
1810904: Upon landing, we were advised by Ramp control that our gate was occupied and to have Ground Control hold us off of the gate. Ground Control cleared us to taxi north on [taxiway] 1 from 2, make a u-turn in the pad, and then hold short of 3 on 4. We did so and were the third aircraft in line. A B737 was first and an E-175 was second. After a while, the E-175 was cleared to his gate and made a hard right to get out of line and proceeded to his gate. Because the Captain was on the radio with Operations and I was on the radio with Ramp Control, we did not immediately move away to close the gap left by the departing E-175. Upon completion of our radio calls, the Captain dropped the parking brake and began slowly moving forward to close the gap between us and the B737 that was now the first aircraft in line. I noticed Aircraft Y coming from my right at a higher than normal rate of speed but was initially convinced that he was cutting through the pad and would be turning south on taxiway 5 to form a second line of aircraft holding short of 3.Both the Captain and I realized at the same time that the Captain of Aircraft Y was trying to squeeze between us and the B737 ahead. The Captain hit the brakes hard enough to make the aircraft stutter to a stop. Had we not noticed Aircraft Y and the Captain of my aircraft not hit the brakes, it is possible that the left wingtip of Aircraft Y that was rapidly cutting in line might have come across our flight deck window. We were both stunned. No clearance had been given for that aircraft to squeeze between us and the aircraft ahead of us. No heads up had been given on either the Ground Control frequency or the ramp frequency to alert us that he was going to try and squeeze in ahead of us. In my over 20 years of flying for an airline, I have never before seen such a reckless move and it is the closest I have ever come to an aircraft accident. I have thought about this for the past 22 hours and cannot for the life of me think of anything that would cause a pilot to think that taxiing in this manner was safe, a good idea, or in the best interest of anything I know about the safe operation of an aircraft and the protection of the passengers in one's care. I cannot speak for the mindset of the Captain in Aircraft Y. I cannot think of anything that would cause me to operate an aircraft in this manner and therefore have no idea what to suggest. Our gate was occupied, so we were instructed to get in line on the taxiway behind a company aircraft. During this time, the line began to move and I taxied forward. Another company Aircraft Y approached at a fairly high taxi speed and cut in front of us. I was able to stop in time after realizing where they were planning to go. If I had not seen them, their wing would of hit the front of our aircraft. We had switched off ground frequency to get an update on our gate. I returned to the frequency and asked what that was. I believe Aircraft Y answered that there was no room at the end of the line (the reason for cutting in front of us). Later, I asked the Ground Controller what their flight number was, and I was told 'Snitches get stitches'. I asked the Controller if I heard them right and Controller responded that it was a joke. I responded that I didn't think it was funny, I took it as a threat, and asked for the Tower phone number. I believe Aircraft Y taxied in front of us not knowing with certainty that we would see them. They did something that could of potentially damaged aircraft or injured persons. I can't speak for the crew of flight Aircraft Y or why they thought that was good practice and safe to do. As far as my crew, I don't believe there was anything we could of done to change the outcome. As far as the Ground Controller, I believe by what Controller said, Controller saw what had happened and didn't intervene. This created the possibility of two aircraft colliding on the ground. Instead, I believe, Controller thought the best course of action was to make a joke out of the situation.
1810906: First Officer's landing. After touchdown and roll out to the end, we were issued taxi instructions while still on the runway and during transfer of control from FO to Captain for taxi. I heard taxi Alpha to the gate which I read back. As we turned across the hard stand for gate X from Alpha the controller informed us we had been instructed to taxi Alpha Fox. [The cause was] Task saturation. Controllers should not issue taxi instructions until clear of runway. Busy airports should have a standard and understood initial taxi route so that you have time to clear the runway and listen to further instructions. Maybe they could be depicted on the approach plate or in the airport diagram or the controller could issue with landing clearance. On the landing roll out while we were transferring controls we were issued a taxi clearance to gate X. The Captain still had the radios as we were decelerating through about 80 knots. He responded to the radio call and I can clearly remember him saying taxi to the gate via Alpha. There was no correction from ATC so we taxied to the gate. As we crossed the ramp area the Controller advised us the instructions were Alpha Echo Foxtrot. We apologize and proceeded to the gate with no further issues.The inability to hear the controllers instructions clearly at a busy time in the landing roll out combined with the lack of correction by ATC when our read back was incorrect. In the future I will restate the instructions from ATC once I have the radios on the ground after the roll out is complete. I will also plan not to respond the ATC during task saturation like this.
1810918: After gate arrival the flight attendants reported a strong odor like 'dirty socks' on descent. They said it started in the aft cabin and progressed throughout the cabin. No odor was noted on the flight deck.
1810920: On arrival at ZZZ, winds were variable and began to favor Runway XX for landing. We were set up for landing on Runway XY. I, acting as Pilot Monitoring for this leg due to special qualification airport, suggested to Captain that we swap our planned arrival runway due to winds and additional available landing distance (approximately 500 feet) for landing on Runway XX. The FMC was reprogrammed correctly, briefed, and we accepted a heading to intercept final Runway XX. With approximately a 30 degree intercept, approach control cleared us for the ILS XX. Captain selected approach mode early. This caused the aircraft to capture a false glideslope and the aircraft began a descent prior to capturing the localizer. I called this to the Captain's attention, of which he was also aware.Prior to localizer capture I recommended a discontinued approach. Altitude was well above Minimum Safe Altitude and the approach was salvageable but due to my experience level in the jet, I suggested a soft go-around. The Captain elected to continue, to which I agreed and remarked that our subsequent protected altitude would be 2,600 feet, which we were currently above, and that I would monitor. The Captain, slightly flustered about the false glideslope capture began to fiddle with Auto Pilot disconnect, Flight Director reset, and approach mode was re-armed. The new capture mode now is LOC but with a failed Glideslope. The aircraft has defaulted into the current vertical speed. I call slightly below glideslope, Captain again resets Auto pilot, Flight Director, and re-arms the approach mode. Localizer captures, Glideslope has been armed, and we are currently in a 700 to 800 FPM descent, very slightly low on Glideslope, at a safe speed, and safe altitude.I call attention to our protected Final Approach Fix altitude and glideslope intercept at ZZZZZ 2238 feet. If I remember correctly, we were approximately 3 miles from ZZZZZ when I remarked that at our current Flight Path Angle would have us slightly below our target altitude without any correction at ZZZZZ. Let me be clear, the aircraft was, based on our current descent rate, projected to be only slightly below 2,300 feet at the Final Approach Fix. A minor correction would have rectified the approach path angle and captured the glideslope. I called our altitude to the Captains attention once more approximately 1 to 2 miles prior to ZZZZZ, where we had now reached 2,300 feet, the charted approach value. Right as I was going to call for the Go Around at ZZZZZ, the tower controller issued a Low Altitude Alert, the Go Around was called and initiated, and the aircraft was at approximately 2,100 feet, a little less than 200 feet low at the charted glideslope intercept altitude, as well as above 1,000 feet above ground.The Go-Around was accomplished without error and a subsequent ILS was flown to Runway XX without any additional complications. Upon debrief, I became aware that the Captain was unaware that he had not captured the Glideslope. I re-framed the situation for us to consider alternate action and explained my reasoning for a requested discontinued approach prior to localizer capture. I am still low time and in consolidation. I had no reason to expect that we could not become stable with glideslope capture prior to Final Approach Fix. Hindsight is exactly that and this event began and ended all within 4 miles. The Go-round was completed to qual standards with safety and stable approach criteria in mind.False glideslopes capture prior to localizer capture due to not allowing the aircraft to capture in LOC or LNAV prior to arming the approach mode. Again, I believe I was very clear about our impending altitude deviation, however I don't believe I heard any response from the Captain from 3 miles(my initial call) and 1 to 2 miles(my second que). I could be wrong. The whole event spanned a time frame of less than 3 minutes from 'looks good' to 'doesn't look so good' so I could NOT have fit many more altitude callouts in that span. Due to my low experience in the jet, I incorrectly expected a correction that I did not receive. The go around was initiated at or just seconds after the Final Approach Fix. An assumption of understanding is not the greatest way to handle approaching a go around. I do not believe I was hinting and hoping but I will be more aggressive with my descent planning awareness callouts so as not to enter into a [undesirable situation] in the future. However, the correct decision was made concerning the safe operation of the aircraft and the proper response was executed. Trip was third leg of the day. Landed from second leg at around XA:40 local and got to sleep room at XB:10L. Awakened 30 early of show time at approximately XB:40L. Weather was marginal regionally and at ZZZ. ZZZ1 was filed alternate but also monitored weather at ZZZ2 for second option. First Officer has less than 75 hours and ZZZ is Special Qual field. Identified the CFIT (Controlled Flight into Terrain) hazard, short runway, marginal weather, etc. Pre briefed the ILS XY enroute as winds were favoring that runway. Also talked about EFVS (Enhanced Flight Vision Systems) and auto land contingencies. Upon contacting ZZZ approach, they asked if we wanted ILS XX due to a wind shift. Initially decided to stick with XY but reversed the decision seconds later due to shorter usable runway on XY due to displaced threshold and winds favoring XX slightly.I was flying the approach while the First Officer set up and briefed the ILS XX. We re-accomplished the approach checklist and accepted a clearance direct to the Final Approach Fix to cross at 2,600 feet and maintain until established, cleared for the ILS. We put the 2,600 foot hard restriction at the Final Approach Fix and were navigating LNAV/VNAV. Just prior to Final Approach Fix I mistakenly selected the approach mode. The aircraft immediately intercepted what I believe was a false glide slope and begun to descend before intended. I turned off both flight directors and attempted to get the aircraft out of approach mode. The aircraft stayed in approach mode because I did not disengage the autopilot. So, after re-engaging the aircraft tracked the localizer in LOC mode and Vertical Speed with Glideslope Flight Mode Annunciation struck through as a failed mode. Realizing the error, I disconnected both flight directors and autopilot and immediately re-engaged and re-automated. At this point I believe the aircraft momentarily intercepted a glide path, and almost immediately and simultaneously with the Tower Controller realized we were about 250 feet low of the glide slope intercept altitude. We immediately performed a discontinued approach and climbed to 3,000 feet. We received vectors for another ILS XX and auto landed uneventfully.Fatigue was undeniably a root cause although not the only issue here. Flying two legs and then getting only 30 minutes opportunity to nap between legs was just a little too much for me despite 'feeling pretty good' ahead of the flight involved. In retrospect I should have used LNAV/VNAV to get solidly on the ILS final before selecting approach mode. And, also, I should have and will in the future decide to discontinue an approach as soon as any serious mode switching starts happening on the final approach. In the light of day and after a nap I know this solidly, but it is much more difficult with a foggy brain at XF:00. So, in the future, I'm going to use LNAV/VNAV more and not use APP until later in the approach. Revision of the flight pairing to allow for more rest time...even an hour nap, would help. Also, making sure to use LNAV/VNAV and protect GSIA (Glide Slope Intercept Altitude) at 1 NM prior to the intermediate fix.
1810941: After seeing my flight was delayed, I called Maintenance Control and they said they weren't able to service the hydraulic system I had written up the night before. The local maintenance didn't have the correct parts or fluid. The technician told me they were flying out the parts, fluid, and mechanics from ZZZ. I asked if hydraulic fluid was allowed to fly and they said it was fine. After the aircraft arrived and the mechanics finished servicing the aircraft, I arrived and began my preflight duties. The mechanics said they had one sealed can of hydraulic fluid and the pump tool they used to service the system. I called the on Duty Pilot and he told me it was fine as long as it was sealed and the partially used can was being left. This didn't sit right with me so I tried to find information about it in the manual. Hydraulic fluid wasn't listed but there also wasn't a phone number for the company HAZMAT specialist. I escalated the issue to the Union and they were able to find a reference in the Dangerous Goods Manual (DGM) appendix about hidden hazards. I also googled the hydraulic fluid (Mobile HyJet IV-Aplus) and found the safety data sheet listed the fluid as a Class 9 Dangerous Good. After leaving a voicemail with the Duty Pilot saying I was going to deny boarding to the fluid and equipment, the duty manager called me and asked why I was going to leave the items and that it was going to cost a lot of money to get it back to ZZZ. I referenced the DGM and they said I was good to depart.This [Hazmat violation] was either caused by ignorance of our DG policies or was negligent behavior on the part of operations. I've been told before from them that hydraulic fluid is Hazmat. They once drove 3-4 hours to another airport because of this same issue. Either way, this was a significant safety violation. A comprehensive review of DG policies and the quality of training need to happen. Either they actually didn't know or they disregarded safety policy for the sake of operational convenience. Either is scary in a 121 airline.
1810943: After leveling off at cruise and completing the cruise checklist, my FO noticed approximately 10 skydivers in close proximity to us at an altitude roughly 1,000 feet above us. We were on our assigned routine from ZZZ-ZZZ1, specially on V186 around TANNR. After noticing the jumpers he disconnected the autopilot and initially nosed down the airplane, but I instructed him to stay at altitude and the jumpers seemed to maneuver around us. We reported the jumpers to ATC and maintained physical separation until well clear. Suggest having them jump off airway.
1810944: The flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 was the third leg of our day. We had landed at XA00Z which was an hour advance of planned passenger's arrival. Our passengers soon notified us of late arrival upon which I checked to ensure we would not be affected by EDCT (Estimated Departure Time Clearance) and that weather wouldn't be a factor. I then obtained our flight clearance which included a full route meaning we weren't getting our shorter overwater route. That route would also avoid any of the approaching weather by a wide margin. I re-ran our flight plan to ensure we had adequate fuel as the new one was 110 NM longer and would slightly change winds. The original route required 3,570 lbs total including enroute burn, 45 min reserve, and alternate based on cruise altitude of FL400. No alternate was required though as destination weather was > 5000/5 for the entire day and projected to remain so. Still, we plan and carry alternate fuel anytime we have the ability to do so. I had rounded the final fuel load up to 4,000 lbs total as it's all too common flying in or out of ZZZ3 airspace and suddenly getting significantly different routing or held down below cruise altitude for a bit. That decision would prove critical in preventing a divert later in flight. We boarded passengers at XB30Z and were given taxi clearance to 30. Upon nearing the runway, we were told to taxi to the holding area and would start taxi again at XB50Z for a XB54Z release. Approaching XC00Z, we were cleared to taxi and then into position and hold where we sat for approximately 3 minutes before being cleared for takeoff. Shortly after checking in with departure, we were given a 250 kt speed restriction and then given multiple vectors 90 degrees off of route. During most of this we were held below 15,000 ft. After being cleared back onto our flight plan, we were step climbed 6 times until we reached FL 330 about 30 minutes into the flight. During this time we also had to request deviations for weather. A slight left deviation would've allowed us to safely clear all the weather even at the lower altitude, but all aircraft were being directed that right was the only choice. Based on what traffic we had directly in view and on TCAS, it didn't make sense as it looked clear with all possible conflicts being to the west. We attempted to work right but even with significant deviations directly westward we were going to be boxed in by cells. Both NEXRAD and our onboard radar indicated yellow to red echoes well above our current altitude. We and other aircraft at higher altitudes continued to request eastward deviations and were denied. We also repeatedly requested higher as that would've been a satisfactory way of being able to comply with what they needed, but again were denied. At this point, I told the ZZZ3 Center controller that we had no choice but to go left as there was no place we could safely penetrate the weather. They finally relented and after a short deviation that was within 2-3 NM east of the course line, we were around it and back on flight plan. I was prepared to declare pilot authority to deviate for safety of aircraft, passengers and crew had they not. Between the additional ground time, ATC vectors, deviations, and hold down, we had eaten significantly into the additional fuel and were showing below a 45 min reserve if we remained at the lower altitude. This was even after seeing the deteriorating fuel state early and slowing down significantly from cruise speed to M.65. After again requesting further climb and being denied, I declared minimum fuel. Instead of the controller acknowledging, we were shifted to the next controller. Upon checking in, we were still held down and told to expect some time before climb. I again interjected on the radio that we were minimum fuel which was acknowledged by the new controller by him stating, 'uh..ah...well, ok.' He then stated we wouldn't get any further climb until with ZZZ4 Center. By that time we would be over State andstill at FL330 just over an hour into flight. The PM and I evaluated the fuel state and knowing the potential ATC delays we could face in ZZZ1 area airspace despite the great weather that we may be facing a divert. I kept our home base of ZZZ5 and ZZZ6 in mind should that be required. We set 1,000 lbs as an acceptable, safe fuel state needed to both put us above minimum fuel and give us some additional in the event of further delays. After ensuring ZZZ4 Center knew of our fuel state, we were held down for nearly another 10 minutes and then stepped 4 times from FL330 to FL400. After reaching FL400, we pulled back to M.67 and finally saw 1,100 lbs overhead destination and decided to continue. I considered requesting FL430, but based on less tailwind and the increased burn to climb I decided it wouldn't be beneficial. Fuel state improved to 1,280 lbs as the winds shifted and thanks to a small shortcut by Center. During decent with ZZZ4 Center, we were turned roughly 120 degrees off the arrival and it wasn't until questioning the controller if he knew that we had declared that he stated no and turned us back towards ZZZ1. Even though I had never rescinded the previous declaration, it apparently had not been passed to some of the subsequent ATC sectors. I told the controller that we were currently above min fuel but would not continue to be with continued vectors away from destination. We were shortly passed off to the approach controller and landed uneventfully from the RNAV XX. Final fuel state at shutdown was 1,145 lbs.Our passengers being on time might have alleviated some of this as weather had not moved onto our route at that time. More fuel would've have also created more pad, but the additional alternate fuel that wasn't required by regulation or the situation plus additional contingency fuel should've been more than sufficient to prevent it. Getting held down well below planned cruise altitude until almost halfway through a 2.5hr flight is pretty uncommon but played the biggest role in this.
1810948: After departing we were flying the ZZZZZ departure. At around ZZZZZ1 intersection on the departure, at approximately 18,000 feet, the Captain (Pilot Flying) called the transition, followed by ATC giving us a frequency change. As I (Pilot Monitoring) looked down on the aisle stand to change the radio frequency, I heard the Captain say something while there was a sharp right rolling movement of the aircraft. I looked up and saw a red AUTOPILOT disconnect EICAS message, and the Captain with his hands on the control wheel. I had assumed that we had experienced wind shear, being in the terrain that we were located. After the Captain appeared to have the situation under control, I asked the Captain if he wanted me to report the incident, to which he replied yes. I reported to the controller that we had hit a strong gust on departure, which he acknowledged. The Captain then said something along the lines of did you see that? We almost hit a glider. He had disconnected the autopilot and rolled the aircraft to avoid the glider.I believe I said, is that what happened, to which he said yes. I can't remember my verbiage, but I believe I then reported to ATC that we had almost hit a glider. ATC acknowledged, and then passed along to the aircraft behind us the information. At no point did we receive any type of TCAS alert, nor any warning from ATC about a target in the vicinity. After that last transmission to ATC during which the incident happened, we switched frequencies and continued on with the flight uneventfully. Later when we were over the ZZZ track, we spoke to the aircraft behind us but they said they had not seen the glider. Looking back with hindsight, I should have reported the incident to the controller by saying, 'I wish to report a near-midair collision.' I cannot say enough about Captain's quick thinking and airmanship to bank away from that glider and avoid what would have potentially been an air disaster. During climbout from ZZZ on the ZZZZZ departure at an altitude of about 17,500 feet we encountered a glider. The Pilot Flying turned off the autopilot and banked right to avoid a possible collision. This event occurred just as we were given a frequency change to Departure Control. At no time during this event was there any traffic depicted on the TCAS nor was there any traffic alerts given by ATC. The Pilot Monitoring passed this information to the controller before switching to our new frequency.
1810952: Departing Munich, we were given a push clearance that said, after the crossing Medium Transport aircraft, cleared to push to face north. This was relayed to the push-crew and acknowledged. Push commenced shortly thereafter. We couldn't see, but assumed the Medium Transport passed. A brief time later, Apron control asked us to stop our push, which was relayed to me and the me to the push-crew (there was the lift tug driver and another person on the headphones). I allowed a reasonable amount of time to transfer the stop, but they kept on pushing. I asked them again to STOP the push. The person on the headset seemed confused. I again told them to stop the push, stop the push. The push slowed but never stopped and then began to pick up pace. I then with louder, more stern voice told them to STOP, HALT THE PUSH, figuring the German stop command might do the trick. Nope, the push just continued. After we came to a stop on the start spot, I asked him if he understood what STOP meant - he was flustered. I overheard the FO talking to apron trying to convince them that we had told the push crew to stop multiple times. They mentioned it was a reportable event, hence the filing. This is very rare for Munich or any German airport. I am convinced, this was purely a language issue and the gentleman on the headset did not understand the bigger picture. The tug driver was also dependent on what he told him and I don't think he was aware of what was going on either. Upon receiving our push clearance Ramp control instructed us to wait for an aircraft to taxi by, then push. This was relayed to the push-crew, and they immediately began to push. Ramp control instructed us to stop, as the aircraft we were supposed to wait for had not yet passed by. The Captain instructed the push-crew to stop and had to tell them several times, before they would stop. When they did stop, they just paused and began to push again. This happened, I recall about 3 times, and ramp control kept instructing us to stop, but we could not get the push-crew to do so. The push-crew eventually just pushed us all the way back, contrary to our instructions to 'halt.' No explanation was given, as to why they would not stop. Ramp Control informed us of our deviation, and their intention to write a report regarding this. We gave them our apologies and explanation that the push crew was not following our directions to stop as they requested.
1810963: Departed ZZZ 4L in windy gusty conditions with a normal takeoff. Passing approximately 500 feet, a Rudder Ratio EICAS caution message appeared. I followed the QRH procedure after doing the 'after takeoff' checklist. This procedure stated: Above 160 knots avoid large or abrupt rudder inputs, Crosswind limit is 15 knots, Do not autoland. I made a maintenance write up and we continued. Climb was in IMC with light chop since there was a weather system moving into the east coast.Approximately an hour and half into the flight at FL340 received a Cabin Alt EICAS warning along with Cabin Altitude light and aural warning. We performed the immediate actions: Donned the oxygen masks and established crew communication. I followed the Cabin Altitude checklist and when I came to the decision tree: Cabin altitude is controllable (I switched to the other alt controller without any change) or Cabin altitude is uncontrollable, I felt that I was in between the two since the cabin was slightly above 10,000 feet and HOLDING STEADY. I advised ATC and asked for a lower altitude to the mid 20,000 feet thinking the cabin would decrease below 10,000 feet. I was also reluctant to go any lower because there was weather and turbulence below us. I called the purser and asked if the cabin oxygen masks had dropped and she informed that they had not confirming that cabin altitude never got above 14,000 feet. The cabin altitude decreased below 10,000 but the EICAS message was still illuminated so I asked for lower again. Passing 20,000 feet the Cabin Alt warning went out and the cabin showed approximately 6,000 feet so I elected to stop at FL190. This kept us right above the weather with the FO deviating around the tops.I informed the purser of the situation and made a preliminary PA. Contact with Dispatch was next with Maintenance Control on the line. Maintenance Control was not able to rectify our situation so the Dispatcher and I started looking for a divert airport. Due to the weather and the cross-wind limit of 15 knots due to the Rudder Ratio issue I was very limited in airport selection since the cross winds were in excess of 15 knots in ZZZ1, ZZZ2, ZZZ3, ZZZ, ZZZ4. ZZZ5 was the only option with calm winds, 400 Feet broken, 3 MI visibility and rain.I made the decision to divert to ZZZ5 with dispatch concurrence. I informed the purser and made another PA.We began planning for landing into ZZZ5 and was told of moderate turbulence ahead. I seated the flight attendants. Approaching the IAF for [Runway] XXL ATC informed us of an aircraft ahead of us Going Around since they were unable to see the runway at mins. I inquired about XXR and was told there was another aircraft on approach for that runway. That aircraft landed and we proceeded to a normal landing. Fire and rescue greeted us and after getting the all OK we taxied uneventfully to the gate.
1811004: Planned fuel was 6,040 and got fueled to 6,200. We took off with roughly 6,000 pounds of fuel and minimum fuel was 5,564. So we left with well above minimum required fuel according to release. We were enroute and about halfway to 2/3 of the way through as I monitored our fuel burn. I noticed based on current conditions at that time (winds aloft were greater than planned and ATC requested Mach .77 or greater while .76 is planned), that we would be about 700 pounds under planned landing fuel. So as a crew we quickly setup for long range cruise and contacted ATC that we needed to slowdown even though they insisted we maintain a high speed. So we slowed to Mach .63 for long range cruise and then ATC descended us to 27,000 feet from 31,000 feet starting down early because we were slower than surrounding traffic.Then we get instructions shortly after to change arrivals keeping us away from other traffic. Once we finally got situated with the changes, dispatch beat me to notifying them and sent us an ACARS asking about the route changes and fuel. So we told them current plan and situation and based on the information back from dispatch, we had sufficient fuel as long as we maintained LRC (Long Range Cruise speed) to ZZZ allowing us to land with just 100 pounds of fuel more than planned and dispatch had us landing at roughly 1,850 pounds. At some point ATC also queried us asking about why we would be taking off with less fuel than we need to do the flight, even though we didn't. We actually took off with more fuel than planned. ATC was actually being unprofessional about the whole thing and giving us a hard time, because we asked to slow down to conserve fuel as stated over the radios in order to avoid getting into a bad fuel situation later or having to declare minimum fuel, and then he put us on different arrival and etc. It just created more workload and pressure by his attitude and questions as if it was our fault than it needed to be and ATC did not help with that even though they're there to help us.He made us sound bad on the radio as if we didn't know what we were doing about our fuel. Then sometime later while setting up for new arrival, ZZZ does a runway change as well after we got our LDR (Landing Distance Required) and brief, so that added more workload trying to update everything and re-brief in addition to ACARS taking longer than usual to respond. During all of that, Center then instructs us to level at 19,000 feet after getting the first descend via due to VFR traffic at 17,500 feet! After traffic passes Center then gives us descend via again with immediate handoff to Approach in the same transmission. So First Officer does the handoff while I'm assessing and starting down seeing how quick we need to descend. I saw we needed to do 6,000 feet or more a minute in order to meet the crossing restriction. I knew that wasn't going to happen so right as I was going to tell First Officer to let ATC know we can't make the restriction because of the level off earlier due to traffic as he was checking on, Approach immediately on initial contact asked if we would make the crossing restriction and we said no.He immediately then got upset and asked if we told the previous controller who would be Center and we said no because we didn't have time as we literally just switched and got the clearance at the same time and literally a few seconds later discovered we couldn't make it work. So we explained that to Approach but he wasn't accepting that and blamed us for not making the restriction or notifying Center before talking with Approach. But we literally had no time between the clearance and handoff at the same time and during the frequency switch that's when we noticed the issue and first transmission with Approach we weren't given the time to tell him that before he asked and queried us. So Approach then gives us two small delay vectors and rejoin arrival. But Approach said we should've told them early on we couldn't make itbut again we explained the situation and that we were not given that chance to do so. So we then continued on after that with no further issues.Insufficient fuel planning on release as it never reflects the actual fuel burn since release doesn't account for delay vectors or vectors on approach. The issues with ATC and last second changes to arrival and runways were a result of not having enough fuel at normal cruise followed by slow ACARS affected our ability to fly the planned arrival causing a higher workload for us and ATC which then caused the hiccup with crossing restrictions and with crossing traffic as well. For fuel, we slowed for LRC and got a couple shortcuts once on the banker arrival. We were able to gain most of our fuel back because of LRC and landed with 2,200 pounds. For the crossing restriction, we just explained the situation to ATC and along with Center, Approach gave us a hard time and we notified them we couldn't do it, then we carried on with no further issues after that.For fuel planning and fuel contingency, we should be doing a minimum of like 500 pounds and 750-1,000 pounds extra on IFR days. Also for holding fuel, that should be 600 pounds minimum as we realistically burn more than 400 pounds on a go-around on a VFR day. As far as ATC goes after discussing with my First Officer as the situation that unfolded after another as a result, we maybe should have declared Minimum fuel early on knowing we wouldn't have enough unless we slowed down. But because of LRC and little to no delay vectors we determined to have enough hence why we never declared. However, if we declared min fuel early on that would've maybe given ATC more understanding even as frustrating as it may be, and allow us priority to slow and not have to descend via and etc. And that maybe would've avoided the issue with crossing at ZZZZZ1 and etc. One thing led to another, so next time maybe declare min fuel and decline a descend via to stay up high longer and to reduce workload. It was a good learning experience except for lack of professionalism and help from ATC.
1811005: While being vectored for the visual approach to runway XX at PHL the captain noticed a white drone pass along the left side of the aircraft. Captain observed drone pass the left side of aircraft. Unknown person operating drone near aircraft. Notified ATC. Suggestions: More closely monitor the position of drones in relation to aircraft. On Approach to XX in PHL a drone flew past the aircraft. It was at 5,000 feet, straight and level and heading westbound. I saw it pass off the left side of the aircraft. It didn't cause us to change course or altitude. Suggestions:Be aware of drones by airports. Second trip in a row now.
1811010: We departed on a Class II international trip. The previous day (with a different Second in Command), we had tested the HF radios by receiving a time hack on the WWV atomic clock HF frequency. We had a good operations check and assumed the HF radios were working properly. The day of the trip, we again tested the HF by receiving a time hack on the ground, however, we could not transmit on the primary and secondary frequencies at the time due to our close proximity to the FBO hangars. After departing and prior to coast-out, the Second in Command (SIC) (also an experienced Captain who happens to have a lot of experience with HF in the military) attempted to test the HF radios using the Primary Frequency and a Secondary frequency while I flew the plane and managed the VHF radios. Prior to coast-out, the SIC determined that the HF radios were not transmitting. We reviewed the Operations Manual to make sure we were operating the HF radio properly and to make sure we weren't missing anything. We determined that we were operating it accordingly and that we had tried everything we could in order troubleshoot the problem. We briefly discussed our contingency options again prior to coast-out (including returning to our departure airport) and informed Center of the issue. Center informed us that there was a flight right behind that we could relay our position with until we got back in radar contact. After that, there would be a southbound flight that was paralleling our course that would relay for us until we reached our destination.After discussing this with ZZZ Center, the controller also assured us that this was a legal option. We made radio contact with the relaying flight on the VHF air-to-air frequency. After we were confident we could continue to communicate and relay, the SIC and I again discussed our options and contingencies and we both elected to continue. We relayed our positions successfully until we reached ZZZ Center on VHF again. Our next contingency plan was that if we couldn't relay with another flight we would divert as ATC did not have any northbound traffic for us to relay with in order to return state-side. During this time, we briefed the passengers on the possibility of [diverting]. I transferred the controls to the SIC so that he could fly while I coordinated with ATC, relayed our position, plotted our course, and kept up with the NavLog in an effort to reduce each other's workload. He had worked hard attempting to troubleshoot the HF radios, meanwhile having me manage the radios and navigation allowed me to handle the lost HF event. Once talking to ZZZ Center, we made VHF contact with the southbound flight and we were confident that we could continue relaying position reports, we elected to continue to our destination via relay.We recorded each waypoint along the route on the NavLog and plotting chart, and successfully relayed each one. The other flight in turn would verify that each reporting point was received by ATC. Once we were within range of ATC, we contacted via VHF, they confirmed radar contact, we again exchanged the flight controls (I resumed pilot-flying duties and the SIC resumed pilot-monitoring duties) and we continued the rest of the way to our destination on VHF radios in the radar environment. The rest of the flight was uneventful. After deplaning our passengers at the destination, I called Maintenance Control to create a write-up and MEL the HF radios. The MEL restricted us to VHF communication. The log was completed and the MEL was complied with. My next call was to Operations to inform them of the issue and restrict the aircraft to 'Class 1 navigation only' until maintenance could fix the HF radios. The remainder of our scheduled trips were within radar service areas, so there were no additional operational issues concerning the HF radios and the MEL. As a side note, despite being a stressful situation, I believe the SIC (another Captain) and I handled the situation quite well all thingsconsidered. We communicated, risk assessed, and split duties effectively. If ATC hadn't assured us this was a legal option (it sounded like we weren't the first one to have this problem) or other flights had not been willing or able to help us relay our position, then we would have definitely had to have returned to our departure airport or diverted after burning off a bunch of fuel to get the plane below landing weight.These HF radios probably have not been exercised in over a year due to COVID-19 international travel restrictions and lack of Class II flying. While we did test the HF the previous day by receiving a time hack, we did not check the transmit function of the HF radios. We checked the HF radios reception the previous day by receiving the time hack, however, we did not test the transmit function of the radio. Checking the transmitter the day before would have allowed us to MEL the HF earlier and prevent this trip from occurring on this tail number. Also I would recommend that as we continue to develop training scenarios as part of our recurrent training programs, that we include Class II navigation scenarios to supplement that training. In a normal year (without pandemic-level travel restrictions), we don't individually get to perform very many Class II trips. I believe including Class II training scenarios, including what to do during lost-comm events as well as other emergencies such as single-engine failure, depressurization, and medical emergencies), would be extremely beneficial in building decision-making processes in a Class II environment. During the departure, I told the PIC that I would conduct the FMS navigation check and the HF check. The FMS navigation check was conducted almost immediately using a VOR. The HF check was another story. On deck at departure airport, I was having issues getting a radio check on the ground with ZZZ Radio, but after discussing with maintenance, we collectively thought it was interference from the hangars right at the ramp. An air check was required. We could hear the HF clock on 10000 MHz but just could not raise ZZZ Radio.As the departure airport is very close to the ocean, we coasted out as I was attempting to get the HF to work. Both HF radios seemed to be having a common issue with transmitting, this despite being able to hear intermittently HF traffic. I was able to tune the radios but continued to fail in any contact with ZZZ Radio. (HF1 seemed to not electronically tune as I pressed to transmit, HF2 seemed to tune pressing transmit, but no one could receive). While the PIC flew the plane (and spoke with ATC), I continued to trouble shoot the radios exhausting all system knowledge. We even pulled the manual out to make sure I was not missing anything.During my troubleshooting of the radios, the PIC was provided an option from ATC of relay with other aircraft. Specifically, there was another aircraft very close by our position. The other aircraft pilots agreed to take our HF relay if we needed that option. At this point, I reported to the PIC that our HF radios were failed. We were pretty much at the final fix prior to HF operations (20 minutes after takeoff). We both discussed the options prior to committing to the HF relay. We could turn around and head back. We could relay with other aircraft. We could also pick up another relay that could take us all the way down (or perhaps back to ZZZ if we wanted that option). We decided to continue with company to keep the flight going safely. The clients were kept informed. ATC was kept completely in the loop.As we entered radar control, ATC called to tell us that there were no northern flights that could help us get back but there was an Air Carrier flight which was willing to relay HF the remaining way. Since the remaining oceanic airspace had 3 more fixes, we decided that this was a safe option allowing us to keep the mission on track. With ATC facilitation, we contacted the flight while in radar control and established the link for our HF relay. The HF relay with the Air Carrier took us into ATC airspace. The rest of the flight was uneventful. Primarily, we both felt comfortable that we could continue to our destination safely. Secondly. This HF teaming, thanks to ATC, [and other flights] allowed our passengers to get to their destination with all the COVID restrictions compliances intact for their entry (a significant travel issue). Cause, aging equipment. I am not sure that this HF failure can be avoided. Perhaps we need to do more checks of our equipment and keep them at a higher standard of repair and readiness.
1811016: Emergency deplaning at Gate X after passengers were all boarded, initiated by flight attendants due to extensive smoke in the cabin. As passengers were being rushed off the aircraft it was determined that a passengers Lithium Ion iPhone battery overheated and was the cause of all the smoke. All passengers safely deplaned through the front entry door to the terminal. ARFF (Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting) called by flight crew. ZZZ flight attendants did an outstanding job handling the emergency deplaning![Smoke was caused by] overheated Lithium Ion powered passenger Iphone.No way to know if a passenger's iPhone spontaneously starts to combust. Emergency deplaning at the Gate X. Plane was fully boarded. Deplaning was initiated by the flight attendants due to excessive smoke in the cabin. During the deplaning the #1 Flight Attendant notified us that the smoke was caused by a Lithium Ion battery on a cell phone. All the passengers deplaned to the terminal. We called airport Fire Department and Ops to tell them of the situation. The flight attendants did an excellent job in their duties and in handling the emergency deplaning.The phone overheating was out of our control. The flight attendants did as they were trained. We as a cockpit assisted them and directed them as needed.I believe everything went well. Everyone did as they were trained. Training is key.
1811045: On approach to land in LAS from vectors, and cleared for the visual my Captain had just turned final at approximately 3,800 feet and was on a stable descent to land. At about 1,150 feet our RA dinged 'traffic' which indicated about 200 feet below us. We couldn't see the traffic. At 940 feet to land (3,000 AGL), we had an RA warning go off due to a helicopter. The warning was to our right. We still couldn't see the traffic, but the warning soon turned into an announcement from our aircraft systems to 'pull up' at 940 feet on the RA. My Captain immediately decided to call for a go-around and we executed the maneuver appropriately, were radar vectored back to land, chose the left runway to allow for some additional distance, and landed safely without incident.Cause - A busy weekend post COVID time when the helicopter industry was seeing a lot more activity. This particular situation was out of our control to avoid. We don't generally have issues with helicopter traffic, and in this situation at such a busy airspace, we could not disregard the RA instructions so low to the ground and at such a critical phase of flight. Considering the busy nature or the weekend and the idea we are experiencing such high post-COVID activity in Las Vegas, perhaps we as a crew could have suggested the left runway for some extra separation, but it's never been an issue in my time flying before. On visual approach fully configured turning final at approximately 3,700 feet, when rolled out on final an RA was enunciated and a subsequent go-around was performed. We returned to fly visual to the left runway with no further issues. Helicopter traffic operating too close to the active runway approach path. Either keep helicopter traffic further west or make the left the primary runway for south landing traffic.
1811113: Upon landing and arrival at gate a strong odor engulfed entire cabin. Started as a manure/organic smell then changed to chemical/sulfur type smell. Captain was notified and maintenance was called.
1811174: I was operating a flight from ZZZ to IWS with two passengers on an IFR flight plane and talking with Approach. Approach cleared me for the Visual Approach into West Houston Airport, untowered field and approved my frequency change. Before I switched to CTAF, I heard a traffic alert as Approach asked if I was still on the frequency. I heard the traffic call for crossing traffic 500 feet below me, I'm not sure what lateral separation was with the initial call. I acknowledged the traffic alert and stayed with Approach instead of flipping to CTAF.I saw that I had a nearby ADS-B target converging with my flight track and was scanning furiously for that aircraft but could not see him. The other aircraft was climbing, and was converging vertically as well as laterally. I have a low-wing aircraft and dipped the left wing and slipped to try to make visual contact but did not find it, as it was already quite a bit inside the wing in my line of sight at that point. As I saw the ADS-B track continue to converge and pulled up and right sharply to evade the target. As I did that, the other plane unmasked from behind my wing and I was able to maintain visual separation for the 10 or 15 second we were closest to each other. Approach called the traffic as no factor at the same time and I cancelled IFR with West Houston in sight as we were in VMC and set up for downwind entry overflying midfield.I explained to my passengers that we had to move the plane away from another aircraft which had failed to yield and that we were not in danger. On reflection, I should have positioned the aircraft more aggressively to drop the left wing to see the other plane earlier. I also could have immediately asked for a vector from Approach to keep me clear, although this traffic appeared to be climbing out of Dan Jones (T51) or Dry Creek (TS07) and presented a late radar contact for the traffic call.
1811182: During departure climb the airplane experienced a failure of the right engine. The prevailing environment in the cockpit promoted a breakdown in CRM (Crew Resource Management) prior, during and after the incident which led to a failure of complying with established procedures. Also, the Pilot in Command failed to declare an emergency after the engine was shut down. Although the airplane was under control the whole time and an eventual landing without incident was conducted, under different circumstances the breakdown in CRM could have led to a worst outcome.
1811204: I departed ZZZ1 bound for ZZZ as Aircraft X. After reaching cruise altitude of 8,000 feet I observed the right wing tank fuel gauge showed an increase of several hundred pounds of fuel. I then observed that the filler cap for the right tank stuck BELOW the right wing attached to its lanyard with fuel being vented from the fill opening. The wing tanks feed the main tanks and there was plenty of fuel to reach the destination ZZZ. I diverted with concern that spreading jet fuel over the most populous city in an environmentally conscious state might not be well received. ZZZ2 provided a close alternate over sparsely populated mountains without need to fly over the city proper.As I slowed and descended into ZZZ2 and put approach flaps down, the cap that initially dangled below the wing moved up to the top of the wing still attached to its lanyard and fuel stopped venting from the open filler hole in the tank. This was not a situation where a faulty fuel cap vented fuel 'in place'. I had 30 gallons of fuel added to the right-wing tank in ZZZ2 by an experienced fueler who opined that the cap was secure and apparently worked properly. I was not aware that I should have had a mechanic inspect the cap - and continued the flight to ZZZ in violation of company and FAA policy.
1811208: I conducted preflight in accordance with checklist and prepared for flight. Normal startup and taxi to run up ramp. Conducted run-up and everything checked out okay. Set up for normal takeoff. Pulled out onto the runway and added full power. Airplane was accelerating on center line and approximately 500 feet down the runway, the nose began to drop down. I cut power and the nose dropped to the ground and airplane came to stop near right edge of runway. Notified FBO who sent crew to assist in removing airplane from runway.
1811222: On go-around Aircraft X had a gradual loss of power which resulted in having to land in a nearby field. The airplane had been sitting (pickled) for three years a week before but had recently been flown from and to maintenance for the annual inspection (at ZZZ) and back to ZZZ1. The same day the off-field landing occurred, I had performed several landings and had no problems at all with the aircraft until this last takeoff/climbout.The RPM seemed to drop and the aircraft was not producing thrust. The engine has a massive carb heat system. Carb heat was used and possibly left on in the climbout however nobody thinks that carb heat would cause enough power loss to cause a catastrophic thrust - lift scenario in low density altitude flight conditions (sea level 65 degrees).Other issues might have been debris in the recently fueled tank, carburetor float issue and then possibly a prop governor issue. We could not reproduce the problem on the ground. So far, the issue is unknown as to the continual loss of power.In looking back at this event, I think that it would have been prudent to take a newly run aircraft that has been sitting for a while and just out of annual to a large airport where there is more room for errors. Only after several hours or days of 'testing' should you exercise an aircraft to other shorter riskier areas. You just never know what can go wrong. They say hindsight is 20/20 but I will need to take a better look at risk management when it comes to flying an aircraft that has an unfamiliar history or has just come out of hibernation and or annual inspection.
1811226: Flew to a job sprayed a field and was returning to ZZZ. Called El Paso (ELP) Tower on [my] cell phone to let them know I would be flying on the [edge] to pass through the airspace they approved. They informed me of Aircraft Y in the area. Did not visually see a helicopter. Aircraft Y saw me and said he had to take action to not get near me. The event happened west of the ELP airspace. Exiting the El Paso airspace El Paso Tower (Name) asked for my phone number just in case he needed to get in touch with me on the incident.
1811235: I was returning to my home base of ZZZ from ZZZ1. I am flying my newish Aircraft X, of which I have about 19 hours in. It should be noted that most of my flight hours are from 25 years ago. I knew ZZZ had some crosswinds but I thought they were manageable and I felt I needed to push myself a bit. If I remember, the winds were about 13 at 260 (260 at 13). Part of my challenge was that they were not reporting winds on METAR only ATIS. Upon approach the winds started gusting to 19. This would give an 8.4 kt. crosswind gusting to 12 knots, something I should be able to handle. So, on the first attempt, I think my approach was OK, but I flared high, bounced and quickly realized a go-around was the best option. Not perfect but decent decision making.The second attempt is where things went very wrong. This time I came in with 20 degrees of flaps. My approach was probably a bit fast, but seemed OK as I got closer to the airport. First of all, I flared too high again, bounced, but then made the mistake to try and salvage the landing. On the second bounce I recognized that the plane was proposing and I'd have a prop strike if I let it drop again. So, I started another go-around, but the plane would not climb, more importantly I wasn't facing down the runway but more towards the left side. At this point the helicopters parked left of the runway are getting bigger in my windshield but I know I've got to gain air speed. The one correct decision I made was to keep the nose down until I gained some airspeed. Eventually I got the speed and was able to climbout. At some point in this I realized why I couldn't climb, I had raised all of the flaps! I then came around and successfully landed the plane on the third attempt. It was bad enough that after I parked, the fire department came over to 'congratulate' me on my recovery, but I really think it was to make sure I was OK.I learned the following on this landing attempt. I need more time with my instructor with landings, especially crosswind landings. I need more practice on Go-Arounds focusing on flap management and right rudder.
1811246: After flying a practice RNAV (GPS) approach into ZZZ, I was climbing through 2,000 feet on the missed approach when I checked in with Approach. Approach provided an altimeter setting (30.12, which had changed since my last check-in of 30.11) and a few seconds later provided a heading for vectors for the ILS at ZZZ1. I leveled off at the assigned altitude of 3,000 feet and shortly after, ATC asked me to maintain 3,000 feet. Considering my altimeter was reading 3,020 feet, I knew this call meant something was not right. I scanned the instruments and saw the altimeter setting was now set to 29.92. I requested the altimeter setting again and when I entered the correct setting, I was approximately 300 feet above my assigned altitude. After landing I was able to determine the sequence of events that caused this deviation.My airplane has an Aspen Avionics Evolution 1000 PFD. I have had this for the last X years and feel I am proficient in operating it. It has a feature that, in my piston powered general aviation airplane, is not used. If you press the 'baro' button and then push the right knob, the altimeter setting will change to 29.92. Since I never climb to FL180, I have never used this feature. In this situation, when I contacted ATC, they gave me the altimeter setting, and since it was different, I pushed the 'baro' button and turned the right knob to the correct setting. When ATC then provided me a vector, I needed to move the heading bug almost 180 degrees (it had been set during the southbound approach and now I was flying northbound). Instead of spinning the heading knob (the same right knob) 180 degrees, I pushed the knob which automatically sets the heading bug to the current heading. What I didn't realize was that when I pushed the right knob, the 'baro' function was still active and therefore set the altimeter to 29.92. The heading bug also aligned to the current heading, however since I was in turbulence, I assume I bumped the knob twice instead of once. I didn't notice the change in altitude because I was in a climb. When I reached 3,000 feet, I leveled off like normal without being aware that I was higher than I should be.Moving forward I will need to be more careful and aware of what function is active in the PFD before making changes. However, my fear is that it may be another X or more years before something like this happens again and as time moves forward, we tend to forget these events. I do think this is an opportunity for Aspen to make a software revision. If this baro reset feature is meant for aircraft passing through 18,000 feet, it would be nice if this feature could be disabled for installations in aircraft that cannot reach that altitude. Alternatively, if this feature is meant for aircraft passing through 18,000 feet and it is utilized at an altitude well below that, a flashing yellow flag (similar to what happens when approaching the selected altitude) would help to visually annotate the change that was just made. I'm not trying to remove responsibility from the pilot, but the pilot has hundreds of things to remember when flying. Modern avionics should not be adding to the list of quirks that need to be remembered.
1811264: With one passenger, took off from ZZZ1, was circling the west side of [the island] intending to land back at ZZZ1. At 2,000 feet MSL, abeam ZZZ, lost 400 RPM engine power, engine got very rough, with bad vibration. Requested priority handling for Runway XX at ZZZ. Upon reaching threshold, aircraft was much too high and too fast for landing, was still at maneuvering speed from descending from cruise, made low pass and went around for another attempt at Runway XX, at about feet 200 AGL, with throttle at max power setting, and barely able to maintain altitude. Runway surface was shortened to about 2,600 feet by construction. There were two orange construction barriers, one at the end of the shortened runway length, and a second one about midway within the remaining 3,000 feet of runway closed for construction. Construction barriers were not apparent to me as such from the air. I was not able to touch down at the threshold, and touched down just beyond the first barrier, within construction area.At that point, I still did not see that the barriers were barriers (they looked like flat tarps or orange police tape on the ground). Still at high speed from rollout and heading towards the second barrier, my passenger called for me to go to the left. Steering to the left side of the runway, I passed beside the barrier, and avoided hitting it, and with full braking, came to a stop at the end of the paved surface, and shut down. Nothing was damaged, nobody was hurt, but I had barely avoided the construction barriers, made of concrete. But only on the ground and nearby are they visible as barriers. From the air they look like orange flat tarps or bags. The potential for catastrophe in the event of [a] landing is great. If construction barriers used on runways were made of soft rubber, like traffic cones, or constructed to be collapsible on impact, there would be no hazard, and they would still fulfill their purpose.On my part, my landing was poor. My speed and altitude were too high. Reducing power and using a large amount of flaps, or planning on making a downwind to Runway XY instead would have been necessary to avoid the overrun into the construction. My mindset at the time of the accident was one thing 'get on the ground in as few seconds as possible', based on training for the total engine failure scenario, where there truly is no time. This scenario was not like that, and needed essentially a normal landing procedure. A partial power loss, like this, is a more common [event] than a total complete engine failure. But the general training syllabus based on the FARs emphasizes the total engine failure scenario, almost to the exclusion of other emergencies. I thus suggest that the training syllabus mandated by the FARs be changed to put more emphasis on a partial power loss, and assessing the difference between that and a more total power loss. I intend to take a flight review in the short term, with emphasis on practice for a partial power loss, like this scenario, and being on proper approach speed for short field landings at the threshold in such scenarios. Next day, mechanic found electrodes had been bent away from contacts in both spark plugs on one cylinder, causing that cylinder not to fire. He repaired those plugs, and we did a successful ground run, and per his determination that it was fixed, I took off again, from Runway XY, at the beginning of the usable runway surface before displaced threshold, to return to home base, ZZZ2. At 1,200 feet to 1,300 feet MSL (about 400 feet to 500 feet AGL) after takeoff, the problem recurred. I did a 180, reduced power, and with flaps extended, made safe landing touching down at threshold of Runway XX, and came to a stop within the usable runway.The following day, mechanic prepared to pull the affected cylinder, whose spark plugs had been affected the same way as before, to investigate the problem. He found a small black cylindrical object, 1/4' diameter and 3/8' long, out of hard plastic or scratched metal, in the cylinder, and concluded that it was knocking against spark plug electrodes and bending them. Neither he, myself, nor FAA could identify object or its origin. Mechanic is certain it did not originate from within the aircraft, and concluded that it had to have come in through the carburetor heat intake, which is unfiltered. This is unlikely to have happened during operation as carburetor heat inlet is far off the ground. I believe a careless operator did a run-up beside where my aircraft was parked at an outside tie-down, and that run-up kicked the FOD into the carburetor heat intake. On an earlier unrelated occasion, similar carelessness caused my entire windshield to get pitted by kicked up FOD (I had to replace the windshield), making the scenario plausible as my aircraft is always tied down outside. Pilots are taught to avoid doing runups near persons or other aircraft or vehicles due to this danger. But as I cannot control the carelessness of others while I am not present, and hangaring the aircraft is unfeasible, I intend to get cowl plugs for when the aircraft is parked, to avoid this. While I don't feel that they should be mandated, perhaps the FAA needs to officially recommend them for those who must park outside. The FOD removed, I departed from Runway XY again, and this time, there were no problems, landed safely at ZZZ2. Hence, the FOD had been the cause of the engine problem.
1811273: Aircraft X departed ZZZ approximately and almost immediately returned due to low fuel situation. Upon entering the ramp the aircraft was being taxied close to 30 to 40 knots. Upon marshalling the aircraft and giving the command to stop the pilot continued to taxi albeit at a reduced speed disregarding the signal to stop and almost running over and killing me. Pilot was visibly upset and was altogether negligent about the safe operation of the aircraft and preflight check due to not doing a thorough preflight inspection and checking the fuel.
1811279: I departed ZZZ, climbed normally, received vector for a right turn to a heading of 290 and a climb to 10,000. I complied with all of the uneventfully. West of the airport was cell of precipitation that I couldn't see through. It was depicted as yellow on my weather display. The precipitation was west of the airport and oriented along the axis of about 290 to 300 west of ZZZ.I was doing the ZZZ4 departure. The tower controller advised in the initial climb that in substance that I'd be boxed around on vectors for the climb before being going to the route.A previous departed reported the ceiling at about 6,500 which was basically true. I changed frequency to ZZZ TRACON and got a heading of 290. When I entered the IMC the rain was very intense and it was turbulent. I noticed changes on the vertical speed indicator up and then later down. The temperature was near freezing, but I did not see any actual ice. While climbing in IMC, the radio frequency began to screech such that I couldn't hear anything. That ultimately occurred on both radios and both frequencies. The marker beacon lights were flashing. I received a traffic alert for traffic on my left. It was very turbulent, but I stayed at 10,000 feet as assigned. With no communications (coms), I squawked 7600.I decided to turn 90 degrees right still in IMC because that resolved the traffic, would get me out of the precipitation, was a heading basically on course, was consistent with the expectations from the departure briefing and ZZZ4, and would restore coms. The precipitation was aligned with the vector so remaining on that heading was not viable. There was traffic there. I didn't change altitude (I was at 10,000 ft. the whole time).After the right turn, I exited the side of the precipitation, I was able to hear ground responding to one of my calls (on COM2 on the bottom antenna), so I went back to the departure frequency on COM1 (on the top), re-established communications and departed.The ATC TRACON controller was upset seemed to think that I was in VMC and just turned randomly or something. I've flown through 'yellow' precipitation many times uneventfully. The lost coms procedure when you're on a vector is to either stay on the vector or turn on course. I turned on course because it solved all of the problems, but seemed to surprise ATC. I think that the confusing thing for ATC was that it was fine weather straight over the airport, which is probably what he has on his computer. But west of the airport was unexpectedly intense rain.I'm not sure that this incident could have been avoided given what everyone knew at the time, although once I squawked 7600, the turn on course shouldn't have been a surprise.
1811286: While being vectored for the visual approach at ZZZ, approximately while descending through 5,000 feet, the Amber CAS message (ENG CTRL SYS (L-R)) appeared as well as the Master Caution System light, I referenced the Manufacturers Emergency/Abnormal Checklist which dictated the first step is to reset the FADEC to the affected side, which in this case was both sides, the checklist goes on to say if the CAS message clears then no further action is required, or if the CAS message remains, to land as soon as practical. The checklist also goes on to advise of the possible effects that may be encountered, they are:- Degraded or lack of response to throttle movements including possible surging or flameout.- Possible inability to restart.- Possible inability to achieve ground idle.- Loss of automatic Interstage Turbine Temperature (ITT) limiting during ground idle.- Loss of automatic ITT limiting during ground or windmill starts.- Loss of ITT indication.The message did not clear after the reset, and given the possibility of a flameout, I chose to land ASAP, I notified ATC and requested to proceed directly to the final approach course for landing. ATC complied with my request and gave me priority.
