The landing was uneventful, but on the landing roll out, the L Engine Fail Warning CAS message came up, it distinguished about 15 seconds later, then appeared once again about a minute later during taxi and stayed on for 10 seconds then went away.Once I arrived to the ramp at the FBO I shut the engines down and powered down the aircraft with no further incident.
1811292: I experienced an electrical issue while flying through the (ZZZ SFRA). I was flying south-eastbound at 3,500 feet MSL per the procedure depicted on the ZZZ TAC chart. As I was passing directly over ZZZ and making a radio call on the air-to-air frequency to report my position, my intercom and a number of other electrical systems simultaneously failed. My radio transmission was cut short mid-sentence. Immediately thereafter I noticed a burning electrical smell. I quickly shut off the master switch to reduce the risk of an electrical fire. At this point it was clear the flight could not continue and a landing at a nearby airfield would be necessary. My home base, ZZZ1, was only 20 NM north of my current position. I elected to execute a climbing 180 degree turn to reverse course within the SFRA, north-westbound at 4,500 feet MSL. Once north of the SFRA, I remained clear of Class B, C, and D airspace, staying well west of ZZZ2 and the ZZZ3 Class C shelf. As I approached ZZZ1 from the northwest, I contacted the Tower Controller from my cell phone, and he cleared me to land. The no-flap landing was uneventful.As for lessons learned and next steps, I have a handheld radio, but the battery was unfortunately dead. I need to check this more regularly so that it can be relied upon in the event of lost comms. I've also printed out a list of ATC phone numbers in case I need to reach other facilities using my cell phone (I luckily had ZZZ1 Tower saved as a contact on my phone). I also think I should have more seriously considered descending immediately and landing at a closer airport, such as ZZZ4. By climbing to join the reverse course of the SFRA, I put myself in a more dangerous position if an inflight fire had actually developed. Additionally, I have a fire extinguisher in my airplane, but it was secured under the back seat, and I never touched it. I should have removed it from its harness and had it ready to go in case it became needed.I think it's extremely important that pilots regularly think about what they would do in these types of abnormal situations. These situations don't happen often, but when they do quick action is sometimes required to avert a real emergency. I'm lucky this occurred during a daytime VFR flight. A couple weeks ago I was flying at night in IMC on an IFR flight plan. Had this occurred then the situation would have been far more serious.
1811302: Departing from ZZZ. Initial Climb on runway heading with intention to remain in pattern. Aircraft Y was crossing ZZZ VOR before our takeoff and had announced on CTAF that he was going to cross midfield, make a teardrop entry to the left downwind for the runway. He specifically stated that he was going to enter downwind behind us. When climbing through 600 feet, I received a traffic warning from ADS-B stating that traffic (Aircraft Y) was nearly overhead with 500 feet vertical separation. Upon reaching 800 feet the traffic (Aircraft Y) was directly overhead with 300 feet vertical separation. This event caused us to temporarily suspend the climb until Aircraft Y had passed. Aircraft Y was below pattern altitude, 1,200 feet, by 100 feet when he was closest to us. This aircraft flew nearly the entire teardrop maneuver off the departure end of the runway at pattern altitude and below. Then proceeded to cut across the upwind portion of the pattern to join the downwind from the inside, rather than the intended 45-degree entry.
1811311: We began the day at XA:00, the plane had 13 gallons of fuel on the pilots side, and 11 on the other. Generally we plan for 5-6 gallons per load of jumpers. After releasing jumpers I descended down from 9,000 feet AGL a couple miles east of the airport. Under 3,000 feet AGL on a 2/3 mile straight in approach to Runway XX @ ZZZ, I continued losing altitude as plane with the throttle fully out to lose airspeed. (It was put in every couple thousand feet descending to 'clear' the engine.) When the desired speed and altitude was reached, I pushed the throttle in with no response. I enriched the mixture and pumped the throttle, and that also made no change. Checked fuel selectors, mags, etc, all with no luck. I realized the aircraft would not make the runway fairly shortly. Continuing straight in, I would have hit the side of an adobe hill.Right was rougher terrain, so left was the best option. I made an announcement on CTAF but may have been too low at that time. I navigated to the smoothest looking area i could find given the very short amount of time I had to deal with the situation. Dropped full flaps, and slowed down as best I could. The plane touched down, bounced over a few hills, and came to rest slightly upward on another hill. I exited the aircraft thru the pilots door, and looked over the plane, then called Person X to inform him of the situation and was able to text him GPS coordinates While waiting I checked the fuel level in the aircraft, and the passenger side was empty, while the pilots seemed to have about 7 gallons, however the plane was at a slight angle so could have been inaccurate.Burning 17 gallons of fuel for 3 flights is about normal. Especially considering the slightly lengthy times to climb today.
1811312: After making a left base at ZZZ call over CTAF, the R66 stated over communications they were '3 miles NE of the field', after hearing this we asked if they could see us. They replied they saw us right over them. After hearing this we decided to take evasive action and discontinue our approach and continue straight west of the field, away from the other aircraft. We did not see the aircraft until they were short final of the field. They did not adhere to standard taxi pattern procedures and came in right underneath us on our base leg. The pilot of the Robinson did not state they saw us and were number 2 for the runway or anything so we just decided to get out of their way and try again later after they were no longer a safety factor for us.
1811317: Upon safely landing I noticed that the battery had become partially dislodged during flight. Using Google search words of 'dji mavic pro 2 battery popping up' I found that multiple people have had problems and crashes due to the batteries coming out during flight. I believe this is a design flaw in the battery attachment method that could easily be corrected if the battery clip design was changed slightly, such that it provided a more captive interlocking engagement. I believe that a crash during flight, which according to various forums many people have had as a result of a battery becoming dislodged, represents a significant design safety flaw that should be corrected.
1811318: I'm writing because I have concern over the quality of the DJI Mavic Air 2. During my post flight inspection of my drone, I noticed fatigue cracking in the body of the UAV. The cracking is right around the pilot point for the front motor supports. I've done some research online and noticed that this apparently is a common problem among other DJI Mavic Air 2 operators. I did some digging and I noticed that the FAA currently doesn't regulate small UAVs, and I have concerns over the process to close any safety concerns with these manufacturers. There seems to be a gap as the FAA really would like to regulate the operations of the vehicle, but they currently don't have standards in place for the certification of the vehicles. From my perspective there needs to be some sort of regulations in place to ensure the UAVs will operate safely and the burden of airworthiness should not be bore solely by the operator, but OEMs need to take responsibility for their equipment as well. Note, that I did land without any incident, and have reached out to DJI on the matter and I will not be flying until the issue is resolved.
1811368: When I got to Aircraft X, it had a writeup for (paraphrasing) '#4 tire worn'. We were scheduled to take aircraft from ZZZ to ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 to ZZZ to ZZZ3. On our second pass through ZZZ with about five minutes to push the Ops Agent informed us of a Maintenance lock on the Release. About that same time we got an ACARS message from Dispatch saying the same thing and that it was something about a tire change. I called Dispatch and the guy answering the phone said he had tried to call Maintenance and no one answered so he would try again and let me know. I called back seven minutes later and asked to be transferred to Maintenance Control to talk to them directly. Maintenance Control said the tire was allowed only three cycles and the aircraft was 'dead' until it was changed, that it was supposed to be done the first time we went through ZZZ but somehow it didn't happen. This is five minutes before push with no one in sight to change the tire. Five minutes or so after scheduled push, a crew came out to change the tire. The guy that changed the tire took the logbook and came back about 45 minutes later with it saying we were good to go.(As an aside, I informed Maintenance Control the aircraft was coming back to ZZZ for the night and could they change it then. Maintenance said it was only good for three (3) cycles. In 15 years I've never seen a tire written up that wasn't changed immediately and the first I've ever heard that a 'worn' tire is good for only three cycles. This information would have allowed us as a crew to be more proactive to get the tire changed the first time we went through ZZZ or at least set up for the next pass through. This could have prevented over an hour delay.I looked at the logbook and saw in the lower right corner 'MTO W/O Closed' with the 'YES' circled. I didn't look for any narrative in the pink Maintenance part. That is my bad but I took MTO W/O Closed to mean the work was done. We did the 'Before Start Originating' checklist and departed without incident. I noticed a missed call and a text from the succeeding Captain about the logbook having a problem. Being out of the aircraft and in the hotel room by then, I have no way of knowing what the problem was for the logbook but apparently the Captain had to call Contract Maintenance to verify the #4 tire was changed and enter it in the logbook. The long and short of it is I may have flown an aircraft with an open writeup because of improper documentation and my ignorance in seeing that.
1811376: Prior to takeoff we had a Left GPS fail. We stopped, ran the QRH, contacted Dispatch and Maintenance and MEL 34-53-01A(C) was issued. We completed the logbook, ran our checklists and departed for ZZZ. During cruise I began to setup for the ILS approach that would be required due to low ceilings. When I switched the frequency to active, I immediately got the LOC / G/S caution flags on the primary flight display. We ran the QRH, which told us we could not do an ILS. We also could not fly an RNAV because of the GPS inop MEL. We called Dispatch and decided we would divert to ZZZ1. We continued without further incident. Here is my issue. Had part of the procedure for the GPS inop had us check other navigation systems (ILS) we would have found the ILS to have also failed. From what I understand they are part of the same (box). Could that be added to Maintenance procedures for MEL 34-53-01. Thank you.
1811457: During our taxi-out and takeoff role, the Captain and I noted a Number 1 Fuel Filter Bypass Master Caution Light. We both felt this was part of a MEL condition entered into the aircraft's ELB, but feel the MEL procedure to be both ambiguous and poorly written. The condition should not be available for ER [Extended Range] operations.During our pre-flight planning activities, the Captain and I noted a defect of 'Repeat. LH Fuel Filter Bypass warning light was on for 5 minutes' written up on the Electronic Log Maintenance Logbook (ELB). Maintenance indicated that 'Fuel Filter Signal Disagree' on EEC #1 was the actual issue causing this light to indicate. Maintenance deferred the fault by placing the #1 Fuel Filter Bypass Light on MEL 7304A.The ELB indicated that maintenance replaced the #1 engine fuel filter, did an engine idle run, and noted no gross contamination of the fuel in the filter. No further CDU faults were noted by maintenance. The number #1 engine 'Fuel Filter Bypass Light' was placarded. Upon referencing the 737NG MEL, as far as we could tell, this is all the maintenance action items that need to be completed.As for the flight crew actions to be completed for MEL 7304A, we must only assure that the:1. 'Remaining fuel filter pressure warning system must operate normally.'2. 'Maintenance is required to verify malfunction is in fuel filter bypass warning system on initial deferral.'We noted that the flight crew actions for this MEL are rather sparse: Our normal pre-flight activities would ensure that the #2 Fuel Filter Bypass Light was extinguished and maintenance indicated they performed step 2.During our pre-flight briefing the Captain and I discussed this MEL, verified that the system was not needed for ER operations - as our flight to Destination would, of course, fall under this category. Unfortunately, a complete discussion and briefing about this item may have fallen slightly short as we became mildly distracted with a separate and unrelated new maintenance fault in the parking brake accumulator system that was noted during our flight deck pre-flight activities. In turn, our flight became delayed at the gate in ZZZ as the parking brake system needed to be deferred using another MEL. Additionally, we waited for connecting passengers from an inbound ZZZ1 flight.We pushed back from the gate in ZZZ started to taxi out for a departure on Runway XXR. During a turn on our taxi to the runway, we both noted that the Master Caution light illuminated for the Number 1 Fuel Filter Bypass Master Caution Light. I canceled the light and the Captain decided he wanted to stop in a safe area to deal with the possible issue. I agreed and ground control in ZZZ allowed us to stop on Taxiway 1.As the Captain stopped and set the parking brake, we both stated how confused we were about the fuel filter bypass light illuminating. I checked the 737QRH for this light and it only indicated that 'erratic engine operation' may occur 'in flight'.The Captain and I discussed how it was extinguished after engine start, and only illuminated momentarily on taxi out, during a turn, and it was now extinguished again. We referenced MEL 7304A again from the 737NG MEL. Nowhere could we find whether the 'inoperative/placarded' light should remain illuminated, extinguished, or momentarily indicate. We discussed that most MELs similar to this deferral would explain to the flight crew that a caution light may illuminate. (See example MEL 78030: 'NOTE: The 'Master Caution' and 'ENG' MAY illuminate when performing master caution recall.')The Captain decided to call Dispatch and conference in maintenance while stopped on the taxiway. We told our Dispatcher about our issue and he brought in Maintenance on the phone line. The initial maintenance personnel transferred us to the 'Specific area.' The 'Specific area' advisor told us that this momentarily illumination was normal and part of the MEL, the write-up was already in the ELB, and that it is 'OK to continue.'During our conversation the Captain, Maintenance, Dispatch, and I came to the conclusion:1. There is no maintenance procedure to deactivate this light.2. The issue is already indicated in the ELB.3. Maintenance stated that was a normal and 'very common' occurrence on the 737 fleet and we are OK to continue.After finishing our conversation with maintenance and dispatch, the Captain and I amended our takeoff briefing to be prepared for this light to illuminate during the takeoff roll. I, as the PNF, would indicate it was this light, cancel the alert, and the takeoff would continue in both the low speed and high-speed regimes.During the takeoff roll, at approximately 120 kts (at least 20 kts below V1), the Number 1 Fuel Filter Bypass Master Caution Light did illuminate. I called out that the fault adding 'expected!', canceled the Master Caution Light, and we continued the takeoff. The light extinguished itself shortly thereafter. The light never illuminated again throughout the rest of the flight. The flight continued uneventfully to ZZZ2. The maintenance release had an open write up for the 'fuel filter differential pressure warning system'. We read both the maintenance release and the MEL (7304A). Not much information other than the other system must be operative and if you do get the other filter bypass light, you should assume both engine filters have an impending bypass condition. Startup was normal. On taxi out, we got the left fuel filter bypass light, the side that was written up. It caught us off guard, because no where did it say that the light might come on. We pulled over and got a phone patch to Maintenance Control to discuss the light. Maintenance Control said it was normal with the problem and we were OK to continue. The light went and we taxied for takeoff. At approximately 120 knots, the light illuminated again. We continued the takeoff and the light went out shortly after we were airborne. The light did not illuminate again until taxi in.
1811463: While flying flight ZZZ - ZZZ1 the gear did not come up on takeoff when the gear handle was raised. I was flying and immediately recognized that something was wrong. I kept the airspeed at 220 kts. while we climbed out to 4,000 ft. MSL. I put the auto pilot on and checked the Aux Gear Extension Door, it was down. I called for the QRH and the FO ran the checklist for Gear Disagree with the handle in the off position. It did not help. I gave the aircraft to the FO and directed him to inform ATC that we were going to return to ZZZ. I then contacted Dispatch. Maintenance Control and the [Chief Pilot] were brought on the line as well. While all the parties were assembling, I talked with the Flight Attendants and the passengers. Maintenance Control and I ran the Gear Disagree checklist with the gear handle in the up position. This checklist had me lift and reseat the Aux Gear Extension door. As the checklist was completed, the gear was able to be raised. In conference it was decided to land overweight versus burning down fuel to 157.3. Dispatch sent landing data for our weight on Runway XXR. I took the aircraft back from the FO and then flew an approach to Runway XXR in ZZZ. We configured early and got a normal gear extension. We landed normally with max auto brake set. Our landing weight was 168.0, 10.7 overweight. We taxied clear, the fire trucks checked our brakes and we then taxied back to gate. I was the pilot monitoring on the flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. The flight departed the gate and taxied to the runway for a normal takeoff from [Runway] XXL. The visibility was slightly reduced due to rain, and there were overcast clouds at 800 ft. After rotation, the Captain called for gear up and I retracted the gear. We started the right turn on the departure, and the flaps were brought up on schedule and the Captain called for the after takeoff checklist. I checked in with Departure and we were given a 270 heading and 6,000 ft. Departure then gave us Direct to XXXXX, which I programmed in the FMC and LNAV was selected. This was a relatively high workload time, in IMC. I completed the after takeoff checklist flow, electing to leave the engine anti-ice on, ensured the flaps/slats were retracted, and placed the gear handle in the off position. I completed the after takeoff checklist and noticed that there were lights illuminated at the gear panel. At this time, the Captain and I both noticed that the plane did not sound right, and we started trying to diagnose the issue. The Captain used speed intervene to set the speed to clean maneuvering speed of 225 kts. I mentioned that it sounded like a gear door was open, and we looked at the gear lights and that the landing gear lights indicated 3 green on the instrument panel as well as the overhead panel. There were also 3 red lights on the gear indication. The Captain called for the QRH, and I completed the QRH for landing gear disagree. The QRH was completed and we determined that the gear was in the down position. At this time, we both looked at the alternate gear door, which was closed. During my preflight, I had confirmed the alternate gear door was closed visually, and then by stepping on it. I had also confirmed the gear pins were present on the flight deck.At this time, we advised ATC that we would like to stop at 6,000 and get some delay vectors for a landing gear issue that we needed to work on. The Captain transferred controls and radios to me, while she contacted Maintenance Control via the radio. Maintenance Control instructed her to place the gear handle in the up position and then open and close the alternate gear door. Then the gear handle was placed in the down position, and back to the up position. At this time the gear retracted and all gear lights went out. From the time we took off, until this moment was approximately 15 minutes. We decided to [advise] ATC and requested that fire rescue meet us at the runway. We decided that a return to ZZZ was our best option. Due to the fact that we tankered an extra 16k [lbs.] of fuel we were overweight for landing. The Captain talked to Maintenance Control and Dispatch to see if they wanted us to burn off fuel or land overweight. Were sent overweight landing data and determined that a safe landing could be made back in ZZZ, and used auto brakes MAX. During this time, the Captain made several announcements to the Passengers explaining the situation and also briefing the FAs on our expected plan of action. We briefed the approach, and discussed our plan in case the gear failed to come down on the approach. A normal landing was made and we exited the runway and stopped to allow our brake temperatures to be read. Fire rescue said everything looked normal and followed us to the gate.
1811483: We were cleared for the Visual Approach. The FO (First Officer) was PF (Pilot Flying) and briefed a visual backed up with the ILS. ATC brought us in on a 4 mile final from a left base which was inside the final approach fix on intercepting the final/Localizer we were slightly low but as it was a visual I told him he was a little low but I let him continue since we were stable and spooled up just below the Glideslope. At about 800 ft. the FO was still descending and we got a Glideslope aural Emergency Ground Proximity Warning (EGPWS) to which he stated correcting and he leveled off to get back on profile. We continued to a landing.I noticed he was low and called it out and then the EGPWS called it out as well. [The] cause was the First Officer misjudged his height and continued descending. I assumed he would correct expediently but he only shallowed his descent rate slightly. The Pilot Flying took corrective action. I'll be more assertive next time and suggest the FO go outside the final approach fix while doing the visual so he has time and isn't rushed.
1811512: On a visual approach to Runway 16L while descending to 7000 ft. we received a GPWS warning. I leveled off around 7,100 ft. and had the terrain in sight the entire time. After passing the hill I started a descent and was unstable so we went around.We were expecting the RNAV Y 16L but were taken off because of departing traffic on Runway 34R. This lead to an extended downwind and base to final. We were much farther out than we briefed or expected. When we finally turn final I used the RNAV 16 X approach plate for distance and altitudes. Over 'BADPE' fix the altitude is 6900 ft. I set 7,000 and started to descend my rate was too much and we received the GPWS warning. [Pilot flying suggests] when operating in mountainous terrain on an RNAV approach and you are taken off that approach see if there is another approach that is better suited for your new location and situation, and familiarize yourself with it before even starting a visual approach.
1811516: First Officer flying through FL200 on way to FL270, in IFR conditions. First Officer and Captain's airspeed indicators [were] unreliable. Standby airspeed indicator correct. Captain's airspeed indicator came back, but First Officer's out for 5 minutes and EEC (Electronic Engine Control) Systems went to Standby. QRC and QRH procedures accomplished as well as followup procedures. Anti-icing systems working, Engine and wing heat on. Stayed as much out of weather, ZZZ closed, ZZZ1 still in VFR weather and location of heavy maintenance for the B-737. Briefed flight attendants and passengers. Captain flew to ZZZ1, safety vehicles checked out aircraft.Good crew coordination of verification of the unreliable airspeed indicators.Don't fly into clouds with icing conditions. May have been multiple problems that happened at the same time. EEC Systems went to standby while in heavy thick clouds, on climb out, through the freezing level.
1811535: Received a Level 1 'Emerg Power On' message while at cruise, FL380. We referenced the QRH, which states moving the Emergency Power Switch to OFF, and then to ARM, which we accomplished. The message remained. We monitored the Electrical System Synoptic for battery status, and created a plan in case the battery started depleting. Per the QRH, we had the option to deploy the ADG. During descent, the battery started losing charge, and we deployed the ADG. It came on-line without issues. Approx 2 minutes later, we received multiple messages on the EAD indicating an electrical system failure. The Capt lost his 3 MFDs, however I still had my 3 MFDs. I assumed PF duties, the Capt took over PM (Pilot Monitoring). We lost Radio #1, and maintained comm on Radio #2, where we notified ZZZ center of our electrical issue. No flight control issues were noted. No other system issues were noted. We [requested priority handling] passing through 10,000 ft. We received vectors for a visual approach to Runway XXR, with a 5NM final. Landing, roll-out, and taxi were uneventful. Electrical system malfunction.A systems problem, that I don't know how it could be prevented. The ADG worked as advertised, and we were prepared for the loss of some systems if the ADG became the sole source of electrical power. During cruise at FL380 we received a level one alert 'EMERG PWR ON'. We went to the QRH which told us to cycle the Emergency power switch to see if [the] alert would go away, which it did not. It said to monitor battery power and if needed to deploy the ADG. Power stayed steady at 26 for the battery for 35-40 minutes. Then [the] battery started to deplete and the decision was made to deploy the ADG while we were descending on the arrival. When ADG was deployed Captain's instruments and radio went away and control was given to the F/O and radio 2 was used. We [advised ATC] and were descended to 2,000 ft. and became visual with the airfield. My HUD was working and I decided to take the aircraft on base leg in case any other unforeseen problems arose. Normal landing and [priority handling] was called off after landing rollout.Battery system and emergency power malfunction. ADG deployment reduced systems available but was handled according to emergency procedures.I am not sure if this could have been avoided as far as the flight deck was concerned. The [incident] was handled according to the QRH and flown to an uneventful finish.
1811543: On the arrival into the ZZZ area, ATC kept us high due to departing IFR traffic. We heard the departing traffic calling ATC on the radio after departure, but got no response. Because we were getting very close to the airport, we elected to reduce speed in order to make the impending descent easier to manage. We were monitoring both the ATC Center frequency and the CTAF frequency at ZZZ. There was a significant amount of General Aviation traffic operating in the vicinity of the ZZZ airport. As the speed was reduced below 200 knots, the First Officer, who was the PF, asked for Flaps 8 and 20. I verified that the speed was below 200 knots and selected Flaps 8 and 20. As soon as I selected Flaps 20 I realized we were still at 16,000 ft., and said, 'We can't do that yet;' and immediately retracted the Flaps back to 0. At this point we were only six or seven miles from the airport, still at 16,000 ft. We had identified the traffic threats on TCAS. In order to initiate our descent to the airport, we canceled IFR. After descending through 15,000 feet the First Officer again asked for Flaps 8 and 20. Because we had extended the flaps earlier above 16,000 feet, I was focused on the altitude. Due to the fact that we had slowed to below 200 knots the first time we extended the flaps, I failed to look at the airspeed indicator, thinking we were still below 200 knots. We were discussing the maneuver we would need to make to circle around and descend to the airport at the time. ATC and CTAF radio traffic was also heavy at the time. As soon as the flaps were selected the overspeed clacker started up. I looked at the airspeed indicator, saw that we were above 200 knots, and reached for the flap lever with the intent of retracting the flaps. At this point I'm unclear what EXACTLY happened next. There was some turbulence, we were beginning our turn, and there was a lot of radio traffic. We were also focused on the traffic displayed on the TCAS. All of this created a great deal of distraction. My hand was on the flap lever at the time, with the intent of retracting the flaps. Whether it was because of turbulence causing me to inadvertently move the lever, or me simply moving it the wrong way because of the distractions, I did, in fact, move the flap lever to 45. The overspeed clacker, interestingly enough, added to the momentary confusion. In fact, at one point I believe the First Officer said, 'What the hell is going on?' I was mortified to see the indication that the flaps were at 45, because there was no intent, plan, or call for further flap extensions. It was simply a mistake. I immediately retracted the flaps to zero. We did not receive any message associated with a flap problem, i.e. 'Flaps Fail', etc. After everything calmed down and things were back in order, we continued the approach, which ended up resulting in a go-around because a general aviation aircraft cut us off on short final. After landing and proceeding to the gate, I wrote up the flap limitation exceedance. Maintenance arrived later, inspected the flaps, performed functional checks, found no irregularities, and returned the aircraft to service.In my opinion there were several factors contributing to the event. Distraction was probably the primary cause. We were distracted by all the radio traffic on the CTAF frequency. Sometimes it was difficult to differentiate between the CTAF traffic and the Center traffic. Also, being left so high so late on the arrival created a self-imposed sense of immediacy...'We need to get down'. Interesting to note that this urgency was never 'real', but rather something we imposed on ourselves. Assumption was another contributing factor. Because we had originally slowed to below 200 knots, I assumed we were still at that airspeed when flaps were requested the second time. This assumption caused me to neglect the airspeed indicator before selecting the flaps because I was more concerned about the altitude.This is primarily an exercise in self-discipline and patience. The training and procedures are all in place to help prevent these types of events from occurring. It simply becomes incumbent on each pilot to be disciplined enough to not allow external factors to get in the way of simple, straight-forward procedures that can and will keep the aircraft, passengers, and crew safe.
1811548: I was [the] pilot flying, headed into ZZZ. It was VMC, severe clear, and in the afternoon. We were being vectored toward Runway XX in ZZZ. I was in green needles, with the [Runway] XX ILS frequency active. My FO made a comment [that] we weren't picking up the right identifier, but because it was visual, and we had just called the field in sight, I was not going to reference the glideslope anyway. I could clearly see the PAPIs and was going to reference that since I had a visual. We were then cleared for the visual for [the] runway, so I kicked off the autopilot, and began a stable descent. We had noticed the glideslope and the PAPIs were not lining up, so I made a comment I was just going to fly it visually and use the PAPIs as the guide, not the glideslope. After all, it was only being used as a back up. Well, as we proceeded along, even though I was 2 white/2 red on the PAPI, the glideslope annunciator started yelling at us (later, we found out the ILS was OTS, which explained why it was not working correctly). Instead of asking the FO to switch his and my frequencies back to standby, I elected to fly higher on the PAPIs to shut the annunciator up. I ended up being 4 white about at about 300 ft. Because the winds were calm, the runway was clear and dry, and I knew a safe landing could be accomplished, I elected to continue the approach. I still landed softly and safely in the touchdown area, and stopped in the usual amount of runway required. It was an uneventful landing.When we taxied clear of the runway, I asked Tower and asked about the frequency and asked the FO to pull up the current ATIS to see if there was a NOTAM about the ILS frequency, and sure enough, it was OTS. In hindsight, I'm not sure how I missed that on the ATIS, but I should have read it more carefully and I could have avoided this situation altogether. I was the First Officer and the Pilot Monitoring for this flight. Having received ATIS for ZZZ and setting up the approach the CA (Captain) briefed the Visual Approach Runway XX to be backed up by the ILS and I concurred and had no questions on the briefing. When going to green needles on the approach I noticed the identifier for the ILS Runway XX did not match with the identifier on the LIDO chart. I mentioned to the CA that I did not have the proper identifier and I double checked the frequency to ensure that it was correct and it was. The CA acknowledged and [said] that we had been cleared for the visual approach. During the approach the CA noticed that the GS (Glideslope) and the PAPI were not matching and informed me he was strictly using the PAPI for the visual approach. While continuing on the approach the GS annunciator was sounding a notification and the CA ended up high on the PAPI at about 100-200 ft. The CA called he was high and correcting and continued the approach into ZZZ and landed in the landing zone with no issue and was able to slow the aircraft and exit on taxiway. Once on the ground the CA asked the Tower to confirm the frequency for the ILS and the Tower responded it was released to Maintenance. At that point the CA asked me to bring the ATIS back up and that is when we both noticed the ILS was NOTAMed OTS. We discussed the approach and landing and decided to both submit reports.
1811550: After starting engines and running applicable checklists, ZZZ Ramp cleared me for a standard taxi east from the Company A Ramp via Taxiway XX. Upon leaving the parking space, I tested the brakes per the Taxi Checklist. Brakes checked good. Prior to the Taxiway XY hold-short bars, ZZZ Ground cleared me for an expedited taxi to [Runway] XXL via taxiways XZ, XA, and XB, crossing Runway XXR/XYL. Due to the expedited taxi, there was minimal braking. I only applied brakes when slowing for the tight turn from Taxiway XA onto Taxiway XB. There was no problem with the brakes during the turn.On Taxiway XB, ZZZ Tower cleared me for a full-length departure from Runway XXL ahead of a Company B aircraft holding short of Taxiway XB on Taxiway XC. I began slowing for the turn well in advance using ground idle power and brakes. Upon lining up on runway centerline, I noticed that the left brake had lost pressure and was worsening. Immediately following this realization, the Company B crew notified me on Tower frequency that my wheel was smoking. ZZZ Tower confirmed the condition. I notified ZZZ Tower that I would be exiting the runway at Taxiway XD.ZZZ Tower asked if I would like fire services and I replied in the affirmative. I was assigned a discrete frequency for coordination with the fire trucks. The fire crew hosed down my left main gear and I shut down engines. I asked the crew for an update on the wheel's condition and was told that the 'small flames' and smoke had been extinguished and that only steam was left. The crew notified me that they would be approaching the aircraft to meet me if I desired to exit the plane, which I did. The flames had burned through a portion of the brake lines and there was a steady stream of hydraulic fluid issuing from the hosing. The brakes' temperature was continually monitored. I put my hand near the right main gear and noticed no inordinate heat from its brake assembly. I called [the] Ramp Supervisor to coordinate for a tug and was towed back to the Company A Ramp by a Mechanic and escorted by ZZZ response crew.
1811552: We were flying the ZZZZZ RNAV arrival into ZZZ inside of the ZZZZZ1 waypoint when ATC instructed us to descend via except cross ZZZZZ2 at 10,000 ft., 2000 ft. higher than published. We informed ATC that if we comply with the assigned crossing restriction that we will have trouble making ZZZZZ at 6,000, [which was] only 8.2 miles from ZZZZZ2. ATC then replied, 'If you will be high on the arrival let me know.' We then decided to slow down the aircraft to prepare for making the crossing restrictions and recalculate our descent inside of ZZZZZ2 to advise ATC if we will be high or if we can comply with the ZZZZZ restriction.Once the Honeywell FMS reached waypoint passage over ZZZZZ2 and cycled to the next fix, we started down to make the next crossing restriction. Within a few seconds of starting our descent, we received a TCAS 'TRAFFIC' alert followed by a TCAS RA. I immediately disconnected the autopilot to comply with the RA and resolve the conflict. After the resolution advisory was resolved, [the Pilot Monitoring] noticed that the FMS had cycled to the next waypoint early and found that we were still a few tenths of a mile from ZZZZZ2 during the event. The assigned altitude at ZZZZZ2 was 10,000 ft., we leveled off during the RA around 9,750 - 9,800 ft. There was no communication from ATC to us regarding the event. The rest of the arrival and approach was flown successfully and we landed safely.The Honeywell FMS cycled waypoints early, leading us to believe that we had reached waypoint passage. [I suggest] finding a solution to prevent the Honeywell FMS from making premature smart turns/waypoint passage cycles. Operating [the] flight as SIC (Second in Command) and PM, we were assigned to descend via the ZZZZZ [arrival] but cross ZZZZZ2 at 10,000. We leveled off at 10,000 prior to the fix and set the next appropriate altitude. At about 2.5 miles prior to the fix, the Honeywell FMS prematurely sequenced to the next waypoint. We began an initial descent and quickly noticed the discrepancy in distance between current position and waypoint. [There was] an RA to 'monitor descent' annunciation. The Pilot Flying immediately climbed back to 10,000 and we waited until the correct DME was displayed. [The cause of the crossing altitude deviation was the] Honeywell FMS [working improperly]. I have noticed this problem in almost all company aircraft containing Honeywell FMS. The airplane will sequence to the next waypoint prior to the actual position. This can, and does lead to, altitude deviations and potential RAs and possibly worse. I would like to either see the problem itself fixed or the company to implement an SOP or training that covers this issue.
1811597: I was conducting an intro flight in Aircraft X. We had begun our take off roll and got to rotation speed, the aircraft left the ground and was slow to climb. I was pitched at about 10 to 12 degrees.The aircraft then had a reduction in power about 75 ft. off the ground before the engine surged back into full power. Once realizing that we were not going to have sufficient power to maintain the climb I immediately pulled the power back to idle and landed on the remaining runway. Air speed was approximately 95 kts. We landed with about 300 ft. remaining which resulted in a runway excursion of approximately 5 ft. There was no damage to the aircraft or airfield lighting. I taxied the aircraft back to the ramp and was able to shut down, no further incidents.
1811618: We were assigned a trip ZZZ-ZZZ1. We performed the preflight, received our clearance, and taxied out to depart Runway XX. Upon departure both crew members recognized that both comms were not working. We immediately squawked 7600 and decided a left traffic pattern to come back to land was [the] best course of action. In the downwind the pilot monitoring ran the performance numbers and determined we would land overweight and that flying one more pattern would burn off enough fuel to land. We landed [on] Runway XX and taxied to the ramp. After receiving a trip, the crew readied the airplane for flight by obtaining the ATIS, receiving the clearance, taxiing and takeoff all while engaging in two way communication with ATC. Immediately after rotation, the crew lost intercom capabilities between the crew and then quickly realized that communications with ATC was most likely lost due to a red 'X' box appearing over the commutations controls on the GTN [Garmin] 750. Due to still being VFR at the departure airport, a quick decision was to enter left traffic and to return for landing. 7600 was entered into the transponder.
1811626: After canceling IFR on a visual approach into ZZZ, we switched to CTAF and began making position reports. Center had advised us of 2-3 aircraft in our vicinity as we approached the airport. We had one aircraft in sight and were looking for the others. There were several aircraft on the CTAF and no immediate conflicts were noted until a departing aircraft was shown on the TCAS display at 12 o'clock and climbing towards our altitude followed by an automated 'traffic' callout. We could not see it immediately or infer its exact course so started a slight right turn away from the airport to avoid [it]. After several seconds I spotted the other aircraft on a converging course from the left and advised my copilot to increase descent to increase separation as he continued flying and searching out my window. It was difficult to spot due to very little relative movement and it was more difficult to spot from the copilot's seat. During the correction I saw that we were on a collision course and directed a climb/level off before taking [the] controls and beginning a more aggressive climb. My copilot spotted the aircraft immediately after the control transfer and we passed approximately 500 feet above the other plane. I had the opportunity to discuss with the crew of the other aircraft on the ground. After checking in with Center and receiving a traffic advisory, it seems they saw us before our initial ('blind') right turn and began a left turn to increase separation, then a level off to allow us to pass above. The mirrored lateral and vertical corrections contributed to the closure. Our 'blind' turn was initiated due to the TCAS return, which displayed their position and climb, but no lateral movement information. Lateral movement information may have provided better situational awareness in this case. Spotting the aircraft sooner would have also helped prevent the conflict.
1811641: My wife and I were flying to IOW. The nearest airport to IOW with a TAF is CID, 16 NM to the northwest. The CID TAF at our estimated time of arrival was... 4SM -RA BR OVC015We planned on flying the flight VFR with only CID being a little marginal VFR. About 30 NM from IOW we encountered light rain and the OVC015 ceiling started to drop. We maneuvered right and left as we made our way toward IOW. The IOW ASOS at the time was reporting the ceiling 1100 scattered. At 15NM west of IOW at 500-600 feet AGL skimming the cloud bases, I turned around to get back to better weather, but found that the weather had closed in behind me, or my route in could not be duplicated out. I knew there were antenna towers in the area and got a visual on one of the towers which appeared to be near my altitude. The safety of the flight was now in question. I called CID Approach and requested an IFR clearance to IOW. The Controller cleared me to the IOW airport via radar vectors and gave me a heading and instructions to climb to 2,500 feet. I advised the Controller that I wanted to shoot the RNAV (GPS) 30 approach into IOW circle 7. We shot the approach, broke out around 1100 AGL, circled, and safely landed on Runway 7. I hold an ATP certificate, however my last instrument proficiency check I had was a 135 check [several years ago]. Therefore, I was not instrument current.Our airplane is equipped with a Garmin 400W and a Garmin 335 ADS-B out transponder. The 400W had a current procedures data base and the pitot static encoder check was completed [two years ago], making [my aircraft] legal for IFR operations. Additionally, I had flightplan.com app loaded onto my phone, which allowed me to have current IFR low altitude charts and approach plates for IOW, as well as the surrounding area.My brief IFR flight and approach was performed to ATP standards and did not alarm ATC in anyway. I have reviewed my ADS-B track and found that the lowest I got on that flight was 422 feet AGL, which is lower than I recall. The antenna tower I saw is at 320 feet AGL. The low flight occurred in Class G airspace during the day. Complacency on my part was definitely a factor and I have taken steps so as to not repeat this occurrence. I have scheduled an Instrument Proficiency (IPC) check.
1811646: While approaching the OCF VORTAC station I witnessed what looked like some sort of drone at 7,000 ft. MSL. The object looked like cylinder about a foot and half long, with thick ends rotating around rapidly at a 45 degree angle. It did not appear to be moving laterally at all. It was black and a hazard to navigation.
1811655: During a training event, my student was learning to judge height above the runway, and the landing went long due to our duration in ground effect. We were asked by Tower to expedite our taxi down the runway and clear [the runway]. During the turn, my foot became entangled in my headset cord. In an effort to manage the aircraft, I pulled my headset plugs from the ports and dislodged my headset on my head. It is a very confined area and the ports are under the center portion of the instrument panel. I made every effort to stop the aircraft prior to the hold short intersection and crossed the hold short line that guards the runway. Factors that affected my performance include a small cockpit environment leading to cord entanglement. Small area that does not favor any ability to clear a runway, and stop the aircraft if the pilot finds them self in any kind of predicament. Faded hold short markings on taxiway. Plan of action is to review this scenario with local instructors. Incorporate this situation into 'real world' training for my students. Renewed priority for 'hotspot' training.
1811664: While training on South Radar, my trainee was vectoring Aircraft X for a Visual Approach to ZZZ. Aircraft X was assigned various headings for the approach, and assigned 8,000 feet in accordance with the Minimum Vectoring Altitude that they were currently above. Aircraft X was observed descending to/through 7,000 feet and issued a climb to 8,000 feet. In the future, I will issue a low altitude alert and a climb to the appropriate altitude.
1811674: I cleared the aircraft at pilots discretion to 5,000 feet. He was entering a 4,400 foot MIA (Minimum IFR Altitude), then a 3,200 ft MIA. Aircraft was cleared for approach and told to maintain at or above 3,200 feet until inbound at the Initial Approach Fix. Aircraft descended to 4,000 feet in 4,400 foot MIA. I need to re read approach clearance phraseology, I believe there was better phraseology available to clear the aircraft.
1811682: As PM, the Captain and I were nearing BERBN intersection on the COKTL 1 Arrival into LAS. After receiving the ATIS for LAS, and before beginning the descent on the COKTL 1 Arrival, the Captain briefed the COKTL 1 Arrival, along with the visual approach, backed up with the ILS to Runway 26L. Conditions at the time were VMC DAY (15,000' few/10SM vis). Prior to reaching BERBN intersection, Approach Control asked us if we had the ILS loaded. I looked over to the Captain and we both nodded, at which time I stated that we did indeed have the ILS 26L LAS loaded into the FMC (from the direction of PRINO intersection). The Approach Controller cleared us to fly the ILS 26L with a clearance to cross BERBN at or above 7,000 feet MSL. I then queried the Approach Controller about whether or not they would like me to call our base leg for Runway 26L. The Controller replied that our base leg would be visible on their radar, and that a call was not necessary. Not realizing that there was INDEED a transition from the BERBN intersection to HUXAR on the ILS 26L, we proceeded turn north whilst descending to intercept the Runway 26L localizer just outside of RELIN intersection (D7.2 IRLE) Runway 26L.Shortly thereafter, we were told by the Approach Controller that we had initiated the turn too soon, and we were given a heading to the East in order to avoid traffic (other carrier) that was already established on final for Runway 26L. We did receive a TCAS TA (no RA), and after completing the turn to the East, the TCAS TA was resolved. After the turn to the East, and with proper separation between our aircraft and Aircraft Y, Approach Control vectored us back to the north to join the localizer and clear us for the visual to LAS Runway 26L. We were then handed-off to LAS Tower. Landing was uneventful. After landing, we were provided a phone number to call LAS TRACON. The COKTL 1 Arrival and the latest ILS 26L charts for LAS are dated (date). I can tell you that I was certainly not familiar, nor had I ever been assigned the ILS 26L from the COKTL 1 Approach (I wasn't even aware that there was a transition from BERBN intersection, as that transition is located on the new ILS 26L Approach chart). My apologies to the LAS Approach Controller for our misunderstanding.As an added measure, I would prefer to see more information added to the COKTL 1 Arrival, like a ball note referring Pilots to the BERBN transition on the ILS 26L LAS. An added note within our company pages may help bring attention to this transition as well.
1811687: While on approach into ZZZ, we were descending from 6,000 ft to 5,000 ft on the runway localizer tracking inbound to runway, and were cleared for the ILS . While descending through approximately 5,300 ft, on the Localizer, a larger sized, square 'Quad-Copter' drone suddenly went past our right wing, (from aircraft front to back) missing the right wingtip by, in my estimations, about 50 ft. The event happened so quickly that there was no manual reaction to the event (autopilot / auto-throttles stayed engaged, etc). I immediately told my Captain that we just had a near miss with a drone since he did not see it, and we immediately notified Air Traffic Control as to the exact location, altitude, and description of the drone/event. We proceeded on the ILS as normal, for landing. The Captain contacted the Chief Pilot once parked at the gate to report the matter.
1811697: Aircraft was dispatched with an inoperative Pack #2 due to a regulator fault and [the flight] was in full compliance with the MEL at departure. Flight was completely full in the cabin. Due to Pack #2 being inoperative it was difficult to cool the main cabin temp using only Pack #1. Using only Pack #1 at FL370 we were able to maintain 72 degrees in the cabin using max cold and high flow. Approximately 200 nm west of ZZZ at FL370 we received an ECAM AIR PACK 1+2 FAULT. ATC was notified and [priority handling was requested]. Upon checking the pressurization and bleed air page, it appeared that Pack #1 was overheating showing an output temperature in amber yet we never received a Pack 1 OVHT ECAM. The cabin altitude was still under control. A descent to 10,000 ft. was initiated without exceeding the cabin altitude before we complied with the ECAM to turn off Pack #1 leaving us unpressurized. Contact was made with Dispatch and Maintenance Control to discuss the situation resulting in a diversion to ZZZ. Approximately 240 nm from ZZZ, at a cruise altitude of FL350 and while in communication with Center, an ECAM aural and Master Caution sounded for AIR PACK 1+2 FAULT. The CA (Captain) said he noted a momentary amber overheat temp in Pack 1, but it did not trigger the PACK 1 OVHT caution. I (Pilot Monitoring) did not see this indication that had subsequently returned to a green inlet temperature. Pack 2 was previously secured and turned off per the MEL deferral on our 2nd release. Pack 1 showed a fault light. The AIR PACK 1+2 FAULT ECAM directed us to secure Pack 1, descend to 10,000 ft. MSL or MEA and then turn on the RAM Air when the pressure differential was less than 1.0. Even though Pack 1 had a fault light in the overhead panel, it appeared to be partially functioning, the cabin pressure holding and the cabin altimeter only increasing at a very slight rate. A flight crew decision was made to begin an immediate normal descent to 10,000 ft. without the use of oxygen while closely monitoring the pressurization page to ascertain the true nature of the Pack 1 malfunction. The CA directed me to assume pilot flying duties and ATC responsibilities while he coordinated with Operations, Dispatch, flight attendants and the passengers. We began a coordinated 1500-2000 fpm rate of descent via two ATC-assigned step down altitudes of FL300 and FL200 before ultimately reaching 10,000 ft. The aircraft was lowered in a steady continual descent with no pauses which I believe helped our situation. Cabin pressure held steady around 8,000 ft. during the normal descent. Upon reaching 10,000 ft., Pack 1 was secured, differential pressure reached less than 1.0, RAM AIR was selected on and the cabin altimeter climbed from approximately 8,000 to 10,000 ft. as expected. We completed all remaining ECAM items until the screens were normal. The rate of fuel burn at 10,000 ft. MSL made reaching our initial destination of ZZZ1 impossible, and it was decided that ZZZ was a suitable diversion while 200nm away and with 11,600 pounds of fuel aboard along with the best Maintenance, aircraft and passenger accommodation options. We informed ATC, Dispatch, Operations, and proceeded accordingly. We switched to the next Center and the Captain [requested priority handling] and returned to the pilot flying role while we coordinated an uneventful arrival via the ZZZZZ to Visual XX approach at ZZZ and ultimately parking at gate XY. We were then met by the ZZZ Chief Pilot at the gate and proceeded to fill out a risk mitigation form following the event. We then accepted a new aircraft and release at gate XZ and ultimately brought the same passengers to ZZZ1 two hours later than originally planned.In totality, I felt the event was handled safely and professionally. The CRM skills taught and utilized allowed both the CA and First Officer to properly divide duties while ensuring sufficient cross checks and communication. At no time did I feel rushed or stressed. I believe the deliberate delay in securing the faulty Pack 1 that appeared to be functioning along with the continual scanning of the pressurization page allowed us to avoid an unnecessary priority descent, use of pilot oxygen, or the deployment of passenger oxygen that might have accompanied a rapid depressurization. All in all, I felt the CA was composed and handled the event in line with Company desires. While I regret the delay the passengers experienced, I believe we handled the event in a safe and caring manner.
1811735: I was the PF (Pilot Flying) on this flight from ZZZZ1 to ZZZZ. On arrival into the ZZZZ terminal area, we were cleared direct to ZZZZZ and cleared for the ILS XXL approach. Weather at ZZZZ was reporting winds 280 at 12, few clouds at 3,000 ft., altimeter 29.62, and no other significant weather. The initial approach was uneventful and we were fully configured and stable by about 1200 ft. AGL. At approximately 800 ft., I turned off the autopilot and began hand flying. Then at approximately 700 ft. we received an audible wind shear warning that lasted for 3-4 seconds. This caught us both by surprise as there were no other conditions that would be associated with wind shear. There was no convective activity in the area, the weather was good, and the wind readout showed stable at 12 kts. The aircraft showed no airspeed fluctuation nor an increasing or decreasing trend vector, the thrust setting was normal, pitch attitude and vertical path were stable. During the alert, the weather radar showed a lot of red radar return that wasn't previously there, and did not correlate with what we were seeing visually out the windscreen. We both assessed the situation, and agreed that the alert was erroneous. At this point we were at about 300 ft. AGL, and the Captain told me to continue. I agreed with this assessment and decision, and continued to land normally. Not once did we receive any other indication that wind shear was present, it wasn't even 'choppy'. It was smooth all the way through landing. After reflecting on the event, I still believe that the alert we received was false. With that being said, as a crew, we probably should have discussed making a logbook entry and discussing the alert with the mechanic once we were parked at the gate in ZZZZ. Going forward if I encounter something like this again, I will handle it differently for a couple of reasons. First, the FOM does state that if a wind shear warning is received, to follow wind shear escape maneuver or to execute a normal go around. Secondly, I do not want to get into a habit of second guessing the warning systems on board the aircraft. Regardless of a suspected error, and as long as safety is not compromised, follow procedure then once at the gate, make a logbook entry for a suspected error. We were operating this flight from ZZZZ1 to ZZZZ arriving approximately XA:30 UTC. Captain was PM (Pilot Monitoring) and FO (First Officer) was PF (Pilot Flying). We were set up for the ZZZZZ1 RNAV arrival for the ILS XXL. The aircraft (a B767) was empty and our landing weight was 198,100 lbs. VApp was calculated at 122 and VRef at 117. The weather was VFR. There was no convective activity, a few clouds at 3000 ft., winds 280 at 12 reported on the field, and altimeter at 29.62. We were cleared to the fix ZZZZZ to begin the ILSZ XXL at 4000 ft. We intercepted the localizer and armed the APPCH. We continued to configure the aircraft for landing maintaining VFR conditions. With the aircraft fully configured for landing (Stabilized Approach criteria met) at approximately 700 ft. AGL we received a wind shear alert. The weather was VFR, and the winds at our altitude were showing stable at 12 knots. There was no airspeed fluctuation (including the airspeed trend line), the throttle position did not change, the thrust setting did not change, and the aircraft pitch attitude did not change. As PM, I did not elect to call 'Go Around' as the aircraft was fully stabilized, fully configured for landing and we were passing through approximately 300 ft. AGL with the PF hand-flying the aircraft. Given the situation with all of the present conditions and the state of the aircraft, I believed the alert was erroneous. I should have made a logbook write up on the EPGWS (Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System) to check for errors. There were no reports of any wind shear activity in the area and the weather conditions were VFR. Also given the location and state the aircraft was in, I thought it would create an unnecessary 'non-normal' situation that could have potentially caused more problems than just continuing the approach and landing the aircraft. As I stated above, the aircraft exhibited no indications for us to believe that there were any type of wind shear occurrences at the present time or in the immediate time prior to landing.
1811745: We were on a visual approach to Runway XX at ZZZ. During the approach we received a GPWS Caution 'Terrain' or 'Too Low Terrain' just after the '500 ft stable' call. As the PM (Pilot Monitoring), I failed to call for a go-around. The PF (Pilot Flying), Captain completed the approach and landing uneventfully. Everything about the approach was normal and I have seen it many times in my 3 years here. PF was stable at 100 ft above field elevation as well as at 500 ft above field elevation, the only exception was that the winds that had recently shifted and gusting were causing the airspeed to deviate by plus or minus 10 knots, but not dramatically. The fact that we were visual with the runway, on path and speed and properly configured, made the GPWS caution surprise me. After hearing it, I reverified that we were within all our approach criteria and it appeared safe so I did not call for the go around. However, being that it was not day VMC, I should have called it. In the future I will be sure to comply with the GPWS alert immediately and call for the go-around.
1811750: Original First Officer (FO) called out from the trip. I was assigned a new FO, he informed me that he was low time FO and hasn't flown much during the past few weeks. I took the first leg to ZZZ1, and I let him [have] the leg back from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. He flew really well during the entire flight. We were cleared for the visual approach Runway XXL with great weather. FO did a great job during the approach and he was properly configured and stable at all times. It looked like he was going to have a great landing because he was doing everything by the book. Unfortunately, when it came time to do the flare he barely flared and took the power out a bit too quickly and the main landing gears made contact with the runway firmer than normal. Everything happened too quick, I saw him initially starting to flare but then at the end he let the nose drop a bit and the mains contacted the runway. I didn't get a chance to note the VSI at the time. As soon as we arrived at the gate I called Maintenance and informed them of that I was writing the aircraft for a possible hard landing with minimal flare. We originally had a plane swap, while on the swap I grabbed some dinner. And eventually received a call from the Chief Pilot confirming that there was damage to main landing gear and he wanted to hear from me what had happened. I explained to the Chief Pilot what had happened, and Chief Pilot took notes and said to follow up with an Ops report.A firmer landing than normal due to minimal flare that caused the main landing gears to come into contact with the runway quicker than normal due to minimal flare. FO barely flared during a visual approach at Runway XXL in ZZZ that ended up causing a hard landing situation.[Reporter recommends] possibly rotate brand new FO's and make them fly more often. FO informed me he had not flown in a while and was still low time FO. 1811758: Got a terrain warning coming into LSE. We briefed the company page on it before descent. Cleared for visual approach and entered downwind leg. Descended too low on downwind and got the terrain warning. Climbed higher and dropped the gear to get out of the terrain caution area.[Suggest] Make a higher and wider pattern, brief the company page closer to landing so it's fresh in our minds.
1811768: During Flaps 45 landing, my NH (New Hire) First Officer (FO) OE student retarded the thrust levers too early setting us up for a hard landing.
