1811773: While briefing the arrival and approach into Norfolk (ORF) we noticed a discrepancy between the data in the FMS database and that depicted on Jeppesen FD Pro. The RNAV Z RWY 5 missed approach as shown in the FMS database has us going to TECHI intersection and then proceeding to the CCV VOR and holding. The missed approach procedure as shown in the Jeppesen Approach Chart shows the missed approach as going to TECHI and then proceeding to OUTLA intersection and holding. On this flight, we spotted the airport almost 10 miles away, called 'field in sight' and were cleared for the visual approach so not a big deal. The supplier of the FMS data needs to be made aware of the discrepancy and the FMS data updated accordingly.
1811778: I loaded the route into the FMC. We received and acknowledged revision 1 sent from Dispatch asking if we had received the revised flight plan. It was the route I had loaded earlier. It started with the ZZZZZ departure. But the route assigned in FD Pro did not match the route from Dispatch, but it too started with the ZZZZZ. I assumed the FD Pro flight plan was the original flight plan. We received the PDC clearance which stated 'Cleared to the ZZZ airport ZZZZZ then as filed, climb via SID. Expect FL340....' After takeoff, prior to completing the ZZZZZ SID, BOS ATC requested we fly direct to ZZZZ intersection as a short cut. We searched our legs page in the FMC but could not find it. We advised ATC we had no such fix. They had us go to ZZZZ regardless. They then asked to confirm the route we were flying. The route we had loaded from Dispatch was NOT the route ATC had on file. But it was the route that was originally in FD Pro for [us]. ATC then had us fly that earliest FD Pro flight plan to ZZZ. We were asked later during our flight to call BOS Center once on the ground. I did. They wanted to figure out what might have been the reason our flight plans did not match up. They said we had not deviated off course as we were on the filed ZZZZZ which was on both flight plans. I stated to him I had loaded the revised flight plan from our Dispatcher and that I accepted the PDC flight plan clearance message as it appeared to match our revised flight plan. I called our assigned Dispatcher and informed him of the problem. He thinks PDC did not load the revision but he should have gotten some kind of rejection notification if it was kicked back. Which he did not. So we do not know why ATC did not get the revised route that we flew. I would suggest that if the ATC PDC message that acknowledges our clearance was a complete route, not 'as filed', I would have caught the discrepancy in the flight plans. It was unique in that both flight plans began with the ZZZZZ. It worked out in our favor that ATC gave us a short cut before we left the ZZZZZ. If not, somewhere after the ZZZZZ we would have deviated off the ATC filed route. The route that Dispatch sent us matched the route in [our] flight plan. The PDC acceptance message was not enough to make us doubt we had a route difference. PDC clearance could read the full route instead of 'as filed'.
1811787: Clean configuration. Airspeed 280 knots. Autopilot on. IMC conditions. Being radar vectored around significant squall line. Anti-ice on. Climbing to cruise altitude and passing altitude about 20,000 feet when my airspeed indicator suddenly went erratic with plus or minus several (at 30 knots greater and less than commanded) indications. Airspeed indicator never reached stick shaker or over-speed warnings limits. Immediately took control of aircraft from autopilot and crosschecked the primary flight display with the Captain and standby indicator. Recommended Captain become pilot flying as his indications were consistent with standby indicator and airspeed indicator was not as erratic as mine (more consistent with turbulent air flying in the 737). After transfer of aircraft control to Captain, I completed the Quick Reference checklist (QRC) and QRH for unreliable airspeed indicator. When double checking the pitot heat was on I notice both Engines Electronic Control (EEC) were in soft alternate mode. During the entire time the aircraft was in IMC the airspeed indicator was erratic and EEC remained in soft alternate. A few minutes later, at level off at cruising altitude (low 20;000s) and out of IMC the airspeed indicator returned to normal along with EEC. Remained clear of clouds and landed uneventfully at ZZZ1. We did not return to ZZZ after [Notifying ATC] because we were more than half way and the squall line was over ZZZ.Unknown as to why airspeed indicator was unreliable and erratic in IMC turbulent air and then returned to normal when clear of clouds. Also did not know why EEC went to soft alternate and then returned to normal.
1811820: During arrival into ZZZ we received 4 runway changes in about 5 minutes time. We were then broken off the arrival and vectored around for a visual approach to XXL. Reaching the ZZZZZ fix we received a fuel imbalance caution message. We then switched the fuel selector to the correct side to balance fuel and landed within limitations for a fuel imbalance. We felt rushed and focused on flying the visual correctly. Upon receiving the caution, we felt like going around was a more unsafe decision than continuing on the approach, due to the distraction and complexity that were that we were experiencing. Always go around whenever a caution message appears. Run the QRH as directed. After a rushed departure due to company operations. The aircraft was initially over fueled (may have played a role). Descending on the ZZZZZ arrival we were assigned multiple runway changes and arrival transition changes in sterile. This caused task saturation. Finally we were assigned RNAV visual for [Runway] XXR. On the approach we received a fuel imbalance message turning onto final at ZZZZZ1. We were able to promptly balanced and corrected the issue. We landed with the selector off and a imbalance within limitations. Cause was gusty wind condition, multiple runway/transition changes, rushing because we were 'leading the pack', and no clear reason why the fuel imbalance was caused (pilot error, mechanical, etc.) I feel we should have considered a go-around. I was behind the airplane and task saturated. I should have verbalized this to the captain. We could have requested delay vectors and potentially broke of the approach to fix and trouble shoot the issue.
1811826: The incident happened during our descent on the ZZZZZ arrival into ZZZ. As far as I remember, we had been cleared by the previous Controller and told to do the XXL transition. I had already programmed the FMS for that specific arrival and pre-loaded the ILS XXL. The weather was not an issue with a clear sky and great visibility. I briefed a visual approach for XXL, backed up with the routing of the ILS for that same runway, and made sure we had the discontinuity between the last point on the arrival - ZZZZZ1 and the first point on the approach - ZZZZZ1. We were then told to contact the next Controller and assigned different altitudes on the arrival while maintaining the routing. For some reason, at one point, I thought/assumed we were cleared for the visual and got rid of the discontinuity by linking the first point on the approach with the last point on the arrival - ZZZZZ1. I turned to the Captain to ask him to 'confirm' and proceeded by removing the discontinuity. Because we were not cleared for the approach yet, the aircraft proceeded past ZZZZZ1 on a XXX as expected, but because it was now programmed to fly the approach it started turning at ZZZZZ2. The Controller asked us if we were flying the RNAV, we responded that we were doing the XXL transition and as the Captain said these words we realized we had made a mistake by leaving the XXX. The Controller kindly reminded us what we were expected to do and gave us a heading to intercept the localizer for the visual XXL. What led to this mistake is mostly my fault. I was fixated on flying the visual, and I forgot to actually make sure we had been given the clearance before getting off the arrival. My mind was too focused on the preconceived idea of what was expected rather than what we had actually been cleared for that I failed to properly communicate with my Captain. I was complacent, and this led to confusion in the cockpit and with the Controller. During our descent on ZZZZZ arrival into ZZZ, we were cleared to descend via ZZZZZ , XXL transition. We programmed the FMS for that particular arrival and transition and preloaded the ILS XXL. The weather was good with clear sky and great visibility. Pilot Flying, briefed the visual approach XXL back it up by ILS. We made sure the discontinuity between the last point on the arrival ZZZZZ1 and the first point on the approach ZZZZZ1. We were told to contact the next Controller and assigned us different altitude on the arrival while maintaining the routing. I contacted the next Controller and for some reason we thought, we were cleared for visual via ZZZZZ1 transition. As we past ZZZZZ1, we continue to fly heading XXX as we approached ZZZZZ2 the plane was about to transition to the new fix. At this point ATC assigned us a heading 350 and asked us if we are flying the RNV transition? Which responded yes and I realized the error. At this point he assigned us 310 heading to intercept the localizer and cleared us for visual to XXL.We were both fixated and our mind was set on the preconceived idea of what was expected rather than what we had actually been cleared for, especially when the proceeding traffic receives that clearance. I (we) failed to confirm and communicate with each other and ATC. I got complacent and side tracked, the combination of these two led to the confusion in the cockpit and with the Controller.As a (Captain/Pilot Monitoring) I should have communicated and confirmed that we are both on the same page and understood the clearance and when in doubt ask the ATC for clarification. I want to make sure and get the confirmation before removing the discontinuity and not to rush. Do not assume if previous aircraft receives particular clearance we will get the same and avoid complacency. I will emphasize this on my future arrival briefings to ensure this doesn't happen again, FOOLISH ASSUMPTION/MISTAKE.
1811827: During the pre-start check, the crew confirmed that all three altimeters were set properly. I have a clear memory of personally checking all 3 altimeters. As Pilot Flying I was hand flying a vectored departure and given a clearance to climb and maintain 10,000 ft. Approximately 200 ft prior, as I was leveling off, I was given a new clearance to climb and maintain 16,000 ft. I continued to hand fly and completed a smooth level off at 16,000. As I was doing so, ATC gave us a notification of opposite direction traffic 1,000 feet above us which we had on TCAS and immediately saw visually. All appeared normal and I believed ATC was simply letting us know why we had not been cleared higher and was giving a normal notification of traffic. The transmission was partially garbled, and the Pilot Monitoring (PM) requested that ATC repeat it. ATC simply responded with 'maintain 16,000' which the PM acknowledged. The PM then noticed that our altimeters did not agree and informed me that my altimeter was set at 29.92 instead of the local altimeter setting. I reset the altimeter and discovered that I was actually at 16,180 ft, which likely had prompted the call from ATC. We were just short of 200 ft high. I descended and was at 16,000 before passing under the opposite direction traffic. We did not receive a TCAS TA or RA. I have no memory of resetting my altimeter to 29.92 but surmise that I must have done so as it would be very difficult to have hit the button accidentally. While allowed to set 29.92 once assigned a climb above 18,000 ft, my normal practice is to wait until the altimeter setting flashes approaching 18,000 ft to reset it. Normal practice meaning I don't recall ever doing it differently. I cannot explain when I reset it to standard, except that it was after the pre-start check and prior to leveling at 16,000. My best guess is that I did so at 10,000 for some reason, as that was the only altitude I passed that I would have considered significant, although I was on profile in a 250 knot climb both before and after 10,000 ft. In this case, the local altimeter setting was close enough to standard that I did not exceed the 300 feet limit for a flight violation or cause a traffic conflict. This was just luck however. Had the altimeter been significantly different from standard, I don't believe I would have been more likely to notice the error and could have been responsible for a conflict.I'm not sure what the cause was except that I simply made an error. Why, how, or when escapes me. However, I did have to call in fatigued that morning as we were on a late in the day pairing but had been delayed overnight to a morning departure two time zones to the east. When I called in fatigued unable to fall asleep early, I was given my 10 hours and a later show time, though to make the later show time I still needed to get out of bed two hours prior to when I was accustomed. After I woke up to my alarm, I was notified that the aircraft was still in maintenance and was given an even later show time, and I took a short nap. In the end, the error happened during a time I'd normally be awake, but I did not get my normal sleep routine. I had legal rest and did not feel particularly fatigued, but I can't discount that fatigue very well could have contributed to such an unusual error. I utilized the Fatigue Risk Management Plan (FRMP) to the extent I felt necessary and neither Crew Scheduling nor the company pressured me in any way to fly fatigued. Perhaps I should have insisted on an even later show time. My feeling of responsibility to our customers who had already been delayed over 12 hours was a factor in making a show time that was earlier than normal for me, considering time zones, but again, I didn't feel overly tired at the time. Obviously, having made this error for the first time, I'll be more cognizant of when I hit the button to bring the altimeter to standard going forward. As far as the possible fatigueaspect, our promise to our customers to transport them to their destination at the time we say can sometimes conflicts with our promise to transport them as safely as possible. I have availed myself of the risk management plan several times in the last year and have never received any negative feedback or pressure to fly fatigued. There are times when I feel the probability of losing pay has pressured other pilots to fly with less rest than they needed, but in this case pay was not a factor as I was the only pilot available to fly this leg to an outstation serviced only once per day. So, I was going to be paid for the leg no matter when I flew it. Therefore, I can't recommend any changes to the risk management plan. I simply need to do a better job of anticipating and assessing my own fatigue level. Climbing out we were assigned to maintain 16,000 ft. First Officer (FO) was pilot flying. Altitude was verified at '1,000 to go' call. As we went through 15,000 feet, I said 15,000 climbing 16,000. FO was hand flying, as we near 16,000 (about 100ft to go) I noticed he wasn't slowing down the climb rate. I looked over and his altimeter was set to 29.92 instead of the altimeter we've gotten when I checked in of 30.16. As I looked over ATC asked if we had the 16,000 ft altitude assigned which I replied affirmatively. As I was done talking to ATC I told the FO he had the wrong altimeter setting, and that our Altimeter was 30.16. FO did level off at 16,000 ft but he had a wrong altimeter setting. FO may have pushed the standard 29.92 altimeter inadvertently at some point after initial departure. As the altimeter were set and cross checked for departure on the ground. We had checked our level off altitude on the 1,000 to go call. But I didn't notice at that time he had a wrong altimeter setting. I think on the 1,000 feet to go call we should have notice this discrepancy, but I was looking at my PFD and not his. FO should have mentioned that his altitude did not match with mine at the 1,000 to go call.
1811848: We received a request to go direct to ZZZZZ. Dispatch had filed us on a southerly track to avoid significant weather on the H-track. The only options given were to accept or standby. We were not going to accept the re-route so we hit standby. The standby was accepted. We sent a message that we could climb instead of a re-route and ATC gave us a climb.Sometime later, the re-route request showed up again but this time the only option we were given was to accept. We ignored the request but that left the ATC icon up on the Upper DU [Display Unit] (so future ATC alerts may not be noticed).This annoyed me so after crossing ZZZZZ1 we noted that accepting the persistent direct routing request would only bypass our next waypoint by about 10 NM. I accepted the ATC routing but waited for a reply from ATC before proceeding. ATC responded with ROGER. So, we went direct ZZZZZ per the clearance. ATC then sent a message asking us to confirm request. We never sent any request so we followed up with a direct message stating we were accepting the previous direct routing from ATC. Shortly thereafter we asked to call ZZZ Center.I talked with the controller and explained the situation. He closed it out on his end with no action but quality control will still review.With CPDLC, ATC cannot ask a question but only provide one answer (accept). That leaves us with an open request. There should be a CPDLC option to accept, reject, or standby. Not just accept or standby. If you don't accept, the message stays open, and the ATC alert never extinguishes. This could cause a future message to be missed.
1811895: This was a maintenance reposition flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. I was flying as the PIC with a Captain in the right seat. Pushing back from the gate, we had a zero fuel weight (ZFW) of 52,000 lbs. The gross weight on the performance was off by over 4,000 lbs from the data received, and we were out of balance. The aircraft had no passengers, no flight attendants, no baggage, just 14,700 lbs of fuel and two pilots and all galley carts. We called the Dispatcher to inform her that we were out of balance. She told me on the phone that she was [gone] the previous week when we were transitioning to 5 zone weight and balance and she didn't know what was going on, and literally just handed me off to the pilot on duty to figure out. This was totally unacceptable. She is the dispatcher of record, has equal legal responsibility for the planning of this flight and upon being informed that we're out of balance and had our ZFW change by thousands of pounds in a few minutes time, she just hands me off to an unrecorded phone line with the pilot on duty?! My head is still spinning. At the gate, our ZFW was 52,000 lbs. Now we are being told to put numbers in the box for ballast but I have no idea what it means 1.0 2.0 3.0 etc, what does that correspond to? We are not actually moving any ballast anywhere etc. The pilot on duty and some other manager on with him, and myself went back and forth for a good amount of time trying to figure out what the accurate zero fuel weight was, what an accurate gross take off weight was, and my main concern, if our stab trim, and V speeds were accurate and safe. I want to reiterate, this was a total and complete debacle. There was so much confusion on the phone as to how we got these numbers from computer and what they meant, and if they were accurate. I had to ask the pilot on duty and manager point blank on the phone, are you telling me these numbers are accurate, and safe for us to depart, before I would continue this flight any further. This 5 zone weight and balance makes no sense how we could be out of balance with only fuel on board. It does not seem like this 5 zone system was well thought out, or that ferry / reposition flights were accounted for. How this got approved by the FAA is beyond me. Additionally, our FOM states that 'the amount to be considered unusable shall be noted on the dispatch release and be considered as unusable by the flight crew', no such comment on this release is present. If were using fuel for ballast for CG limits which is totally news to me seeing as we never had a problem with CG on 3 zone weight and balance, then the PIC must be notified because if that fuel is used, an in flight emergency would have to be declared because the aircraft would no longer be within CG limits.
1811927: Aircraft came in with MEL for two wing stub fuel tank pumps running together and unable to isolate pumps from each other. Trouble shot problem down to the fuel pump selector switch in the cockpit overhead panel. Canned fuel selector switch panel from Aircraft X which is currently in heavy check. When part was canned there was no physical indication on the part, which was still installed on Aircraft X, that there was a discrepancy written up against part in [the] maintenance software. After installation in aircraft OPS CHECKED GOOD NO DEFECTS NOTED IAW EMB 145 AMM 28-XX-XX as documented on Maintenance Logbook page 47XXXXX ITEM XX.When performing [the] maintenance software search for any open discrepancy's against the fuel switch panel search results were negative. However upon installation of new fuel switch panel in Aircraft X it was discovered that there was an open discrepancy located in the task section of [the] Job Card, which is not displayed or indexed in [the] maintenance software search parameters. Without opening each individual Job Card item there is no way to search through the task descriptions section of the Job Card. Canned fuel switch panel had no physical indication that there was a discrepancy against it and panel was still installed on Aircraft X.Add in a function to search task descriptions in [the] maintenance software.
1811942: The aircraft Boeing 747-400 Freighter, Aircraft X, is equipped with two life rafts. I noticed that one life raft was missing and informed the Captain who contacted the Maintenance Department. In addition the aircraft logbook was showing the following MEL XX / FLOTATION EQUIPMENT (Crew and Passenger) (Life Vests) removed one raft for use on Aircraft Y, expires: Date. After we received confirmation from the Maintenance Department, that it is legal to operate the aircraft with just a single life raft, we conducted the flight from to ZZZ to ZZZZ crossing the Pacific. Meanwhile and after reviewing all applicable regulations, I found out, that this was in violation of 14 CFR 121.339(a)(2), which requires, that there are enough life rafts to accommodate all occupants of the airplane in the event of a loss of one raft of the largest capacity. The Maintenance Department further confirmed, that the second life raft was removed at the maintenance station, because it was needed on another aircraft. Furthermore the MEL is incorrect and about operating the aircraft without the required number of life vests, but not about the required number of life rafts. I also contacted the Director of Operations by email and informed him about the violation.
1811967: I Departed ZZZ IFR with 3 passengers (family) for a personal trip to ZZZ1 around XA:00 this morning. Climbing through around 5,000-6,000 feet using radar vectors to join airway, the EIS warning light came on, and the oil pressure, oil temperature gauges started flashing. Oil pressure had dipped into the yellow and then erratically into the red. I reduced power and notified ATC. It was VMC conditions above 1,600 feet. I requested the ILS for ZZZ2 and was vectored for the approach. I maintained as low power settings as possible per the Pilatus procedures, and requested a shorter turn to final below the normal vectoring altitude: my goal was to get the aircraft on the ground as soon as safely possible. After joining the localizer, there was no glide slope, and the ID was barely audible. I then asked for the RNAV approach, was vectored to final, cleared for the approach, broke out at 500 feet and landed.
1811982: I was working the arrival and final position with an arrival rate of 22 [aircraft] sent in the NTML [National Traffic Management Log]. However, at the time of the incident I had 19-20 aircraft in my sector landing MCO. So, needless to say, the Center was not complying with the 22 rate. Which for sure contributed to this because my supervisor called Miami Center to slow the COASTR [COSTR] arrivals down to 210 kts. Aircraft X was on the COASTR [COSTR] arrival. I was fed Aircraft Y from TPA Approach at 11,000 [feet], and normal speed. I descended Aircraft X to 9,000 [feet], not realizing that Aircraft Y wasn't given 210 kts by TPA. When I descended Aircraft X there was probably at least 5-6 miles between the aircraft. As Aircraft X was descending, the CA [Conflict Alert] went off. I issued an immediate turn to Aircraft Y and called the traffic. Aircraft Y read it back and said they were responding to an RA and then subsequently, Aircraft X keyed up saying they were responding to an RA.First of all, the rate is not a joke!!! This is a normal occurrence, here at F11, we ask for one rate and get fed way over the rate. It's been okay until now when something happens. I would encourage you to look into this, and stop the games, because safety is being compromised. The rate is there for a reason. It wasn't being followed, no one will be held accountable for it. When the rate is established, that is the rate. The rate is there to ensure safety. This is a shining example of why the rate is necessary. The advertised rate was 22, and I had 19 aircraft landing MCO in my sector at the time of the incident. That's not a 22 rate. I can assure you, that if the rate was being followed, that situation would have not occurred. Because Aircraft X would have been normal speed over the COASTR [COSTR] arrival, and Aircraft Y and Aircraft X would have been compatible. And the two airliners wouldn't have to respond to RAs, and make it uncomfortable for the people in the back, and safety wouldn't have been compromised.
1811991: ETOPS X day, all legs Aircraft X. Initially Day 2, transmitted ZZZ twice at Gate X. Jetbridge Gate. Checklist Pitot Tube Cover Installation/Removal Procedures, were not applied either time. That is...no covers, no notification to the crew. None. Not done. The next day, ZZZ Gate Y, the aircraft was shutdown for almost an hour. Crew went for food and drink.Returned, pre-flighted aircraft, and began the push uneventfully. There were at least three Operations people at the jetbridge observing our push. The Operations Agent, and Instructors, Managers, and no one alerted us to the pitot covers that had been attached to the aircraft while we were in the terminal.There were no streamers provided. The Captain was not notified. During the push, thankfully the alert Tug Driver asked me why there were 'streamers on the nose.' The PARKING BRAKE WAS SET. Operations was called and we asked who did what during this push and why were we not notified? And how dangerous this was. Specifically, the Checklist and Standard Procedures, Item XX (ZZZ Standard Procedures).During the pre-flight walkaround, Ground Operations will remove the pitot covers. This did not happen. Ground Operations will display all covers to the Crew. This did not happen. The Operations Agent will confirm with the Flight Deck Crew that they received visual verification the covers were removed, at which time the Operations Agent will collect the Probe Heat switch streamers. [This] did not happen. Only the alertness of the Tug Driver, daylight, helped us trap a potentially catastrophic error. When I called Operations to inquire about their process, and I mentioned the danger and seriousness of this event, the person on the radio responded as follows: 'Mr. Pilot Man, I apologize for the Inconvenience.' Inconvenience??!!
1812004: We were cleared the RNAV (RNP) Y 16 L inside of HLDMM (I believe) on the KENNO 2 RNAV. 0.3 was entered into the LEGS Page and 4,500 feet was placed in the MCP (Mode Control Panel) window. Inside of KLOCK, zeros were entered into the MCP. By the time we sorted this out, we were too high above the glidepath for a normal approach, so I directed / executed a go-around.We subsequently flew a visual approach backed up by (a different RNAV) the RNAV GPS X Runway 16L. Mugu Sea Range) centered on the SXC248/058 and possible impact areas, but RNO was not in the listed area. RAF coverage was 0.3 or better. 1812020: Pushed back without the final DG (Dangerous Goods) summary, realized it and stopped the aircraft until the issue was resolved. When I initialized the ACARS during preflight there was a DG sent see printer message but no DG on the printer. My normal procedure is to put this between the throttles until the final is received so I won't forget. The printout was eventually located but I didn't put it where I normally would. We pushed back and I realized we had not received the final. We told ramp we would have to stop until we resolved the issue. 1812040: While enroute to ZZZ we experienced unusually high LP vibrations, still within limitations. No amber indication was observed. However, the vibrations were strong enough to be felt in the aircraft. Descending into ZZZ ATC cleared us to descend to 16,000 and cleared us for the approach. We began to descend when we noticed the vibrations were getting worse. While running the QRH we encountered sudden turbulence, shortly after we received a terrain alert and immediately executed the escape maneuver. We continued to ZZZ without further difficulty and to a safe landing. Crew became task saturated by increasing engine vibrations, sudden unexpected turbulence and QRH checklist.Suggestions - Terrain awareness chart or company jepps. Company awareness video regarding descent and approach into ZZZ. ATC cleared us for the approach into ZZZ and notifies us of no radar coverage under 16,000 feet. The Captain set the initial approach fix and we began a descent on a VNAV path toward the airport. During descent we were handling an engine vibration issue with the QRH along with some unexpected turbulence, when we received a terrain notification. The Captain executed an escape maneuver and we continued to a safe landing on Runway XX at ZZZ. Crew became task saturated with the engine vibrations, QRH, and unexpected turbulence in descent.
1812044: I had a disruptive passenger on board and needed to communicate with the station to coordinate the removal of the passenger. We called for the station several times to inform them we would be returning to the ramp. After several attempts we did not have any answer. After we got parked on the ramp a few agents came out to the airplane looking confused on why we returned back to the ramp. We again tried reaching the station on the published frequency. After several attempts we were still unable to communicate with them. As a last resort I typed on my iPad and held it up to the window to communicate with them that we needed stairs and a supervisor. Once the supervisor was on board and the situation was under control. I asked if they monitor the ops frequency. The supervisor told me the radio only works sometimes. This is a safety concern of mine. We were not able to communicate with anyone. ZZZ is uncontrolled, so no ATC, ACARS doesn't work there, and the station's radio did work. If we were to have a more serious issue for example a medical emergency or needing firefighting services we would be left by ourselves with no assistance. The ops radio at ZZZ doesn't work. Fix the ops radio.
1812051: On arrival into EDF we were on ANC Approach. After initial contact, ANC asked what approach we wanted at EDF. The Pilot Monitoring replied the Visual 34. ANC instructed us to turn left heading 260 and descend and maintain 8,000 (we were at 13,000.) While rolling out on a 260 heading and still descending, ANC came back and said they were going to take us the other way and to turn back right heading 330. We rolled out on 330 still descending. At around 9,000 descending, ANC asked us if we wanted Runway 16 and that the winds were 330 at 5. Taking into account our position and high altitude relative to EDF Runway 34 and our weight, I decided that this would be acceptable, but wanted the IRO to double check the numbers before accepting this change. I said 'standby' and the Pilot Monitoring transmitted 'standby' to ANC. ANC immediately instructed us to descend and maintain 3,000. At the same time of ANC transmission, we were leveling at 8,000, and I was asking the IRO to run the numbers for 16. The Pilot Monitoring replied '3,000, Aircraft X'. I reset the altitude selector to 3,000, verified the altitude with the Pilot Monitoring, engaged FLC, set speed and we began to descend. This clearance seemed logical considering we were clearing terrain, there was no traffic on TCAS, no terrain indicating on the HSI (I was in terrain mode) and we needed to lose altitude to make the airport. There was no further contact with ANC ATC until they instructed us to maintain 8,000.Descending through approximately 6,700, ANC contacted us and instructed us to maintain 8,000, low alt alert and that the MVA in that area was 8,000. After landing and block in, I was notified by EDF Tower (via the military) that ANC TRACON wanted me to give them a call (which I did after speaking to the Chief Pilot.) They took my info and said he would be forwarding to quality control (assurance?) and they may contact me as they were looking into it. There was either an error by ANC Approach or we mistook instructions for another aircraft. After the flight while discussing with the crew, myself and the Pilot Monitoring thought we heard the same instructions. Considering we may have accepted a clearance for another aircraft on frequency, I later looked at the flights in and out of ANC at the same time. There was another flight that arrived in ANC shortly after we landed. It is possible that the instruction were meant for them. It is also possible instructions were meant for an entirely different aircraft and we mistook it for us. There was high workload at the time while considering a runway change, configuring the aircraft and checking landing data.The Pilot Monitoring immediately replied to maintain 8,000. I rolled the altitude selector back to 8,000, clicked off the autopilot, added power and hand flew the airplane back to 8,000 and then reengaged the autopilot. If in fact we did accept a clearance from a different aircraft, caution must be used when similar flight numbers are on the same transmitting frequency, especially during high work loads. Unfortunately, we were unaware of the other aircraft at the time of the event. As International Relief Officer, I heard ATC instruct us to descend to 3,000 feet. Pilot Monitoring (PM) readback 3,000 feet on the radio to ATC. Pilot Flying (PF) entered 3,000 feet into MCP. PM acknowledged the entry of 3,000 feet into MCP. As aircraft descended below 8,000 feet, ATC instructed us to go back to 8,000 feet. PF reset 8,000 feet in MCP and flew aircraft to 8,000 feet. After landing, PIC was instructed to phone call ATC when he was informed that we flew below the instructed altitude of 8,000 feet. It is possible that we heard and responded to an altitude instruction for another aircraft. However, PM did read back the altitude and wasn't, subsequently, corrected. The situation was corrected quickly after being instructed to do so. The conditions were VMC. There were no terrain hazards at our altitude. There didn't appear to be any traffic conflicts.
1812070: Upon arrival to the aircraft, an ACARS message from our dispatcher was already on the printer asking if we had Revision X to our flight release. I opened and downloaded the flight release to my iPad. The release was indeed Revision X. We replied to the Dispatcher telling him that we did have Rev X onboard. I never saw the original Rev Y. When uploading the flight plan to the FMC, the route that loaded was consistent with Rev X. This route was: BLZZR4 BLZZR BAF Q480 CANDR RAV J64 [...]. I logged into the CPDLC and we received the clearance via CPDLC. The CPDLC clearance was: 'CLEARED TO ZZZ ARPT BLZZR4 THEN AS FILED. [...]' We accepted the clearance. From this point the flight progressed normally. After departure while flying the BLZZR4 departure we were talking to Center, we had not yet reached the BAF waypoint. The controller gave us a shortcut and cleared us directly to TRIBS intersection. We couldn't find that fix on the legs page and replied that we were not showing TRIBS on our route. The controller inquired as to what our route was and I replied with the route that was on our release (noted above). Controller replied that they had a new route for us and cleared us from our present position direct to TRIBS Q406 BWZ J6 HVQ J78 FAM SGF [...] to ZZZ. We accepted the new clearance, entered it into the FMC, then notified Dispatch via ACARS of our new route. Later in the flight, while talking to the next Center, the controller notified us of a possible pilot route deviation and gave us a phone number to call Center upon arrival in ZZZ. The flight continued uneventfully to ZZZ. Enroute to ZZZ, the Captain and I discussed what possible route deviation could have occurred. We could only speculate that there was a difference between the flight plan on our Rev 01 Flight Release and the route that Center had cleared us via CPDLC and expected us to fly. We were confident, however, that we were never off course since both the CPDLC clearance and Rev X flight plan had us flying the BLZZR4 departure, and the shortcut and subsequent reroute issued by Center occurred while we were still on the departure route. At BAF (Barnes VOR) is where Q480 & Q406 diverge).After the Captain called Center from ZZZ, we suspected that the cause of the problem was that the Rev 01 route wasn't processed by BOS prior to issuing us our CPDLC clearance. Since both the Rev X route, and the original route that BOS expected us to fly both began with the BLZZR4 departure, we had no idea from the CPDLC clearance of 'CLEARED TO ZZZ ARPT BLZZR4 THEN AS FILED.' that there was any discrepancy. We are unsure why the updated route wasn't processed by BOS prior to issuing our CPDLC clearance. Perhaps there is a cut-off time where changes are no longer accepted or processed. Even when being issued a 'Cleared As Filed' CPDLC, listing the entire filed route at the end of the message would be another way to confirm that the ATC facility has the same route as the crew does on their flight release. In addition, being able to print the entire CPDLC message would also be helpful to not only have a hard copy of the clearance, but also to avoid having to step through multiple pages on the FMC and potentially miss something. This would be especially helpful when there is an unexpected reroute as part of the CPDLC clearance.
1812089: We received an ACARS message that told us a box of horse tranquilizers may have been left on the aircraft from the previous flight. We did a search of the cockpit and found it in the storage area next to the Captain's seat. This bin usually contains the EFB charger and cable, extra headset, Ipad mount, and maybe a water bottle or two. It was a small black box, it blended in very well with the other jumble of black things. I missed it on the my cockpit inspection. Horse charters are unusual. Flight crews don't do them often and the requirement for the PIC to maintain control of the dangerous drugs the handlers carry is easily forgotten on block in. Treat that box of tranquilizers in the same way we deal with gear pins and pitot covers. Place a light weight, bright orange, pouch with a long orange flag in the logbook. The pouch and flag should say 'DANGEROUS MATERIALS' in big letters on the outside. Require a logbook write-up when the pouch is used. The write-up is cleared when the pouch is re-stowed. If the flight crews, AMTs, and cleaning crews see that pouch and flag, they will notify OPS.
1812101: Due to construction in the southeast portion of the airport, I did not enter the ramp for [the] gate at the correct entry point. Even though I thought I was intimately aware of the LGA environs, my expectation bias, compounded with non-standard taxi marking that made it appear that I was at the end of the taxiway, caused me to make a mistake. The irony of this event is when we departed Runway 31 earlier, both of us noted the crazy construction and the potential for mistakes that could happen in the close quarters. Prior to operating out of LGA for the first time in a long time, I reviewed the company notes/memos and our 10-7 pages. Both of us had our taxi charts up. When I noticed we were in the wrong position, I stopped the aircraft. We coordinated with the Ramp Control and was safely marshaled out after we restarted our left engine. Causes included expectation bias, poor taxiway markings, construction congestion. This was in daylight. Experienced crew. While I take responsibility, better markings would have made the difference, especially since we are all not at the top of our game with the reduced flights. Even though taxi configurations change during construction, this does not alleviate reasonable signage or markings. It is the cost of doing the work. I am sorry for the mistake. However, if this is the worst thing I do----it has been a good career. For me, it illustrated that I can always do better. Taxied down wrong alley in LGA.Cause - Taxied down wrong alley in LGA, expectation bias combined with new construction and unfamiliar with temporary entry points.Suggestions - Just try to stay current with the extensive and dynamic new construction at LGA.
1812103: Showed up to the gate at XA am from being assigned trips off reserve, met the Captain and the gate agent where we learned from the Gate Agent we had 2 non rev maintenance guys coming along with us. Went down to the aircraft where I started doing my checks and setting up my stuff, I came round from my walk around and started doing my 1st flight of the day checks. In the middle of while I was doing my 1st flight of the day flows the maintenance person asked me if he could bring his stuff up to the aircraft instead of the cargo bay I said sure (I heard him say tools and something else) as he walked out the jet bridge I paused for a minute and the Captain walked into the cockpit, he asked me where the maintenance guy was going. I told the Captain he went to get his tools and I think he said something about hydraulic fluid, I told the Captain I haven't read DG (Dangerous Goods) in a while but don't know if we can take it he agreed and went outside to tell the maintenance personnel to hold on for a second, he came back in sat in his seat pulled out the FOM and searched [but] could not find anything specific so decided to ring the duty pilot, at this point I carried on with my first flight of the day flows over hearing the conversation the Captain was having on the phone with the duty pilot, I heard something along of the line as it being explained as a hydraulic pump by hand in a little crate basically a little hand pump, and Captain was assured we are not taking any hydraulic fluid it's been emptied out might have a drop or two that was missed with a paper towel that's all... Captain looked at me and said don't know if you heard most of that which I replied I have he assured me we are not taking any hydraulic fluid and if I was comfortable going in which I told him in that case I have no issue going to fly. Well I believe we did everything that could have been done to ensure we were following SOP and company policy and procedure but there was a breakdown in communication between duty pilot / Maintenance Control and base Maintenance Manager where they forget to tell us we're taking canisters of hydraulic fluid. I was given Aircraft X on my first day of a four day reserve stretch. When I arrived at the gate I was informed that this was a maintenance (MX) reposition flight for an aircraft in ZZZ1. The two mechanics were sitting in the gate area and I went over to speak to them. I was informed the aircraft in ZZZ1 had issues with its hydraulic 2 quantity and that they had to head over and look at the system. I went back to the gate and got the paperwork, met my First Officer (FO), [Name], and went down to the aircraft. As we began doing our first flight of day items and loading the flight plan, I told [name] that I would go upstairs and inform the gate agent he could let the mechanics board. Unfortunately the agent was having issues with scanning the mechanics on, so I called our Dispatcher so we could have them put on the release and they could come down. On the jet-bridge with the mechanics one of them told me he wanted to go check if they had got the tools out to the aircraft yet and that he wanted to also 'make sure the pump would not be leaking'. I immediately asked him if he was referring to a hydraulic pump and he confirmed he was. I told him I had to contact the Operations Controller because there should be no hydraulic fluid on the airplane, especially not any that could be leaking. at XA:01am I called the Operations phone tree and connected myself to the Chief Pilot, [Name 2]. I told [Name 2] that Maintenance told me they were worried about a hydraulic pump that could leak in the cargo compartment and needed to know exactly what was going on with this reposition and the equipment I was bringing. [Name 2] agreed with me that no hydraulic fluid was allowed to be transported and we went through the FOM looking for any guidance on hydraulic pumps and transporting that type of equipment. Our joint search of the FOM was in [the] chapter under the Hazardous Materials and Dangerous Goods section. This call lasted 13 minutes and 7 seconds and we agreed that there was no exceptions about equipment such as a hydraulic pump and [Name 2] told me he was going to talk to the Maintenance Head in the Operations. at XA:18 am I missed a call from [Name 2] and he left a message saying 'I just got a little more info on that hydraulic pump so to speak on your guys repo flight. Apparently it's a ground servicing pump, basically a tool we are bringing down there for maintenance.' I called back at XA:19am and he explained to me that we were bringing a pump that Maintenance would use on the ground to pump fluid into a hydraulic system on the other aircraft. He told me that Maintenance confirmed it was washed out and did not contain any hydraulic fluid. I then went back and spoke to the mechanics to confirm this was the correct information. They said yes, the pump was indeed a servicing pump and it had been cleaned thoroughly prior to transport. With this information I and the conversation with Maintenance and the Operations Controller I decided that this was indeed a legal fight with cargo that was permitted in accordance with our FOM. On Date 2, I received a call from [Name 3] from the safety committee. He informed me that a Captain on the return flight for the broken aircraft was being asked to transport canisters of hydraulic fluid from ZZZ1 back to ZZZ and asked me if I knew anything about how they got there. I told [Name 3] that I had not transported any canisters from ZZZ to ZZZ1 and was under the impression that the pump and two tool kits were the only items aboard my aircraft. [Name 3] told me he would investigate further and call me back. [Name 3] called me back and informed me that we had unknowingly transported 2 canisters of Hy-Jet IV-A+ to ZZZ1 and informed me to fill out an ASAP with all pertinent details. Two Canisters of Hy-Jet IV-A+ were brought aboard Aircraft X ZZZ-ZZZ1 without knowledge to the flight crew. There was clear confusion and either misinformation or lack of information between the flight crew, Operations, and Maintenance. In the future on maintenance reposition flights, or any flight requiring equipment to be flown for maintenance, an itemized list of equipment that is being transported should be signed my maintenance personnel, one copy should go into records and the other copy should go to the flight deck to be reviewed by the flight crew. This way there is a clear paper trail of evidence and accountability in the event that anything like this should ever happen again.
1812109: Just prior to the EEP(ETOPS Entry Point) on a flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 we received an ACARS message from Dispatch informing us that a possible 'hoverboard' might have been loaded in the cargo area. It should not have been and with the dual concurrence of us and Dispatch it was decided that the safest course of action was an air return back to ZZZ. We discussed with Dispatch if they wanted us to burn down to a normal landing weight or land overweight. It was decided to land overweight and that Maintenance would met us at the gate and conduct the overweight inspection. We requested and received Runway 8L for landing due to its length and to minimize brake heating. The landing was normal and the overweight inspection was successfully accomplished and the 'hoverboard' was removed. Clearly, there was a breakdown somewhere that allowed an item of non approved Hazmat to be placed onboard the aircraft. How and why this happened is beyond the limited facts that I have available but I think a in-depth review of our processes and procedures with regards to these items would be warranted. Prior to reaching the ETOPS Entry Point and Oceanic Airspace, we received a message from Dispatch informing us of a safety of flight issue regarding some luggage onboard. A Hoverboard (non-permitted item) had somehow passed through TSA screening and had potentially been loaded in a cargo compartment. In conjunction with Dispatch, we felt the safest decision was to return to our departure airport of ZZZ. This required an overweight landing and maintenance inspection. Not only was the item found on our aircraft, but apparently two Hoverboards were found. More extensive checks or passenger questioning during the check-in and security phase. Passengers need to also be made aware of the seriousness of having such Hazmat items onboard a plane.
1812165: It has recently come to my attention that Maintenance performed prior to flight may not have been accurately or timely recorded in one or more of the aircraft's airframe, engine, and propeller logbooks. I have entered the date of the flight (Date 2) as the 'Date of Occurrence' at the top of this report, but I consider this report to be timely because I have only recently become aware that the confusing maintenance records it addresses could be problematic.On Date 1, I delivered my aircraft to an aircraft maintenance facility for an annual inspection, engine change, and related maintenance. During two months, I observed portions of the annual inspection and related maintenance work as that work was performed, and I observed portions of the work performed in changing the engine.After all work (including ground running of the newly-installed engine and ground testing of other aircraft systems) was completed, maintenance personnel advised me that the aircraft was ready to fly and should be flown to assure that its performance was satisfactory. Maintenance personnel asked me to fly the aircraft and I did so, remaining in the immediate vicinity of the airport. During that flight, an alternator bearing failed. I do not ascribe the bearing failure to any deficiency in the maintenance performed. Engine power was not affected and I conducted a normal landing upon observing the illumination of the aircraft's ALT OUT annunciator.The engine, propeller, and propeller governor were subsequently disassembled, inspected for contamination and repaired (or overhauled, in the case of the propeller governor), and re-installed in the aircraft. Following that work, the aircraft and its logbooks were returned to me by the maintenance facility. Those logbooks had remained in the continuous custody of the maintenance facility from the time I delivered them to the maintenance facility, until they were returned to me on or about Date 3.A maintenance-related event occurred with respect to the aircraft on Date 3. It was the subject of a report submitted by me. I have discussed that event with the owner of the maintenance facility. I have also reviewed the confusing logbook entries for the inspection and maintenance work described above. In the course of those discussions and that review, I have become aware of what appear to be errors, inconsistencies, or alterations in those entries, and I have brought them to the attention of the owner of the maintenance facility, for such corrective action as may be necessary or appropriate. Yesterday the owner of the maintenance facility agreed that corrective action may be necessary with respect to those entries, and I am therefore submitting this report today.

1812254: My Controller in Charge (CIC) issued a clearance to Aircraft X on the ground at HCR. The new procedure at HCR is that pilots are required to fly a Visual Climb Over Airport (VCOA) and remain within an arbitrary 5 mile radius of the airport and call us as soon as they're airborne. Aircraft X was given all of this information and chose to fly directly south into the SLC arrival flow. He called me initially at 14,000 feet, 10 miles south of HCR airport, in another sectors airspace. Prior to this his transponder was not on. I gave the pilot radar contact, and asked him to confirm his position, to which he stated he was 'south of the airport'. This procedure is unsafe. Other airports have higher terrain than we do and they have SID's off both directions that actually work when it's IFR.There's no reason that we can't have a Runway 22 SID that goes over NONTY. The aircraft could climb to cross NONTY at 15,000 feet which would deconflict from Sector 32's traffic, and the arrival flows into SLC. Other airports have these procedures and their terrain is much more complicated than ours. This procedure was called completely illegal and unsafe a year ago and all that's changed is you deleted a footnote from the 7110.65. We can't keep pretending this is safe, until someone gets hurt. We have a responsibility to the flying public to do better.
1812267: Training was in play at Local and Ground all day. There was flow with delays to ZZZ. Aircraft Y was taxied to Taxiway L short of M for eventual taxi via M to 1L for departure. Aircraft X was taxied to Runway 1R on the SSTIK4, which requires a red 'R' if requested/required by the pilot. It is unknown at this point if that was the case. My only assumption is that the Ground CPC-IT taxied the aircraft incorrectly to Runway 1R and the OJTI did not notice. As their flow time came up, Local CPC-IT taxied Aircraft Y across Runway 1R at M and LUAW Runway 1L. Aircraft X was given Runway 1R LUAW. The CPC-it then, unbeknownst to the OJTI, launched Aircraft X on the SSTIK4, and shortly thereafter launched Aircraft Y also on the SSTIK4. The only reason I became aware is when I heard the CPC-IT issuing visual separation and the Local Assist coordinating the same with NorCal. When I looked up at the display, the aircraft were approximately 2 miles in trail with Aircraft Y lower and following to SSTIK. Of note, with OJT occurring on both Local and Ground simultaneously, and Local Assist open, but apparently not engaged dynamically, the FLM could not possibly monitor both positions and all that the Local Assist was doing. Subsequent discussion by the Local Control OJTI dictated that they were sorry, as they missed it and 'Use of RNAV To... will save you every time.' This has been my complaint about people who refuse to use it and ignore that its use will in fact keep this exact scenario from occurring. The numbers of neigh-sayers are reducing thankfully and we will eventually have the majority compliance.The traffic has picked up over 700 operations a day a few days of the week and is expected to get busier by the month this summer. Use RNAV To... and, when working as OJTI, pay attention to what the CPC-IT is doing.
1812269: The Captain was flying and after takeoff the white FMC message dealing with the autothrottle appeared and the Pilot Flying noticed an amber EGT exceedance. The autothrottles and VNAV were inoperative at that point after takeoff. The TAT probe was indicating a higher than normal temperature which we determined to be the root cause of all the problems. We consulted with the QRH and Dispatch and all agreed to air return to ZZZ without any further issues. Just after takeoff the aircraft experienced a loss of data from the TAT probe (repeat gripe). This initially manifested itself as an autothrottle limit error and a rapid increase in #1 EGT (yellow backfill on gage but no other indications) and loss of VNAV and related FMC functions. We continued to climb to 16,000 feet MSL and informed ATC that we may need to return to ZZZ. I passed aircraft control to the FO and initiated radio contact with Dispatch. After initial contact, radio communications with Dispatch were lost, but Dispatch replied via ACARS that they agreed a return to ZZZ was prudent. Release was amended. ATC, cabin crew and passengers were informed, no emergency was declared. The aircraft returned to ZZZ without incident.TAT failure is a high workload event similar to unreliable airspeed. The number of items that rely on the TAT is huge, and once the event occurs there is (a) no real clue as to what the causal factor is, (b) no QRH guidance for the NN, and (c) a plethora of conflicting data and flight deck indications. Thought should be given to educating our Pilot group to the risks and indications associated with TAT failure.
1812274: Received a runway assignment change from Runway XX to Runway XYR after initial Runway XX briefing. Re-briefed the Runway XYR ILS and began approach. Between ZZZZZ and ZZZZZ1 intersections PF began descending to 1,500 feet. Altitude deviation was noted and a correction was made around 1,600 feet, shortly thereafter the tower issued a low altitude warning. Altitude was corrected back to 2,000 feet, approach and landing was accomplished without further incident. During debrief, crew agreed that expectation bias was a major contributing factor to the deviation. The PF was still thinking about the altitudes for the Runway XX ILS. It was the last leg of a three-day pairing so the PM did not properly back up the PF due to Pilot Flying's strong performance during the entire pairing. PM should not allow previous performance or experience to impact critical backup role. Initially set up and briefed for the ILS XX. New ATIS was obtained with runway change to XYR just prior to runway transition point on the ZZZZZ Arrival. Re briefed and set up for ILS XYR. Approach Control gave us a vector to intercept the Localizer XYR and then to descend to 2,000 feet from 4,000 feet outside of ZZZZZ [intersection] and then cleared us for the approach. I armed the localizer and set 2,000 feet, localizer captured and upon reaching 2,000 feet at ZZZZZ, I reverted to my previous briefing of the ILS XX and set 1,500 feet and proceeded to descend to 1,500 feet. Several hundred feet into the descent, Approach Control told us that we were low. Upon realizing what I had done I initiated a climb back to 2,000 feet from now 1,600 feet prior to ZZZZZ1. Reaching 2,000 feet prior to ZZZZZ1 and being stable again, we now continued to configure and resume the approach to land with no further incident.I should have verified my actions as I was accomplishing them and verified them with the PM. I was still in the mind set of what I had originally briefed and should have transitioned to the new approach even though we were rushed with the late runway change.
