1812431: Previous flight had reported engine fluctuations on takeoff and climbout. Maintenance took a look at the plane and Ops checked it good. On our takeoff, once takeoff thrust was set we began a normal reduced thrust takeoff with an EPR (Engine Pressure Ratio) setting of about 1.41. Once above 80 knots the Captain called out that the EGT and N1 were fluctuating and took control of the aircraft and performed the Reject. The auto brakes engaged at Max. We made the required callouts, cleared the runway and performed the QRC. We did receive HOT Brakes due to the reject and allowed them to cool before returning to the gate. Advancing power was normal with Flex FMA (Flight Mode Annunciator) displayed and EPR (Engine Pressure Ratio) thrust set prior to 80 kts. As the aircraft accelerated EPR indication on eng 1 began to fluctuate. As takoff roll continued EPR EGT and N1 began fluctuations with EPR going above yellow tick mark and almost as low as 1.3 EPR (TO EPR was 1.43). Reject was initiated at approximately 110 kts and we noticed ATC and cabin and cleared the runway to run the rejected to checklist. After allowing the brakes to cool we returned to the terminal.
1812437: Immediately after rotating we received a STEERING FAIL caution message. The tiller was not touched or contacted by any objects. We accomplished the QRH which did not remedy the situation. We contacted dispatch and decided that a landing in ZZZ was desired. Upon reaching ZZZ a low approach to check the orientation of the nose wheel was offered and accepted. After being notified that the nose appeared straight we made an approach and landing. We did not brace but did have ARFF standing by. While slowing below 80 knots the aircraft began to uncontrollably veer right. We attempted to use differential reverse thrust and braking but the aircraft continued its right trend towards the grass. I applied maximum braking and the aircraft came to a stop before exiting the runway. We advised ATC and ran the system reset procedure. This cleared the steering message and we taxied to the gate under our own power. While taxiing in we missed the turn onto taxiway 1 and received alternate instructions to taxi in via 2.
1812451: During initial climbout, I was the pilot flying. We were flying runway heading off of [Runway] XX to 4,000 feet as assigned. We had not yet received our clearance to climb higher. I began to reduce power and pitch in order to level off at 4,000. At 3,500 feet, and speed 240 KIAS, we were instructed to climb and maintain 10,000 MSL. I then smoothly added thrust and adjusted pitch to continue climbing utilizing FLC. Once I increased thrust, there was a loud bang, followed by the engine indications and crew alerting system indicating engine # 1 was out. Additionally, a yawing tendency towards the INOP engine. Once identified by both pilots, controls were transferred to the Captain and I assumed PM duties. Normal checklists were complete, ATC and company was notified and the QRH procedure for engine out was accomplished. Engine fluid levels were normal, and the engine was shut down, which did not require the pulling of the #1 fire extinguishing handle. Once concluded a restart was not advised after discussion, due to the loud bang and sudden shutdown, we then were directed by the QRH to execute one engine inoperative approach and landing. The FA was notified and provided a [crew] brief, followed by the passenger announcement. We then coordinated with ATC for radar vectors for the visual, backed up by the RNAV XX in ZZZ. Once landed, we stopped on the runway, had the engine inspected by the ZZZ fire department. Verification was made that there was no fire, fluid leakage and we then taxied off the runway and parked at [the] gate for deplaning. Loud bang, aircraft yaw and EICAS indications by both pilots leading to the engine out procedure. Cause is still to be determined, from the initial inspection, the mechanical issue caused small metal fragments found in the compressor blades. After identifying the issue, we transferred flight controls, had a brief discussion and executed the pertinent QRH procedures for engine failure and a single engine approach and landing. No suggestions to report at this time. We were climbing out of ZZZ of Runway XX on runway heading and were just about to level off at 4,000 ft so the FO (PF) reduced thrust. Just before we leveled off we were given a continued climb up to 10,000 ft. While reintroducing thrust at 4,000 ft we heard a loud bang followed by aircraft yaw. I immediately looked at the EICAS and saw an abrupt stop in the #1 engine. I called for my Aircraft. The First Officer and I briefly discussed the situation then promptly ran the QRH for Engine OUT. The engine was shut down and our fluid levels (hydraulic/oil) looked normal so we decided against pulling the fire extinguishing handle. We discussed the possibility of restarting the engine but decided against it because of the loud bang we had heard followed by the abrupt shutdown of the engine. We were then led to [procedure] and proceeded to get set up for the Single engine approach. After finishing talking to the passengers, flight attendant and sending a message to dispatch we completed all other normal checklists. We then executed the visual approach backed up by RNAV RWY XX into ZZZ without any further event. We landed and had the fire department check out our engine for signs of smoke, fire, or fluid leak and then proceeded to the gate.The first indication of the Engine failure was a loud bang followed by aircraft yaw. We then looked at the EICAS and saw the indications of a #1 engine failure. We were not given a definitive cause for the failure. It seems to have been a mechanical issue inside the Engine. Upon inspection after landing chunks of metal were found inside the compressor blades. After noticing the event. We transferred flight controls then briefly discussed our situation and decided to run the checklist for Engine Failure in the QRH .
1812515: Originally departed for ZZZ1, shortly after departure we received a LEVEL l FADEC CAUTION message. Asking for box pattern vectors with departure, we ran the checklist. Checklist called for L engine idle and the possibility of the engine shutting down. As we ran through it a few more times with the left engine at idle, the LEVEL l FADEC CAUTION message turned into a LEVEL l FADEC FAULT STATUS message followed by a R FADEC FAULT STATUS message. We were communicating with dispatch to coordinate a continue or air return, we decided it's best to return to ZZZ as there was a previous issue with the FADEC computer system and clearly something was wrong. Upon vectors to land, the rest of the flight continued safely back to ZZZ airport. No emergency was declared nor was it necessary.Aircraft had a write up from the previous crew. Maintenance ran the engines and could not replicate. Aircraft was signed off and okay to go.Both Captain and FO worked very well together. Thanks to company standards and sim training we worked very efficiently to identify and eliminate the threat. Air return to ZZZ due to L FADEC caution during climb out. Dispatch and Maintenance notified and agreed. QRH completed, no emergency declared, return to ZZZ without incident. After a plane swap original flight to ZZZ1 [was] completed.Previous flight had reported a L FADEC FAULT 1 and a R FADEC FAULT 2 white status messages in climb, intermittent. ZZZ ops checked the engines and cleared the plane for flight. We didn't experience any engine or FADEC issues on departure until we reached 8,000 ft. L FADEC CAUTION lasted for a few minutes while we ran the QRH and communicated with dispatch and Maintenance Control. L FADEC CAUTION cleared when replaced by L FADEC FAULT 1 and R FADEC FAULT 2 white status messages. Decision was made to return to ZZZ (close proximity and maintenance capabilities) without objection or incident.
1812538: On the departure, the First Officer (FO) had requested Heading Mode (HDG), Flight Level Change (FLCH) during the climb out as we were given a heading. It was bumpy and he was trying to comply with the SID instructions to speed up to 250 KIAS while hand flying in bumpy air. As we approached the 5,000 foot altitude restriction, he started to slow his climb for the level off, but didn't pull back on the thrust levers. The autothrottles were on, but we were not quite close enough to the altitude for the flight director to switch to 'ASEL' on the FMA and begin capturing. In a climb, the auto throttles remain at full thrust in green FLCH until ASEL is annunciated, and since the FO was hand flying and beginning the level off before the Altitude Select (ASEL) annunciation, the speed began to pick up. As pilot monitoring, I noticed the airspeed at 255 KIAS with an increasing trend and I called out 'airspeed' to alert him to the airspeed. He seemed confused and did not make any corrections. I then called for him to 'pitch up' which he did slightly, but he mentioned the level off altitude that was approaching. I said to 'pull the thrust back' and he seemed confused again and replied that the auto throttles should do that. I then pulled the thrust levers back myself to slow the aircraft down as the speed was starting to go past 260 KIAS. ATC gave us a 'climb and maintain 7000' and a direct to one of the fixes. The FO pitched up for the climb and I was able to let go of the thrust levers as the speed was again under control. As we were climbing, ATC instructed us to climb to 16,000 and the FO called for 'Autopilot On' prior to the next level off so there were no further issues. I reminded him that there is no speed protection in the level off for the FLCH mode if he is hand flying it and levels off early. ATC didn't seem to notice the increased airspeed, and the flight continued without further incident.The FO said that he finished IOE and for the next month was unable to get any flying from crew scheduling. He had less than 30 hours on the aircraft. The following month, he had to be in Country to check on family due to the COVID pandemic. He said that he had flown earlier that day and seemed to be comfortable in the plane. It became clear that he was rusty on the details concerning the FLCH mode. After I spoke with him about what happened, he said he understood and he did not make the same mistake on his flight the following day. Any time a pilot has less than 100 hours (consolidation) on an aircraft, and doesn't fly for more than 30 days, they should be given a trip with an IOE instructor both to give them recency of experience and to refresh any forgotten material. During take off climbing to the assigned altitude of 5,000 in flight level change plane accelerated to 250K, during last 1,000 ft I shallowed the pitch as climb was getting a bit bumpy due to builds up around [the] area and I was trying to avoid flying through a cloud straight ahead. Captain advised me of speed increasing and passing 250 and I assumed the auto-throttle would have compensated for that as it was engaged. Leveling off to 5,000 speed past 260 and the Captain reached out the thrust lever decreasing power avoiding further deviation. Soon after cleared to 7,000 climb and flight continued with no further deviation. After IOE I was put on reserve and didn't fly for about a month, I then was able to pick up a line and fly just one sequence as a tragic event forced me to drop the rest of the month and travel overseas, as a result in 2 months I only flew 19 hours and that was my first day flying after a long stop. As newly typed on a new airplane I didn't immediately recalled the different ways the autothrottle responds, however soon after the event my Captain explained [to] me what happened and refreshed my memory on it. After IOE it would be good to assign some extra flight to help consolidate, maybe assigning more frequent flights and not letting more than 2 weeks without flying would avoid skills deterioration until the first 100 hours are reached.
1812548: Approaching PVD on radar vectors for the visual approach Runway 23. Small GA aircraft on VFR and not in contact with ATC got into close proximity of our flight path. We reacted with an RA and maneuvered on a climb per TCAS instructions to clear conflict. GA aircraft was believed to be within 300 ft of vertical separation. On final approach the runway had a trash bag and other FOD, so the ground crew failed to clear the FOD from the runway causing a go around instructed by ATC. Go around executed around 700 ft AGL. [Caused by] aircraft flying VFR near complex airspace. And trash bag on runway. Followed per [company] procedures in both cases. Encourage VFR traffic to be in radar contact if flying near complex airspace.
1812549: When we left ZZZ we had to MEL Pack 1 due to abnormal shutdown. Flight was conducted at FL250 to comply with the MEL. When we leveled off at FL250, Captain and I smelled smoke like wires were burning and saw that smoke a white/gray smoke was coming through the vents. At about that time [the] flight attendant called up and said there was smoke coming from the back of the plane and a loud noise from the pack. Captain and I followed the memory items for smoke/fire/fumes. We then contacted ATC, [requested priority] to descent to the nearest station of ZZZ1. While running the checklist we isolated the problem and the smoke went away. Landed safely in ZZZ1. Flight Attendant did a very good job with handling the situation in the back. The Maintenance met us at the gate and told us that Pack 2 had failed.
1812551: The following narrative is due to a complete lack of threat and error management and operation performance. This was the first leg of a 4 day trip and I would be flying with a First Officer for the first time. We were heavily delayed to start our day and weather was terrible. High winds and windshear were reported throughout the whole Company system with several crews diverting. Yet my release for this flight indicated nothing other than I should evaluate the use of Runway XX for ZZZ departure. When the aircraft arrived I met the arriving Captain and he explained to me the auto pilot master warning EICAS message occurred at 1,000 feet on the coupled ILS approach into ZZZ. The Captain stated maintenance refused to take the write ups as it was going to ZZZ1 and they would casually look at it there. I immediately called maintenance and asked why they wouldn't take write ups and said from what it sounded like a write up was not warranted. The maintenance controller asked if I wished to MEL the autopilot and I stated how can I? At this point I should have immediately refused the plane, but at Company, refusing to fly gets us an immediate phone call from the Chief Pilot office. We Were now operating in the red of the threat and error management philosophy. On the way to ZZZ1 we experienced moderate turbulence as expected and when we turned base for Runway XY the field was surrounded by virga. The FO and I briefed a go around and the windshear escape maneuver once more. On final at about 1,200 feet the Autopilot Fail master warning EICAS message appeared and the Autopilot disconnected. I continued to hand fly the aircraft and remained stable to about 300 feet where I encountered increasing performance and the approach became unstable. A normal go-around was executed and we called positive rate gear up, we received the windshear caution. Immediately after we hit severe turbulence. We diverted to ZZZ without further incident. The remainder of the flight was performed without the autopilot.Company maintenance did not take a write up from a Captain. I wrote up the AP failure and the encounter with severe turbulence. All write-ups must be taken by maintenance.
1812556: Shortly after reaching cruising altitude of 5000 ft. MSL I was just about to cancel my IFR clearance and proceed to ZZZ1 with VFR advisories with a decent to 3500 ft MSL. After leaving the ZZZ Class B. I received a Traffic Alert on the Garmin 430 showing a target less then 1 mile and at 12 o'clock but with no altitude beside it. This prompted me to immediately look up and scan for traffic, I noticed a light almost immediately and directly ahead of me, seconds later, I passed beneath the drone by approximately 25 feet. In that moment I was able to determine it was a white, 4 bladed drone, approximately the size of a microwave. The light I had seen appeared to be just that, or a possible camera that the sun was reflecting off of. There was not enough time to react, due to this, I continued on my IFR clearance for a few more miles, while I reported the incident to ATC. After the report to ATC, I notified [company] of the event and asked them to issue a PIREP for those heading into ZZZ. There was one passenger onboard, however, they were unaware of this incident. The flight concluded safely with no aircraft damage. Cause: Unauthorized drone activity.
1812562: After completion of pushback and after receiving salute I flashed the landing light. The push lead and a wing walker were observed walking away as the tug backed away from the aircraft. Approximately 10-15 meters off the nose a small bag which apparently contained the push headset fell out of the tug cab where the bag and the headset fell apart laying on the ramp. The tug driver saw it fall out his side of the cab and stopped. As the tug driver stepped out of tug it began to roll towards our aircraft with the tow bar still mounted on the front like a battering ram. The tug driver immediately jumped back in the cab and stopped the tug and manipulated some controls. The cab driver was the only one in tug and rest of pushback crew was oblivious as they walked back to gate area. I don't know if the tug has a parking brake but the tug driver again stepped out of the tug while it idled away from the aircraft towards the terminal. The unmanned tug continued towards the terminal at a walking pace while the tug driver scooped the headset into the bag and then he jogged back and jumped in the moving tug. The tug now under manned control continued back to the gate are and we taxied out for departure.I don't know if it was complacency or rushing to get out of our way or both but I would like to think push tugs both have a park position as well as a park brake both if which should have been used in this case in my opinion. Emphasize safety to ramp members to protect persons and property.
1812687: I was flying visual by myself learning new autopilot and running it thru the ILS 35 approach sequence but visually. Lots of traffic in the area (at least 3-4 planes). I was making radio calls and position reports and other were also, but it was hard to keep track of everyone. Note BJC was not supporting practice [approaches] due to ATC limits and I think more were flying up north than normal. Right traffic for [Runway] 28 crosses 35 runway. I was watching a plane doing touch and go patterns on 28. I went thru the missed procedure (visually) a little earlier than minimum. I was climbing out on 350 heading, but another plane also crossed from my left and I didn't see [it] until late and until I had climbed to its altitude. I don't know if it was in pattern or traversing the area. I was climbing and turned steep left. They also turned steep to their left. My attention was split mostly outside and but some inside to sequence the AP. I believe I had right of way, but if there is a collision, it won't matter. I had traffic on my iPad and panel. But with so many close targets it wasn't useful. Had I not started climb early, I would not have reached pattern altitude so quickly. Also, even if not under the hood a safety pilot is a good idea in congested areas.
1812704: I acted as the pilot-in-command and sole occupant of a Cessna 402 aircraft on a flight in visual meteorological conditions. Prior to departure, I conducted a preflight inspection in accordance with the manufacturer's recommended procedures, and I followed the preflight checklist. All systems appeared to operate normally during takeoff, climb, and cruise flight.During the approach to landing, I monitored the UNICOM frequency when another pilot approximately 4-5 miles ahead of me, approaching the same runway, advised that there was turbulence on final approach. While on short final approach, I experienced turbulence and added power to maintain a proper glide path. At that point, I noticed that the left (i.e., critical) engine was no longer producing power. As a result, the aircraft nose yawed left (i.e., toward the dead engine) and I applied full right rudder to maintain directional control.Since I was on a short final approach to the runway, I reduced power in order to land while maintaining my airspeed above Vmc (i.e., minimum controllable airspeed with critical engine failure). However, the gusty wind drifted the airplane to the left of center line. Since I had applied full right rudder to maintain runway centerline while in flight, upon touchdown the airplane aggressively spun to the right and departed the runway, which caused the landing gear to collapse.When the aircraft came to a complete stop, I shut down the right engine, secured the aircraft, and exited through the cabin door without incident.
1812712: While flying a survey mission over the area at 15,500 ft VFR we saw a small drone flying below us at about 14,500 ft. The drone was about the size of DJI drone and gray in color. It was moving south as we were going north, so we didn't have much time to make out the exact size. We immediately reported to TRACON. For the remaining two hours of our survey mission we did not see it again.
1812716: During a multi engine training flight, during a touch and go, as full power was applied to initiate the next takeoff, I saw the right fuel flow drop to zero. At that moment the student (who is also commercial multi rated but learning to be an multi engine instructor) rotated and began initial climb. Because of the touch and go we did not have the runway remaining to abort the takeoff or land on the remaining runway, so I took the flight controls expecting the right engine to die while continuing the initial climb. The right engine died within a matter of seconds (at about 300 AGL), and I was able to climb to just below traffic pattern altitude, feather the right propeller, and land safely with proper landing clearance. Maintenance reported failure of the engine driven fuel pump and the likelihood that the auxiliary fuel pumps did not do their job of providing adequate fuel pressure to run the engine at full power. The entire fuel system has since been replaced.
1812726: I was PIC on a Part 91 flight departing Fairbanks. I informed the Ground Controller on initial call up that my requested outbound heading was 232. When I received my takeoff clearance for [Runway] 2L the Tower Controller instructed me to fly runway heading. When he passed me off to Departure Control the Departure Controller instructed me to 'turn right on course.' I thought the right turn was unusual due to my requested heading of 232 but I choose not to further query the Controller because I assumed the right turn was to avoid traffic. Shortly after I started the right turn I noticed an aircraft directly in my flight path that had just departed runway Ski Strip 2. I started turning left to avoid the aircraft and at the same time the Departure Controller said something to the effect of '[callsign] turn left, turn left now.' I estimate the distance was no more than one or two hundred feet.
1812750: Myself and my Captain were flying our final leg from ZZZ to HWD. Conditions were night VMC and we had the Hayward city and airport location in sight. The Captain was pilot flying and I was pilot monitoring. The Captain was manually flying and our clearance was to maintain 4,000 until established on the localizer. I went into my iPad to look at my charts, a few moments later I heard the Controller tell us, 'low altitude alert, check altitude immediately, MVA is 3,900.' When I looked over at the Captain's PFD, I saw we had descended to between 3,300-3,400 feet. The Captain took over the radios and corrected the altitude and continued uneventfully.
1812774: I was in the traffic pattern doing touch and go landings with a student at ZZZ (one of five aircraft in the pattern). We were approaching mid-field right downwind for Runway XX, and tower advised that we were following another aircraft on base, which we advised we had in-sight (which was number two, making us number 3.) As we approached our base leg, tower told us the base turn was our discretion, and we began turning base. As soon as we did so, the traffic we were following (Aircraft Y) called tower and advised that they needed to do a 360 for spacing (it appeared they had turned their base leg too soon, and were too close to the traffic they were following. Tower approved and notified them that once they completed their 360 to watch out for us, and that they would be now following us (making us now #2 for the runway, and them #3).My student turned final and we were on an approximately 1.5 nm final, descending through 700-800 feet, when my student stated, 'I think they're turning right at us!'Simultaneously Aircraft Y had apparently just completed their 360 turn and Tower inquired if they had us in sight and were to follow us, they stated they were looking for traffic.I looked up to suddenly see the other aircraft heading directly across our final approach path, and almost on a head-on course, coming at us approximately from 45 degrees off of our left nose. As I looked, I also simultaneously received an ADS-B traffic alert from Foreflight on my iPad, indicated the other traffic, heading directly at us and at the same altitude.I immediately stated 'my controls', took over control of the aircraft, and quickly began a descending turn to the right to create distance from the other traffic, I looked up again and saw the other aircraft also start a sharp bank to their right, while simultaneously telling the tower that they now had us in-sight. I remained in control of the aircraft and executed an (otherwise) uneventful landing.Tower did not acknowledge the event. It seemed that the controller was very task saturated with the five aircraft in the pattern. It seemed they were also distracted by a King Air 350 that was handed over to tower from ZZZ Approach and setup for a right downwind for Runway XX. Initially tower had told them to enter left downwind, but they were adamant that they wanted right downwind, which I believe both added to the confusion, as well as tied up the tower frequency unnecessarily with their continued back and forth communications. It did not help that the King Air had requested and was then doing a 360 turn for spacing of their own, right on the upwind leg of Runway XX when there were multiple other aircraft in the traffic pattern.It should be noted that while we were on short final, the Aircraft Y involved in this incident had once again turned base too soon, and I noticed that they were less than 0.5nm behind us. They were so close that they in fact were ordered to go-around by the Tower because we had just touched down and were still rolling out when they crossed the runway threshold behind us.I believe contributing to the incident were: The pilot of Aircraft Y failing to maintain situational awareness resulting in inadequate spacing thus requesting multiple 360 turns, their failure to adequately scan for traffic and maintain a proper rectangular course in the traffic pattern causing them to cross our final approach course at a 45 degree angle, tower controller being task saturated with multiple aircraft in the traffic pattern, and the King Air traffic adding to the confusion by adamantly requesting to enter the right downwind (which conflicted with the other aircraft already in the traffic pattern for Runway XX, which is right traffic.)
1812797: It was a busy day in the pattern at LMO and BJC was closed for pattern work. I had already done one lap in the pattern at LMO and was in the downwind for another lap. In the downwind, the skydiving operation announced a few times, 'Jumpers away'. I saw them and told my student to make a slightly wider pattern to accommodate them. Just as we made a slight deviation, an aircraft, Aircraft Y, entered the pattern mid field downwind and my ADS-B indicated they were the same altitude as us. Aircraft Y announced they had 'downwind traffic in sight' but it was likely another plane. They cut us off not only in the downwind, but also headed straight for the jump zone. The jump plane announced frantically 'parachutes have been deployed'. I was careful not to climb or descend while I did not have Aircraft Y in sight because ADS-B indicated they were same altitudes. We did not see them until they were passing just under us. Once I saw them, I asked their intentions with no response. I decided it was best to depart the airport back to BJC. Upon returning to BJC, I spoke with many instructors from different flight schools in the area and it seems like the traffic pattern at LMO has become increasingly dangerous. Many instructors have had near misses with other pilots not making calls or entering the pattern however they wish.
1812824: Tower requested release on Aircraft X, IFR, filed ZZZ.ZZZZZ.ZZZ with a requested altitude of FL230, runway heading. The remarks stated that they were requesting to follow the ZZZZZ2 SID, but the routing was not filed that way. When Aircraft X checked on, the language barrier hindered me from properly understanding what they were requesting to do. I asked a few times what their intent was. In the final exchange, I was able to understand that they were level at 1,500 MSL in a 2,300 MVA (Minimum Vectoring Altitude). I immediately said, '...negative, climb and maintain 080.' No further issues were experienced and I was able to get them on their requested routing.
1812829: All events through pushback were accomplished without note. During pushback, a puddle on the ramp aft of the normal oil spot was noticed behind the #2 engine. Puddle was not present on the walkaround. A stream of drops along the ramp was also noticed while the #2 engine was run. After five minutes the fuel leak had not stopped and we towed back to a gate. Maintenance was called, ran several tests, and two engine runs. The leak dissipated as the tests were completed. No fuel appeared to be leaking while engines were running, except for one within limits from the heat exchanger. Forms were completed to indicate it. Aircraft pushed and started again. No leaks were noted.Shortly after takeoff/cleanup, Captain announced a split in the thrust levers. Autothrottles were used for takeoff with VNAV (climb page 2L adjusted for 202 knots at 1,000 feet AGL). Looking at the engine instruments, I noticed the #2 thrust lever about three knob widths ahead of the #1. #1 N1 was at commanded power with the #2 N1 showing the white commanded power bar of about 95%, but the engine only producing about 88-89%. Further advancement of the throttle lever produced no increase in power. Vertical Speed was selected and we reduced our climb rate to bring the power back. As the power came back, the throttle synced and power matched. VNAV was reselected and as the power returned to full climb, the split reappeared with the #2 indicating a commanded increase without the engine delivering the power.As this was being discussed, the center tank fuel pumps were turned on (750 pounds in the center tank). Immediately after the pumps were turned on, the power matched and all indication were normal. As soon as the center tank fuel was exhausted, the split returned. Crew leveled at FL 270 and elected to return to ZZZ. As power was less than full climb at cruise/descent, and no abnormal indication were present during these flight conditions, no QRH Checklists were run. The rest of the return to ZZZ was completed without note. Engine performed as expected from level off to shutdown.Contract Maintenance expressed an increased level of calls from aircraft coming from the paint shop, fuel leaks were common with these aircraft. Would recommend a Maintenance individual check and run engines prior to returning the aircraft to the line. Origination flight on an aircraft that had just come out of the paint shop. Preflight was uneventful with no fuel drips or puddles noted. We pushed five minutes early. On push back #2 was dripping fuel and did not stop after a short time and engine was shutdown. After consultation with Maintenance Control, we returned to the gate and called Contract Maintenance. Contract Maintenance did four motoring tests as directed by [company's] Maintenance. With each test, the dripping became improved. Then an engine run was completed with decreased dripping, but not to a small enough level to allow Dispatch. Contract Maintenance then opened the cowl and did an engine run to determine location of drip. After that run, the component dripping was identified and the dripping had decreased to an amount that allowed MEL. MEL was completed. This was about a 2.5 hour process. Ground Ops and Operations were very helpful with accommodating the Passengers as well as they could. I had given periodic in-person updates to the passengers. Finally, we pushed-back and the engine starts were uneventful without any drips. Uneventful taxi. We took off on Runway XX with a headwind 20G30. On push up of thrust, #2 lagged a bit and I pushed the thrust lever up to get closer to match and continued my crosscheck. As we approached V1/VR I noticed #2 still lagging by a few percent and pushed up the throttle some more. Normal on centerline liftoff and climbout. After liftoff, I informed the F/O (First Officer) that we had a split throttle situation. We cleaned up on schedule and began to evaluate the situation (again the aircraft had no adverse flight characteristics). With the aircraft cleaned up and climb power set, we observed that although the #2 demand pointer was correct, the #2 N1 lagged approximately 2-5% N1. Once our climb rate was reduced in Vertical Speed and at a slightly lower climb thrust setting, the engine was normal and tracked normally with the demand pointers and thrust lever position. To this point we had continued to follow ATC instructions to keep it simple. We found that the engine reacted the same with the autothrottle On or Off. Also we had 750 pounds of fuel in the center tank, so once established in the climb we turned the pumps on and immediately #2 N1 returned to normal operation at full climb power. When center tank was empty and pumps turned off, the malfunction returned. With this information we leveled off and informed ATC that we would probably need to return to the airport. While level we reconfirmed no other abnormal conditions or switches out of place. Also at level flight in this situation there were no conditions that warranted a QRH Checklist although it was discussed. F/O and I discussed the situation and decided that without the aircraft able to achieve full climb thrust on Main Fuel pumps only, the safest choice was to return to the airport. F/O flew and talked to ATC, while I informed flight attendants and passengers of need to return to the airport for safety reasons and gave them our ETA. I called Station Ops on VHF and informed them of our need to return, get a gate, and asked them to contact Dispatch. We also confirmed via ACARS with Dispatch the need to return due to engine unable to achieve full climb power (or something like that). The F/O did a very good job and stayed ahead of the aircraft preparing for the briefings, descent, and Approach Checklist. We referenced the Diversion Checklist to ensure we had covered the suggested items. We accomplished a normal descent and asked for a long visual approach to increase probability of a stable approach and landing without the need for a thrust needful go-around. F/O flew stable approach and landing with normal braking. No emergency was declared, no special handling requested, and a normal weight landing occurred. Uneventful taxi-in and shutdown. Flight was canceled and the passengers accommodated as best as Ops could. Debrief with the flight attendants yielded that although disappointed in their flight being cancelled, they were appreciative of the Safety of turning back. Immediate notification with XXXXXX was done after engine shutdown with Dispatch, Supervisor, Maintenance, and Chief Pilot.The Location X crews both above the wing and below the wing were very familiar with the Maintenance trouble shooting of engine drips on starts because they have seen it more the once from aircraft coming out of the paint shop. An engine run after paint shop would have found this problem before a revenue flight was disrupted. Maybe this may be a prudent practice--an ounce or prevention may have saved a pound of Customer frustration. Perhaps a faster crosscheck by myself might have allowed a reject option in the 70-90 knot range, but even then there was no decrease in power and I perceived the N2 engine thrust close-enough to N1 engine thrust to ensure a safer option than a medium speed reject.
1812835: We were told to taxi by tower after landing on [Runway] 10L and contact Ramp Control. When we contacted Ramp Control they said we had entered the ramp without clearance, but we were still on a designated taxiway. My First Officer and I tried to find out exactly what is considered 'the ramp' on any of the charts or airport pages, but could not find any description of what is actually 'a ramp' or 'a taxiway' anywhere. We looked for signs on the way out but there weren't any. There were some alternating double-dashed lines in FLL around what I would consider 'the ramp' that were about 100 yards off the various concourses, but we were nowhere near those when we taxied in. One factor in this whole thing is the FO contacted the Ramp control frequency on the 10-9 page for North Ramp but only South Ramp was open. But we still were not in or on the ramp when we got that mess sorted out.
1812840: We finished the first leg of three on the last day of a three-day trip. We pulled into the gate at LAS with a scheduled plane swap. After completing the Parking Checklist and other post-flight duties, I cleared the FO to head out while I stayed with the aircraft while passengers deplaned. Ground power was connected initially but air was not. As deplaning commenced, I asked the agent to call for ground air. It was 106F OAT and I was concerned about cabin temp. I understood from the agent that the aircraft would be on the ground for some time. After all passengers were off, I went outside and asked Ramp to connect ground air. A few minutes later one of the guys came to the cockpit and informed me that ground air was inop. In the meantime, one of the new FAs (flight attendants) came onboard saying she came down early because the terminal was very crowded. As the situation progressed I decided to leave the APU on for cabin cooling, informed the FA and agent and went on to my new aircraft. At the time I didn't give it a second thought. It wasn't until I got to the new aircraft, finished preflight duties and had a few minutes to reflect that I realized my error. Sick feeling. I told the FO that I would be back and hustled back to the previous gate to remedy my mistake. Probably 30 minutes or so had elapsed since I had left it. By the time I got back to the gate The new crew was onboard and passengers were boarding.I must say that I didn't feel any type of particular time pressure or any major distraction. I'm not sure why my thought process went so awry. While this situation is not common, I'm sure it's not unheard of and I should know better than to leave the APU running and Terminating Checklist incomplete. I certainly could have stayed with the aircraft until the new Crew arrived.I am sure that I hadn't reviewed FOM in some time so unless I'm the only one who has messed up this way, adding that to our training profile may raise awareness to this issue and prevent someone else from making the same mistake.
1812850: After starting the #1 engine during a single engine taxi out, I shut down the APU. This was done immediately after my workload increased significantly. Since we were on a MAX we chose to start the second engine early on the taxi out to [Runway] XXR, but engine motoring continued until we were crossing Runway XXL. My attention was split between monitoring the engine start and looking outside during the runway crossing. By the time we were clear I was concentrating on the remaining taxi distance for our three minute warmup. I went through the normal After Start Flow without thinking about leaving the APU running. My mistake was not caught by either of us on the Before Takeoff Checklist, only on the climb out through about 8,000 feet.We should have slowed down. There were many factors causing us to rush. The gate was unusual for (Company) operations, and we had to deal with broken jetway stairs and ground power that was disconnected during boarding. These were both stress inducers, and we should have recognized that we were being pushed into the Yellow before we even left the gate. The Captain was unfamiliar with the airport. I could have done a better job walking him through the taxi procedures. I should have realized this would cause a distraction while starting the second engine. We were on a MAX departing for an ETOPS flight, and fuel is almost always a consideration during taxi out. We chose to delay APU start at the gate and single engine taxi to conserve as much as possible. We even briefed the earlier start because of lengthy MAX engine motoring, but it still wasn't early enough to be complete before crossing [Runway] XXL. We should have started the engine earlier so I could concentrate on one thing at a time. Both the Captain and I were new to ETOPS flying. We were in and out of the Yellow during preflight as we worked through the extra preflight procedures. We should have given ourselves more time to complete these tasks. During taxi out, at an unfamiliar airport, a delayed engine start of engine #1 was performed by the F/O, due to a long taxi to the runway. During the After Start Flow performed by the F/O, he inadvertently shut the APU off, which was required for this ETOPS flight. I missed the fact that the APU was OFF during the 'Before Takeoff' checklist, and a normal takeoff was performed. During the climb, at approximately 7000 feet, it was discovered that the APU was off, so I started the APU prior to reaching 10,000 feet. The flight continued without incident. At no time did the aircraft fly in Class II operations with the APU off.
1812914: The event happened at night on taxi out from gate to Runway XXL. There were significant amounts of thunderstorms surrounding ZZZ requiring the airport to only have Runway XXL for takeoff and XXR for landing. Upon leaving the ramp area, we were given clearance to taxi to XXL via Taxiways '1' then [Taxiway] '23.' We turned north on [Taxiway] '1' and followed a B737. The B737 aircraft stopped holding short of [Taxiway] '23.' After about 30 seconds it proceeded and turned onto [Taxiway] 23 and we followed. It was as we turned onto [Taxiway] 23 that both the Captain and I heard the ATC Ground Controller give excited directions to 'hurry up/go fast.' The key point here is that we never heard our call sign used for any of these calls and assumed he was talking to someone else. As we advanced to a position abeam Runway XXR on our right, the Ground Controller called our call sign and I responded. He then told us, using our call sign, to 'go fast, aircraft on short final to Runway XXR.' We saw the conflict and tried to move faster but it was too late and the aircraft was forced to execute a go-around. The Controller told us the aircraft had to go-around and chastised us for missing several calls. I responded that we 'never heard it.'Ultimately, I believe one of two things happened--either the Controller made several excited transmissions either omitting our call sign or used an incorrect call sign, or both the Captain and I missed several radio calls made to us until a conflict happened. We had been reassigned after a long weather delay and misconnect out of ZZZ. We had to consult with dispatch to confirm our clearance and routing. ZZZ ATC had reconfigured airport and were landing and departing runways XXL/R. At spot X we were instructed to taxi to XXL, [Taxiway] 1, [Taxiway] 23. As we approached [Taxiway] 23 a B737 was stopped ahead of us. That aircraft then turned onto [Taxiway] 23. We followed, no instructions to hold short of the XXR approach was given. The Ground Controller then told the B737 to hurry, then told us to hurry and cross XXR approach, saying that we were expected to hold short of [Taxiway] 23. We were not instructed to hold short of Taxiway 23.
1812952: On approach to landing, engines would not idle. Captain was able to slow and stabilize on profile although it required abnormally low throttle setting. Engines would still not idle on taxi in and throttle settings and thrust were not matched.
1812958: Normal takeoff right seat [as] Line Check Airman. Level FL360 at 10 minutes red Cabin Altitude EICAS with Aural Warning. Cabin at 10,500 feet but not climbing significantly. Transfer flight controls to left seat pilot, ran cabin altitude QRC and started [priority] descent to 15,000 feet. ATC advised. After switching to auto 1 cabin controller, seemed to stabilize at at FL240 and warning light went out on EICAS, cabin seemed to descend. Due to terrain and a stable cabin we climbed to FL190. Thunderstorm avoidance and normal approach and landing to [Runway] XXR back at ZZZ. Left seat pilot made landing. Initially, the Controller did not hear [us advising] had to [re-advise] at 15 minutes into event. Cabin was stable but fluctuating inbound. On the ground, the mechanics came to the cockpit to tell us the main PC air distribution duct was broken and not connected. This caused the inability for the aircraft to pressurize.
1813004: During climbout from CVG, we were given a climb to 13,000 feet and cleared to WADAL intersection. Passing out of 9,000 feet (climbing at 1500 feet/min) we were told to contact Indy Center on 135.57. We checked in with Indy Center (135.57) and stated we were climbing to 13,000 feet. Passing through about 10,000 feet, the TCAS gave an aural TA warning and the display popped up on the MFD. It showed an aircraft 800 feet above us descending at our 12 O'clock position towards us (about 6 miles out). At the same time, Indy center issued a turn 15 degrees to the left. Simultaneously we got a descending RA (indicating 2,000 feet/min down). I commanded my OE student to immediately disconnected the A/P comply with the RA, which he did. As we were descending per the RA, we visually acquired the aircraft as it pop out of the clouds at about 200 feet above us. It passed off our right side and directly over us. This appeared to be low wing aircraft, single engine type. This aircraft was squawking 1200 and appeared to be VFR. They nor Indy Center were not controlling this aircraft at the time. I did speak with the Indy Center manager afterwards, he was unaware at that point what had transpired.Cause - VFR aircraft not controlled by ATC and flying in the clouds without an IFR clearance.Suggestions - I learned the importance of always complying with TCAS instructions in an expeditious manner. Had we not done this and utilized our training, it may have ended poorly.
1813026: At approximately 130 knots I saw a flock of seagulls coming from my peripheral right side and they started impacting the aircraft with multiple strikes. The Captain was diligent and assertive to abort the aircraft at this time and we came to a complete stop with auto-brakes, spoilers and reversers. I notified the Tower of the abort and requested the AARF and made all the appropriate call outs (spoilers, 80, 60) to back the Captain up on the abort. Once stopped the Captain made the PA 'remain seated x3' and I rolled the flaps to 40 once we verified no doors were open. We held position to run the brake cooling chart and determined we needed one hour. We then had the AARF follow us to the ramp as well to be sure no personnel approached the aircraft. Once parked at the gate, we requested chocks to be inserted on the nose wheel so that we may release the brake pedal pressure as setting the parking brake was not an option. When the AARF confirmed it was safe to have the jet-bridge brought to the aircraft we did so and AARF remained ever ready throughout the entire process. Once the brake cooling was confirmed complete, the Captain, the mechanic and I inspected the tires to find #2 tire flat with fuse plug melted and #3 tire scalloped badly. Both would need replacement. No other damage identified. Too many birds on the airport property that were not easily seen. Adding an air cannon to the airport property to scare off the birds for arriving and departing aircraft.
1813027: During Preflight flow was unable to select terrain display. Contacted Maintenance Control and was instructed to check reset several circut breakers. No success. Wrote up discrepancy in logbook. Local Maintenance was notified and arrived. Was informed by ground crew chief that this had been a recurring problem on other aircraft type Flights. Was informed of note regarding this situation. The NOTAM FAI 04/431 indicated there was problems due to GPS interference testing from 30April 21 to 15May21. It was now [after those dates]. Maintenance was unable to make repairs. Dispatch requested we push off gate with revenue. I declined. Off loaded passengers. Was asked if I was willing to taxi aircraft without passengers to see if problem would clear. I agreed in accordance with FOM. Asked dispatch what flight number would be. He indicated it would be XXXX. We pushed off gate and taxied south and continued northbound on runway. Maintenance was observing operation. We tried many attempts to engage terrain display without success. Parked airplane on hardstand. Secured Airplane. Was not sure if failure of terrain display was system failure or continued interference testing. If testing was indeed taking place after the NOTAM effective dates, they should be updated.
1813032: We were operating our flight ZZZ to ZZZ1. This flight operates at close to if not at its max weight where maximum performance from the aircraft and crew are required due to the short runways. Headwind operations, or more importantly, absence of any tailwinds, should be the main concern of ATC and pilots when utilizing this airport when such performance is required.In the hours prior to this flight ZZZ was running a south operation, departing RWY XX, as one would expect with a reasonable headwind (180/7kts). Approximately 20 minutes before departure, they switched to a north operation, now departing RWY XY. This change seemed illogical as it now was using a runway that had a 7 knot tailwind for takeoff. With this change our flight was unable to depart as we were too heavy due to a tailwind weight penalty of 9,030 lbs from our runway limit.I asked ZZZ Ground/Tower Control why they had changed to a north operation. The answer we received was that arriving aircraft on the XXXXX Visual were encountering a tailwind at altitude and therefore the change. This puzzled me. Is this an official procedure that the FAA ATC has at ZZZ or shouldn't runway selection for takeoff and landing be based on surface winds?We had no choice but to wait for an opening for RWY XX, which caused a significant delay to our companies reliability operation, not to mention putting other aircraft in an awkward position of either compromising safety margins or accepting lengthy delays. Switching runways around based on winds at altitude rather than safety of landing and departing on short runways with tailwinds, puts the pilots in the position as the last line of defense for safety. Just FYI, we also only had one reverser. Although RTO does not include the reversers in its stopping distance calculations, it was still a consideration to us.ATC changing runways from a headwind to a strong tailwind. Putting pilots in a less optimal position to operate their aircraft.The additional work load and max performance requirements when utilizing a short runway with a tailwind should be avoided as much as possible especially at ZZZ. Every foot of runway concrete is paramount to operating safely at this airport. Therefore every knot of tailwind compromises that safety margin.
1813046: We were cleared for the visual approach to [Runway] 28R from the arrival. I set the altitude to 6,000 for the FAF of ZIXIP. My original plan was to fly towards the FAF at 6,000 [feet] then turn base leg then final just inside of it to start my descent after being fully configured. I decided to turn earlier and mistakenly followed what I thought to be my glide slope, therefore, I believed myself to be too high and needing to descend for a stabilized approach. Turning base to final, we got an audible alert of 'obstacle' to which I was searching outside but did not see. Then at the Captain's prompt suggestion I tried to level off but was not aggressive enough. The slow descent resulted in a 'pull up' alert and I was able to maintain altitude but the Captain noted the RA of being around 650 AGL. I was able to continue my turn base to final stabilized and had no other incidents with the event. Lack of situational awareness on my part and last-minute decision to keep a tighter traffic pattern which would require compressed time to configure the aircraft. Mainly, my mistake in believing/following a false glide slope which lead to my confusion. Following the ILS profiles even in VMC conditions for terrain/obstacle clearance. Keeping my situational awareness outside of the cockpit more & remaining vigilant especially in VMC conditions.
1813055: I was Pilot Flying. I triggered a stick shaker/pusher at the Final Approach Fix. I recovered per SOP.[There was] a northbound squall line west of the field. A last minute wind shift caused us to switch runways. Although it was fast, we were able to set up and brief before intercepting course. ATC forgot to turn [us] on the ILS, so we went through the localizer course. This led to reactionary vectors and the aircraft doing S turns until we passed the final approach fix. At this point we were flaps 30 with the power reduced. I called for the go-around, but when I pressed the autopilot disconnect button, I became fixated on the lack of a missed approach course. (I didn't press the TO-GA button.) While troubleshooting, the airspeed continued to decrease leading to a simultaneous stick shaker and pusher. I lowered the nose and recovered per the training, paying special attention to the radar altimeter. I briefly oversped flaps 8 on recovery.Stall recovery training works. I was able to accomplish the recovery quickly without having to think about it. However, it shouldn't have gotten that far. It was my first go-around since OE. I was task saturated and in the moment couldn't remember where the TO-GA button was. We were able to handle weather, ATC error, runway changes and an instrument approach at the same time. However, because our go around was triggered at a relatively untrained aircraft state/position, I missed a critical aspect of the maneuver. I don't believe this is a common problem, but incorporating go-arounds during recurrent in various positions may be beneficial.
1813059: Climbing out at approximately 5000 ft, we received an R 14 DUCT warning message on the EICAS followed by a ANTI ICE DUCT warning. While running the QRH, we received a HI PACK Press caution message. I assume it was a left pack since we had to pull power back on the right engine, but honestly I don't remember which side the pack high pressure was. I knew from a previous 14th DUCT warning message that we could not continue and requested a return to ZZZ. I told the FO (First Officer) that I had the radios and the flight controls and asked him to read the QRH for R 14 DUCT. After we finished the QRH, I requested that the FO talk to the Flight Attendant and tell her that we had to return to ZZZ and that we are not evacuating and that she has 10 minutes. We completed the descent and approach checklist. I completed the flaps 20 landing and let the aircraft come to a stop after max reverse thrust use and only needed braking to the end of the runway to minimize brake temperatures. Left inboard brake temp did reach a white 8 and 6 while the right stayed green at 5. We taxied back to the gate keeping an eye on the brake temperatures. I asked the FO to run the pack high pressure QRH on the ground, the message cleared. Once we made it back to the gate, holding short waiting for the ramp to park us, we received a SMOKE TOILET caution message. I asked the FO to call the FA and ask her to check the lav for smoke. We could hear the smoke detector from the cockpit. The FA reported nothing unusual in the lav. The smoke detector stopped going off. In the meantime, requested the fire department inspect the outside of the aircraft. By the time the fire trucks came we had already hooked up the jet bridge and deplaned. On the initial climbout we received a R 14th DUCT warning message. The Captain directed me to inform ATC we needed to return to ZZZ. Shortly after the first warning message, we received an ANTI ICE DUCT warning message and an R PACK HI PRESS caution message. After we were established on a course back towards ZZZ, the Captain took the radios and called for the R 14th DUCT warning QRH. After completing the first half of the QRH procedure, the warning message persisted so I completed the rest of procedure, preparing for a landing at the nearest suitable airport.Shortly after completion of the full QRH procedure, the R 14th DUCT warning and ANTI ICE DUCT warning messages cleared while we were still in the air. Given the potential severity of a 14th stage bleed air leak, we agreed that an immediate return to ZZZ was warranted and prioritized our remaining tasks with that in mind. I called the flight attendant and informed her that we had a warning message and would be returning to the airport, and we had about 5-7 minutes until landing. She acknowledged and requested I make a PA. I made a brief PA informing the passengers that we had a maintenance issue that required us to return to ZZZ and that we would be landing in about 5 minutes.I resumed responsibility for the radios and proceeded to assist in getting set up for the approach, setting frequencies and getting the appropriate landing data requested. We completed all normal checklists and then had an uneventful approach and landing. After clearing the runway, and having no persisting warning messages, we stated that we did not require any assistance and taxied to the gate. After we were safely on the ground, the Captain asked me to complete the R PACK HI PRESS caution QRH procedure, which cleared the message. We also reviewed the QRH procedure for the ANTI ICE DUCT warning message.While holding short of the gate waiting for a parking crew, with no remaining warning or caution messages, we received a SMOKE TOILET caution message and I could hear the smoke alarm sounding. The Captain called the flight attendant, who went to check the lavatory, and asked me to run the associated QRH procedure. I contacted the Ramp Tower and advised that we were getting a smoke toilet caution indication and requested the fire department. The flight attendant called back and reported there was no smoke in the lavatory. The SMOKE TOILET caution message cleared shortly after this with no further crew action. Passengers deplaned via jet bridge. I sent an ACARS message to Dispatch and Maintenance at the gate advising of the situation. While in the air the Captain had mentioned (and I believe attempted) messaging Dispatch of the return, though given the time critical nature of this [event], this message was not sent until we were on the ground.[The cause was] right 14th stage bleed air leak in flight.
1813060: While taxiing into [spot], it was raining with lowered visibility. The ramp agents were standing in position with the exception of the marshaller. The Safedock system was in operation, and I saw an agent by the controls. I followed the line clearly marked [spot], which was between both wing walkers. Directly in front of this line, which was angled to the left, was the door marked [spot]. I had line of sight to Safedock. As a newer Captain, I did not have any reason to doubt that this was my 'J' line to follow. As I approached and passed the large [spot] painted on the ground, I realized that it was a dashed line, rather than a solid. Just as I noticed this, a marshaller appeared to my left. The marshaller then waved his flags at me and pointed to my left. I then realized that there was another [spot] line, and that I was in the wrong one.The marshaller emphatically waved his batons to my left, and I believed he was directing me left to exit the ramp. I had my FO [First Officer] call Ramp Control and got clearance to turn left and swing back around for the correct 'J' line. I received that approval. I conducted the turn after the marshaller again waved me to the left.I was able to gain clear sight of the vehicles on both sides and noticed no impediment to my progress. I turned around on the taxi lane and entered the straight in 'J' line using Safedock.My FO said that he then saw some markings for the slanted line that indicated it might be for an B737.I was approached by a Ramp Supervisor upon exiting the aircraft. He stated that I had 'jet blasted' his rampers during my exit turn. I explained my perspective, given that I believed I was following the ramper's direction. He told me that 'Next time, call for a tug.' I told him that I understood his concerns, expressly apologized for my confusion during the parking, and that I would heed his advice in the future.[Causes]1) My inexperience as a Captain2) The addition of 'J' lines for B737 aircraft that lined up with safe dock, were labeled exactly the same as the ones for Airline aircraft3) Rain and visibility issues4) Last leg of a day that began [early]5) Confusing and very late directions given by marshaller[Suggestions]1) Use this as a learning tool with respect to ground operations2) Given the human factors present in this event, I believe there needs to be changes to the paint for B737 'J' lines.3) More focus in inclement weather4) Recognize that fatigue can play a role at every stage of a flight, including taxiing to park5) Use my own judgment when given instructions that don't seem to be correct/ safe.
1813077: Once on the ground parked in ZZZ1 both the First Officer and I noticed a powered wheel chair being taken out of the forward cargo bay. We were not informed of this wheel chair and it was also not listed correctly in our cargo load report. There were only bags listed.
1813085: While in cruise at FL400, I noticed cabin altitude display illuminate Amber on upper EICAS showing cabin altitude of 8300 feet and rising at 300-400 ft/min. Aircraft was dispatched with one pack deferred, two operating. I brought up the ECS schematic to verify Packs 2 and 3 were both supplying pressure and in High Flow. They appeared to be operating normally, but I then noticed a Status message with a Pack 2 fault, cabin altitude was already 9,000 ft. and still climbing. At this point I requested a descent from ATC to FL 360. They gave us a vector for descent. A minute later, with Cabin altitude of 9300 ft., I informed ATC we had a pressurization issue and needed to descend. We were given FL390 and then a few minutes later, FL360. Pressurization stabilized at 8,500 ft., but began to climb again at 100-200 ft/min. We requested and were given FL 320. I notified Operations Control via ACARS (SATCOM inop), that we had a Pack 2 issue and that we had descended as cabin altitude had been increasing. They were given our fuel and told I would keep them advised. We were at FL 280, where cabin altitude at stabilized, but showing slight increase. I recommended to divert to ZZZ along our route of flight, but they informed me they wanted the airplane in ZZZ1. I informed ATC that we needed to change our destination for 'maintenance' from ZZZ2 to ZZZ1. We were given proceed direct ZZZ1, about 350 miles away, where we landed uneventfully.Cruise flight when cabin altitude appeared amber on Upper EICAS.Strictly a maintenance issue with the aircraft. We had Pack 1 deferred and any issue with the remaining Packs was going to cause pressurization issues.To assess the situation, attempt to bring pressurization under control, and descend as necessary to reduce cabin altitude. QRH was utilized to validate what pressurization reading we should have at the various altitudes.Aircraft was dispatched to pick up freight in ZZZ2, and then proceed with a Pack deferred. Pushback, taxi, takeoff and climb were completely normal. Weather on departure were calm winds and decent VFR in the terminal area. The weather became more marginal upon leveling at cruise. On this leg I myself was the First Officer and Flying Pilot. The Captain was the Pilot Not flying. We also had a Relief Pilot on board and loadmaster. The event began somewhat early in cruise at FL400 when the Captain noticed a cabin altitude display Amber on the Upper EICAS display. He then immediately selected the ECS page and we both were made aware of a 8,300 foot cabin and rising at 300-400 fpm. The aircraft was dispatched with Pack #1 deferred, therefore packs 2 and 3 operating normally. After diagnosing the situation via the ECS page, both packs 2 and 3 appeared to be supplying pressure and in High Flow as designed when one pack is selected off. However on the Lower EICAS we both noticed a Status message with a Pack 2 fault. Cabin altitude was still climbing and at this point showing 9,000 feet and still climbing. At this point we agreed to suggest a decent to FL360 and were given a vector for decent. About a minute later with Cabin Altitude of 9,300 feet the Captain informed ATC that we had a pressurization issue and needed to descend now, we first were given a decent to FL390 and shortly after to FL360. At FL360 we observed the cabin initially stabilizing at 8,500 feet, but shortly afterwards began again climbing at a lower rate than previously of 100-200 FPM. We again agreed to request a lower altitude of FL320 and ATC cleared us to FL320. The Captain then notified Operations Control of the situation via ACARS (SATCOM Inop) that we had a PACK 2 issue and we were descending with a cabin altitude still slowly increasing. The Captain requested further decent to FL280 and ATC complied. At FL280 we experienced a cabin altitude almost stable at around 8,000 feet but still trying to climb at a slow interment 100 FPM. The Captain notified the rest of the crew including the Relief Pilot and load master. The Relief Pilot was taking his rest but immediately returned to the cockpit to help in CRM and dealing with the situation. I suggested the Relief Pilot pull up the cabin altitude chart showing what the cabin altitude should be for our current altitude so we would know how far off from normal we were. All 3 crew members talked about possible diversion airports and relayed our ideas to Operations Control. After communication between Operations Control and us it was decided by Operations Control to divert to ZZZ2 to address and fix the situation. The Captain immediately requested to divert to ZZZ2 and informed ATC as to why, and I put us on a course to ZZZ2 via ATC instructions. At this point we were about 350 miles north of ZZZ2 with plenty of fuel and sufficient weather for landing. We landed at ZZZ2 uneventfully and maintenance was made aware of the present maintenance issues.While in cruise flight the cabin altitude appeared amber on the Upper EICAS.Pack 2 was failing for unknown reasons. Pack 1 was already deferred on departure so any remaining pack issues was going to cause a pressurization issue.Crew did their job in noticing the system fault and working the problem. We were dispatched with Pack 1 deferred so any further pack or pressurization faults would cause a pressurization issue.Dispatching an aircraft with a pack deferred which would and did cause a pressurization issue when any further pressurization problems would happen. In this case pack 2 also failing to perform up to specification, therefore, causing an increasing cabin altitude at a higher level cruising altitude.
1813139: I am reporting an unsafe situation we as an aircrew encountered on the flight back from ZZZ to ZZZ1.We had an APU failure and lost at least one of our packs, so we had no air conditioning inflight and the temps in the cabin became dangerously high, I knew once we got off the ground and we were climbing out that the situation was going sideways, so I formulated a game plan and as soon as we reached altitude instead of using the cart I just pulled every tray of water I had on the plane, it was at that point Flight Attendant who was deadheading on the flight immediately came to the galley and introduced herself and asked what she could do to assist me and I just told her jump in and start handing out water and asked her to make ice packs for 2 moms that were on board.One was an expecting mom around and her husband were seated in X12 and an infant and mom in Y3 the expecting mom became pale and very hot and I was really concerned for her and her unborn child's safety and the infant and mom in 6 were red and very warm.What little bit of ice we had that hadn't melted we fashioned ice packs after emptying the Purell packets out of the zip lock bags they were in for both moms and we together pulled every bottle of water we had on board passed them throughout the cabin until we ran out, our flight crew were miserable as well as the flight became very unbearable.At one point I became so dehydrated NAME sat me in my jump seat and handed me one of the large bottles of water we had left onboard and made sure I was hydrated while she attended to pax needs and then I swapped out with her so she could hydrate as well. The teamwork was amazing and I am so grateful to have had her assistance.We kept everyone calm and hydrated as best we could until we got on the ground in ZZZ1, while I was tending to landing prep Flight Attendant deadheading went ahead and filed her report inflight for me so I could tend to the pax.Together we were able to keep both moms and their babies born and unborn safe the flight deck was very concerned and called me to ask if we needed medical personnel to meet us at the gate but I told them no that everything fine but if the situation changed I would advise as soon as possible.In closing the conditions onboard when we lost the pack was dangerously hot and it was definitely a test of my training but like I said as soon as so realized we had a problem I already had a plan in place to deal with it.
1813181: On final approach to Runway 13 into MDT, we were cleared to intercept the visual final approach course. Due to the haze and unfamiliarity on the airports on separate sides of the river, we mistook CXY Runway 12 for MDT Runway 13. We had the GPS 13 approach loaded for reference due to the ILS 13 being out, but prior to turning inbound on the final we were given a vector for the intercept final approach course. I mistook the Capital City airport (CXY) Runway 12 for MDTs Runway 13. We were asked if we had MDT in sight, thinking we did, and cleared for a visual approach, I made a descent for CXY Runway 12, still not realizing it was not MDT Runway 13. MDT Tower asked then told us we were aligned with CXY and gave a low altitude warning. I immediately added power and climbed. I then aligned with Runway 13 at MDT and landed. We were approaching Harrisburg Int'l from the west when we were instructed to intercept the final course for a visual approach to RWY 13. It was hazy with visibility low enough that the only airport in sight was Capital City (CXY). Its RWY 12 is oriented similarly to RW 13 at MDT, so when we were asked if we had the airport in sight, we said we did. The airport was closer by a few miles than our FMS was indicating so we configured for landing and steepened the approach. MDT Tower then asked if we could be approaching Capital City as we were lower than we should've been. At that point, MDT was also visible. The pilot flying applied power and climbed enough to conduct a normal approach to RWY 13.The haze contributed, as did the vector for a visual. Interestingly, the proximity of these two airports is compounded by the fact that the airport on the south side of the river (CXY) is actually north of MDT, which is on the north side of the river due to bends in the river.We could've avoided the error if we'd been more familiar with the area and/or declined the visual approach.
1813182: I began instructing a student pilot for their private pilot certificate under Part 61. This student had been with 2 other instructors before coming to me. The first instructor he was with was from April to December 20XX and had flown 24 hours dual. The second instructor was from February 20XX to November 20XX and had dual of 50 hours and 3 solo flights, one in June, July and November of 20XX. As I began instructing this student, he had 74 hours total time and had soloed. I asked him if he had his student pilot certificate and medical, and his answer was yes. I did not do my due diligence and physically look at those 2 documents because I assumed with 2 previous instructors, 74 hours and solo flights, he had them. That was 100% my error. I paid more attention to verifying he was a US citizen and getting that endorsement in both our logbooks, then giving the proper consideration to the other documents. I realized this on May XX, 2021 as I was thinking it is time to start prepping for a potential check ride in the next couple months. I asked him to provide a copy of those documents to me, and that is when I realized he did not have the appropriate FAA issued student pilot certificate. He had his medical and he had another form, FAA Form 8500-8, Medical Certificate Third Class And Student Pilot Certificate. His medical examiner told him that Form 8500-8 was his student pilot certificate. Therefore, my student believed he had the proper student certificate, and that is why he told me he had both documents. As soon as I realized that this was not correct, I immediately called him to confirm it and advised him as to what must be done to get the correct FAA student pilot certificate. We met the next evening, June XX, 2021 and completed the application. I told him he could not solo until he received his temporary certificate. His temporary was issued on June XY, 2021. This student had 15.7 hours of solo time up to this point, which will not be counted as his solo requirements. He will complete all the solo time requirements after the issue date of June XY, 2021. As for myself, I learned a valuable lesson, never assume a student has the proper paperwork, regardless of the number of instructors or previous flight hours. I will always do my due diligence, and never assume anything moving forward. Moreover, I feel ashamed and embarrassed that as a professional CFI, this situation occurred.
1813185: I have departed ZZZ airport to the south to practice landings in ZZZ1. On the way back to ZZZ I have contacted ZZZ Tower around 7NM to 8 NM south of the field, the Tower has replied standby so I have tuned to easterly heading so I will not enter the airspace, a few minutes after that the Tower has instructed me to join mid left downwind for Runway XX and to report when established on the downwind, after I have established on the downwind I have notified the Tower. To the best of my knowledge and memory the Tower has replied the following instruction: 'you are number 3 for Runway XX continue', I have given the Tower read back and then I looked forward to visually scan for the traffic in front of me, I remember clearly that I saw 2 aircraft in the final for Runway XX, the first one was an airplane in the short final and the second one was a helicopter that was also in the final behind him. I remember that I have pointed the 2 aircraft to my students and explained to them that these are the aircraft that are in front of us and we will follow them as we are number 3 in the sequence. After the helicopter was abeam to my position, I continued to fly on the downwind for an extra 30 seconds to 1 minute so I will allow some extra spacing between myself and the helicopter as I'm flying with students on their first ever fly day. As I was told I'm number 3 in sequence and I visually saw the 2 aircraft that are in front of me I have continued the traffic pattern and turn left to the base leg, and then when I was in the appropriate position I have turned final. Between 30 seconds to 1 minute after I was established on the final for XX the Tower has instructed me to 'immediately turn heading 090 and break the approach', I have immediately took controls from my student and turned to the heading 090 while giving a read back to the Tower. As I have established on the heading 090 I saw that there was a jet aircraft on the final approach behind me, approximately 1,200 feet horizontally and 300 feet vertically in my evaluation. after that I have continued to comply with the Tower instructions and followed a different traffic that was on the downwind to join the final for Runway XX again for a full stop. Before landing when I was on short final I have verified with the Tower that I had clearance to land.I have strong belief in self critic and self evaluation and after this event has occurred I have come up with the following safety measures that can help prevent this situation from reoccurring:1. When you have been instructed to follow traffic while on the downwind, you should always verify with Tower that you can start your turn towards the base leg.2. When you are told that you are number 3 in sequence and you see the 2 aircraft in front of you, that absolutely does not mean that you should stop looking for other traffic in the area, you still need scan for traffic very frequently.3. When flying on the base leg, even in a controlled airport, you should always try to look for more traffic coming on the final, both behind you and in front of you, and make sure that there is no traffic that can jeopardize the approach before actually making the turn to final.4. Do not think that just because you are flying in a controlled airspace under ATC supervision, you are protected. Always actively scan for traffic and verify ATC instructions.I believe that if I had used these safety measures that I have mentioned above this event could have been prevented. I am glad no damage has been done in this event, and I'm committed to learn from this experience and actively seek to improve myself as a pilot and as flight instructor.
